items.title: How to Solve the Mystery of AI Defense in Depth?
items.summary: Back in 2023, I wrote “How to Solve the Mystery of Cloud Defense in Depth?” and ended it with “Where to next?” Well, “next” turned out to be AI. In 3 years. So this post is a belated sequel, of sorts. Steampunk FTW! So, before reading further, ask yourself the same two questions, with one word changed: Do you understand the concept of “defense in depth” (DiD) in security ? Do you understand how DiD applies when AI is (a) the thing you defend, (b) the thing attacking you, and © the thing you defend with? BTW, my own answers would have been “Yes!” and “Uhm… for (a) mostly, yes, for (b) I thought I did, but now I am very nervous, and for © ‘it depends’.” After the October we just had, I suspect I am not alone. If your answer to question #1 is anything but a yes, please (re-)read “Defense in Depth” by Phil Venables . I quoted it in the cloud post, and it turns out to be even more useful for AI. Phil’s bottom line is that DiD is “about the linkage and collected effect of controls,” not arbitrary stacking. He also offers principles for placing controls, and three of them become critical with AI: Positive duplication. Duplicate controls should not share one common cause of failure, so use different teams, vendors, or designs on a critical path. Full complementarity. Every preventive control should have a detective control that checks the prevention actually worked. Control pressure. Watch at which layer attacks are actually stopped; rising pressure deeper in the stack means it is time for redesign. (and, again, no, defense in depth does not mean “just use more than one security control” … or, in 2026, “just use more than one LLM”) Three schools of thought (again) With cloud, I found three schools of thought. With AI, I found … three schools of thought. Some patterns are fractal, just like Phil says DiD should be ( “Defense in depth should also be fractal” )… “Bolt-on DiD” : AI DiD is classic DiD plus one new AI layer, firewall sandwich with AI mayo, basically (or: “AI-oli sauce” as somebody wisely quipped) “DiD is dead” : AI DiD does not exist and does not matter. AI means “everything changes.” “AI can hack everything” camp lives here. “AI-native DiD” : it exists for sure, you just need to discover it for yourself … The first view is basically “lift and shift DiD,” AI edition. Take your network, host, app, data, and D&R layers, then add “a prompt firewall” in front of the model. Bam! The layer “M” is handled too. Uhu, yeah, right … This may be “correct” if your AI use is a chatbot answering FAQ questions with no data access and no tools (hi 2022 … bye 2023). It is almost certainly wrong the moment an agent can read your mail, call an API, and push code. The new layer was bolted on, but the old layers were never told that a new kind of principal now walks among them. The second view comes in two flavors. The defender-pessimist flavor says prompt injection is unsolvable , so securing agents is futile. The attacker-pessimist flavor says AI attackers find and exploit bugs faster than we patch, so layers no longer matter at all (I particularly disdain these ones, if you care to hear it). A vendor-flavored variant says “only AI can fight AI,” so just buy the AI and stop thinking about layers. Intuitively, but also rationally, I know this camp is wrong. “This layer is imperfect” has been true of every layer since the first firewall. Imperfect layers are the entire reason for DiD, not an argument against it! Finally, the third view is … well, still a bit of a mystery. Let’s try to discover it together, again! What do we know for sure? Now for the fun part! Let’s check what we know for sure so far. Two general points first: DiD almost certainly matters more with AI , not less. More autonomy, more speed, and more probabilistic components all mean more chances for any single layer to fail. DiD is still about layers of controls and interlocking controls within each layer , both technical and procedural. Nothing about AI repeals this; it just stress-tests it really well. At this stage, I hope nobody is throwing a chair at the monitor in frustration. We are good so far, right? When AI is the thing you defend First, AI DiD gets married to a new shared responsibility model . In cloud, the provider owned some layers. With AI, the model provider owns some layers too (safety training, abuse monitoring), while you own the context, the tools, the data, and the agent’s permissions. Know where the line is, since that line is where layers silently go missing. Many of the cloud truths and frustrations apply here. Mostly frustrations, natch. Stacked similar models are less depth than you think. A guard LLM watching your main LLM sounds like two layers. But researchers have argued that guard models often share the same statistical failure modes as the agents they monitor. Yes, “diversity of defense” is an ancient idea — some of us are old enough to remember arguing about dual-vendor AV stacks! What’s new here is why AI layers correlate. The nastiest attacks (clever role-play, indirect prompt injection buried in a Jira ticket) don’t exploit a coding bug; they exploit the exact thing every LLM is trained to do: follow plausible instructions. Swapping Model Vendor A for Model Vendor B doesn’t fix a shared objective. The math is simple: two layers that each stop 95% of attacks give you 99.75% only if they fail independently . So count correlated LLM layers as partial layers at best. And here is the practical twist: diversity of the question matters more than diversity of the model. A narrow check asking “is this tool call within policy?” is a genuinely different layer from a general model asking “is this prompt malicious?” So, don’t laugh at “guardian LLM”, but also don’t assume that “guardian LLM” is a wall, more of an attack poodle… The model is probabilistic, so the agent harness must be deterministic — split across time. In the cloud post, I said IAM plays an oversized role, so you need IAM-independent controls. With AI, the context window plays the oversized role, because everything in it can be attacker-influenced (a web page, an email, a doc, a tool result). So you need security invariants outside the model’s context window that hold even when the LLM is 100% socially engineered: scoped credentials, tool allowlists, egress restrictions, sandboxes (as a layer, not as THE solution!), transaction limits, etc. My favorite idea here: frame modern AI DiD across time: put synchronous, zero-latency deterministic gates strictly under irreversible actions (moving money, dropping tables, sending data externally, changing IAM permissions), and use asynchronous, out-of-band AI supervision for everything else — watching telemetry in parallel and ready to trip a circuit breaker if a session goes off the rails. Put synchronous friction everywhere, and the business will happily route around you with shadow agents … leaving you with exactly zero layers. Defend the verbs, not the words. The set of possible malicious inputs is effectively infinite; the set of actions an agent can take is not (it can get large for “fat” agents ). So depth shifts from filtering prompts to governing actions: what this agent may call, with what identity, on what data, and how reversibly. Phil recently called this going from “shift left” to “shift down” , pushing controls into the platform so agents inherit them. Is “agent identity” a new layer or a sublayer within IAM? Is the tool/MCP layer a new layer? I genuinely don’t know yet, just as I didn’t know whether the cloud org boundary was one. Every guardrail needs a detective twin, and mistakes count too. Phil’s full complementarity says each preventive control needs a detective control checking that it actually works. For agents: log every tool call and alert on actions that should never happen if the guardrail held. And remember my cloud post’s ending, that DiD must cover configuration mistakes, not just threats. An agent that “helpfully” deletes a production table is a configuration mistake at machine speed. If one confused agent causes a breach, DiD was absolutely missing. Finally, a human approval is only a layer if the approver isn’t clicking “yes” 300 times a day. Fewer, better gates beat many gates. When AI is attacking you After unprompted II conference, I can say that things are really fun here in this section. The time layers buy at the edge is collapsing. This is NOT “DiD is dead”, but this is where it takes a good, heavy slap, yet still survives. Classic DiD quietly assumes that each layer delays the attacker long enough for you to notice and respond. For example, “just patch it” is still a layer, but it’s getting dangerously thin (unless you VulnOps , I guess). Here is the catch, though: AI massively accelerated recon, bug hunting, and exploit weaponization at the edge , more than it accelerates post-compromise lateral movement — as of today! Once inside your environment, an AI attacker still needs credentials, still trips identity detections, and still touches systems that emit logs. Probabilistic layers get brute-forced. An AI-armed attacker can try a thousand variants cheaply. Any layer that “usually catches it” will eventually be bypassed by someone who can afford to retry. In Phil’s terms, expect control pressure to shift deeper into your stack. The design implication is clear: harden the edge as much as you can, and invest in containment behind it: blast radius, segmentation, fast+good (sorry, do need both) detection, and fast recovery. Some “boring” layers are back in fashion. If prevention at the edge gets thinner, the layers that limit what happens after compromise matter more: egress control, internal segmentation (I like to call it “mini-segmentation”, not as small as micro, but pretty granular anyway), immutable infrastructure, etc. (Yes, I now work at Cisco, so feel free to discount this point by 20%. But I believed it before I joined!) When AI is defending you Your defensive AI is a new layer and a new single point of failure. If the same model (or vendor) sits in your detection, triage, and response layers, every alert passes through one model’s judgment, which is a hidden common cause across all three. Positive duplication applies here too! The fix is not necessarily two vendors; remember “diversity of the question.” This is not “replace Firewall Vendor A + Firewall Vendor B” with “LLM Vendor A + LLM Vendor B”! For example, let one model triage, and let a different, narrow detector sample-audit what it closed. Also, a SOC agent with response permissions is a privileged identity, and its inputs are logs and alerts … some of which the attacker writes. Defensive agents need DiD as much as any other agent! Over-reliance is a thing. AI moves the cost of depth from tuning to validation. Historically, every new layer cost precious SOC analyst blood and sweat to tune, triage, and maintain — which is why so many enterprises only had “DiD on paper.” AI in your SOC can genuinely cut that tuning toil. Free lunch? Of course not! The cost doesn’t vanish; it migrates. Instead of babysitting brittle detection rules, you now spend cycles auditing the AI’s reasoning , testing its prompts, and catching the moment an autonomous tier-1 agent confidently auto-closes a real breach. Validation never goes to zero for a probabilistic layer, so your SOC’s AI needs its own detective control (full complementarity again). So, where are we, so far In one table DiD skimmable So, where to next? So, is “AI-native DiD” still a mystery? Less of one, I think. If I had to compress it into one line: AI makes your layers more correlated and your edge slower than the attacker, so design for correlated failure and for speed. In practice, that means synchronous deterministic gates in the agent harness for irreversible actions, asynchronous out-of-band AI supervision for everything else , diversity of the question rather than just of the model, and more value placed on containment and recovery. Philosophizing about layers is fun, but what do you actually do on Monday morning? If you want to move from “Bolt-on DiD” to “AI-native DiD,” start with these: Correlated layers & the agent harness : inventory which of your agents’ actions are irreversible (money, deletion, external sends, permission changes), put a synchronous deterministic gate on each, and move heavy AI supervision out-of-band. Time at the edge: measure how long it takes you to patch or shield your internet-facing stack after a critical disclosure. Compare that with how fast exploitation started during, ahem, recent weeks. If the gap scares you , fund containment behind the edge. Ah, and please don’t confuse “deterministic” with, well, non-deterministic controls :-) Is model alignment a layer too? I don’t know, probably “weak yes” from me here. Phil ended his post by saying it was meant to stimulate others to do more work on DiD. Three years after my cloud post, I am still taking him up on it. This time, though, I suspect the answer will come from practitioners who are already running agents in production, not from people like me thinking out loud on a blog… Got any thoughts? Reactions? Back in 2023, I wrote “How to Solve the Mystery of Cloud Defense in Depth?” and ended it with “Where to next?” Well, “next” turned out to be AI. In 3 years. So this post is a belated sequel, of sorts.

Steampunk FTW!

So, before reading further, ask yourself the same two questions, with one word changed:

  1. Do you understand the concept of “defense in depth” (DiD) in security?
  2. Do you understand how DiD applies when AI is (a) the thing you defend, (b) the thing attacking you, and © the thing you defend with?

BTW, my own answers would have been “Yes!” and “Uhm… for (a) mostly, yes, for (b) I thought I did, but now I am very nervous, and for © ‘it depends’.” After the October we just had, I suspect I am not alone.

If your answer to question #1 is anything but a yes, please (re-)read “Defense in Depth” by Phil Venables. I quoted it in the cloud post, and it turns out to be even more useful for AI. Phil’s bottom line is that DiD is “about the linkage and collected effect of controls,” not arbitrary stacking. He also offers principles for placing controls, and three of them become critical with AI:

  • Positive duplication. Duplicate controls should not share one common cause of failure, so use different teams, vendors, or designs on a critical path.
  • Full complementarity. Every preventive control should have a detective control that checks the prevention actually worked.
  • Control pressure. Watch at which layer attacks are actually stopped; rising pressure deeper in the stack means it is time for redesign.

(and, again, no, defense in depth does not mean “just use more than one security control” … or, in 2026, “just use more than one LLM”)

Three schools of thought (again)

With cloud, I found three schools of thought. With AI, I found … three schools of thought. Some patterns are fractal, just like Phil says DiD should be (“Defense in depth should also be fractal”)…

  1. “Bolt-on DiD”: AI DiD is classic DiD plus one new AI layer, firewall sandwich with AI mayo, basically (or: “AI-oli sauce” as somebody wisely quipped)
  2. “DiD is dead”: AI DiD does not exist and does not matter. AI means “everything changes.” “AI can hack everything” camp lives here.
  3. “AI-native DiD”: it exists for sure, you just need to discover it for yourself …

The first view is basically “lift and shift DiD,” AI edition. Take your network, host, app, data, and D&R layers, then add “a prompt firewall” in front of the model. Bam! The layer “M” is handled too. Uhu, yeah, right … This may be “correct” if your AI use is a chatbot answering FAQ questions with no data access and no tools (hi 2022 … bye 2023). It is almost certainly wrong the moment an agent can read your mail, call an API, and push code. The new layer was bolted on, but the old layers were never told that a new kind of principal now walks among them.

The second view comes in two flavors. The defender-pessimist flavor says prompt injection is unsolvable, so securing agents is futile. The attacker-pessimist flavor says AI attackers find and exploit bugs faster than we patch, so layers no longer matter at all (I particularly disdain these ones, if you care to hear it). A vendor-flavored variant says “only AI can fight AI,” so just buy the AI and stop thinking about layers. Intuitively, but also rationally, I know this camp is wrong. “This layer is imperfect” has been true of every layer since the first firewall. Imperfect layers are the entire reason for DiD, not an argument against it!

Finally, the third view is … well, still a bit of a mystery. Let’s try to discover it together, again!

What do we know for sure?

Now for the fun part! Let’s check what we know for sure so far. Two general points first:

  • DiD almost certainly matters more with AI, not less. More autonomy, more speed, and more probabilistic components all mean more chances for any single layer to fail.
  • DiD is still about layers of controls and interlocking controls within each layer, both technical and procedural. Nothing about AI repeals this; it just stress-tests it really well.

At this stage, I hope nobody is throwing a chair at the monitor in frustration. We are good so far, right?

When AI is the thing you defend

First, AI DiD gets married to a new shared responsibility model. In cloud, the provider owned some layers. With AI, the model provider owns some layers too (safety training, abuse monitoring), while you own the context, the tools, the data, and the agent’s permissions. Know where the line is, since that line is where layers silently go missing. Many of the cloud truths and frustrations apply here. Mostly frustrations, natch.

Stacked similar models are less depth than you think. A guard LLM watching your main LLM sounds like two layers. But researchers have argued that guard models often share the same statistical failure modes as the agents they monitor. Yes, “diversity of defense” is an ancient idea — some of us are old enough to remember arguing about dual-vendor AV stacks! What’s new here is why AI layers correlate. The nastiest attacks (clever role-play, indirect prompt injection buried in a Jira ticket) don’t exploit a coding bug; they exploit the exact thing every LLM is trained to do: follow plausible instructions. Swapping Model Vendor A for Model Vendor B doesn’t fix a shared objective. The math is simple: two layers that each stop 95% of attacks give you 99.75% only if they fail independently.

So count correlated LLM layers as partial layers at best. And here is the practical twist: diversity of the question matters more than diversity of the model. A narrow check asking “is this tool call within policy?” is a genuinely different layer from a general model asking “is this prompt malicious?” So, don’t laugh at “guardian LLM”, but also don’t assume that “guardian LLM” is a wall, more of an attack poodle…

The model is probabilistic, so the agent harness must be deterministic — split across time. In the cloud post, I said IAM plays an oversized role, so you need IAM-independent controls. With AI, the context window plays the oversized role, because everything in it can be attacker-influenced (a web page, an email, a doc, a tool result). So you need security invariants outside the model’s context window that hold even when the LLM is 100% socially engineered: scoped credentials, tool allowlists, egress restrictions, sandboxes (as a layer, not as THE solution!), transaction limits, etc.

My favorite idea here: frame modern AI DiD across time: put synchronous, zero-latency deterministic gates strictly under irreversible actions (moving money, dropping tables, sending data externally, changing IAM permissions), and use asynchronous, out-of-band AI supervision for everything else — watching telemetry in parallel and ready to trip a circuit breaker if a session goes off the rails. Put synchronous friction everywhere, and the business will happily route around you with shadow agents … leaving you with exactly zero layers.

Defend the verbs, not the words. The set of possible malicious inputs is effectively infinite; the set of actions an agent can take is not (it can get large for “fat” agents). So depth shifts from filtering prompts to governing actions: what this agent may call, with what identity, on what data, and how reversibly. Phil recently called this going from “shift left” to “shift down”, pushing controls into the platform so agents inherit them. Is “agent identity” a new layer or a sublayer within IAM? Is the tool/MCP layer a new layer? I genuinely don’t know yet, just as I didn’t know whether the cloud org boundary was one.

Every guardrail needs a detective twin, and mistakes count too. Phil’s full complementarity says each preventive control needs a detective control checking that it actually works. For agents: log every tool call and alert on actions that should never happen if the guardrail held. And remember my cloud post’s ending, that DiD must cover configuration mistakes, not just threats. An agent that “helpfully” deletes a production table is a configuration mistake at machine speed. If one confused agent causes a breach, DiD was absolutely missing. Finally, a human approval is only a layer if the approver isn’t clicking “yes” 300 times a day. Fewer, better gates beat many gates.

When AI is attacking you

After unprompted II conference, I can say that things are really fun here in this section.

The time layers buy at the edge is collapsing. This is NOT “DiD is dead”, but this is where it takes a good, heavy slap, yet still survives. Classic DiD quietly assumes that each layer delays the attacker long enough for you to notice and respond. For example, “just patch it” is still a layer, but it’s getting dangerously thin (unless you VulnOps, I guess). Here is the catch, though: AI massively accelerated recon, bug hunting, and exploit weaponization at the edge, more than it accelerates post-compromise lateral movement — as of today! Once inside your environment, an AI attacker still needs credentials, still trips identity detections, and still touches systems that emit logs.

Probabilistic layers get brute-forced. An AI-armed attacker can try a thousand variants cheaply. Any layer that “usually catches it” will eventually be bypassed by someone who can afford to retry. In Phil’s terms, expect control pressure to shift deeper into your stack. The design implication is clear: harden the edge as much as you can, and invest in containment behind it: blast radius, segmentation, fast+good (sorry, do need both) detection, and fast recovery.

Some “boring” layers are back in fashion. If prevention at the edge gets thinner, the layers that limit what happens after compromise matter more: egress control, internal segmentation (I like to call it “mini-segmentation”, not as small as micro, but pretty granular anyway), immutable infrastructure, etc. (Yes, I now work at Cisco, so feel free to discount this point by 20%. But I believed it before I joined!)

When AI is defending you

Your defensive AI is a new layer and a new single point of failure. If the same model (or vendor) sits in your detection, triage, and response layers, every alert passes through one model’s judgment, which is a hidden common cause across all three. Positive duplication applies here too! The fix is not necessarily two vendors; remember “diversity of the question.” This is not “replace Firewall Vendor A + Firewall Vendor B” with “LLM Vendor A + LLM Vendor B”! For example, let one model triage, and let a different, narrow detector sample-audit what it closed. Also, a SOC agent with response permissions is a privileged identity, and its inputs are logs and alerts … some of which the attacker writes. Defensive agents need DiD as much as any other agent! Over-reliance is a thing.

AI moves the cost of depth from tuning to validation. Historically, every new layer cost precious SOC analyst blood and sweat to tune, triage, and maintain — which is why so many enterprises only had “DiD on paper.” AI in your SOC can genuinely cut that tuning toil. Free lunch? Of course not! The cost doesn’t vanish; it migrates. Instead of babysitting brittle detection rules, you now spend cycles auditing the AI’s reasoning, testing its prompts, and catching the moment an autonomous tier-1 agent confidently auto-closes a real breach. Validation never goes to zero for a probabilistic layer, so your SOC’s AI needs its own detective control (full complementarity again).

So, where are we, so far

In one tableDiD skimmableSo, where to next?

So, is “AI-native DiD” still a mystery? Less of one, I think. If I had to compress it into one line: AI makes your layers more correlated and your edge slower than the attacker, so design for correlated failure and for speed. In practice, that means synchronous deterministic gates in the agent harness for irreversible actions, asynchronous out-of-band AI supervision for everything else, diversity of the question rather than just of the model, and more value placed on containment and recovery.

Philosophizing about layers is fun, but what do you actually do on Monday morning? If you want to move from “Bolt-on DiD” to “AI-native DiD,” start with these:

  1. Correlated layers & the agent harness: inventory which of your agents’ actions are irreversible (money, deletion, external sends, permission changes), put a synchronous deterministic gate on each, and move heavy AI supervision out-of-band.
  2. Time at the edge: measure how long it takes you to patch or shield your internet-facing stack after a critical disclosure. Compare that with how fast exploitation started during, ahem, recent weeks. If the gap scares you, fund containment behind the edge.
  3. Ah, and please don’t confuse “deterministic” with, well, non-deterministic controls :-) Is model alignment a layer too? I don’t know, probably “weak yes” from me here.

Phil ended his post by saying it was meant to stimulate others to do more work on DiD. Three years after my cloud post, I am still taking him up on it. This time, though, I suspect the answer will come from practitioners who are already running agents in production, not from people like me thinking out loud on a blog…

Got any thoughts? Reactions?

items.title: Warning: Romance Scammers Are Targeting US Citizens For Money Laundering
items.summary: Threat actors are using romance scams to trick U.S. citizens into acting as money mules, the Wall Street Journal reports. The Journal cites the example of Garrick Stafford, a 50-year-old Texas man who lost $65,000 and unwittingly laundered $50,000 for an international crime ring after falling for an online scammer posing as an attractive woman. Notably, Stafford was texting with the scammer all summer before the individual first asked for money, claiming that she needed $150 to pay her cellphone bill. Stafford immediately recognized this as a red flag and blocked the individual. Months later, however, he unblocked her, and they began texting again.

items.title: How to investigate business email compromise (BEC): from fraudulent email to full scope
items.summary: How digital forensics helps preserve evidence, reconstruct account activity, scope impact, and guide remediation By Jeff Rutherford Key takeaways Business email compromise (BEC) often runs on legitimate credentials and ordinary-looking email, so the fraudulent message is often only the visible end of a longer campaign. A key question in an investigation is whether the sender was spoofed or a real account was taken over. That answer shapes what evidence matters and how far remediation needs to go. Containment and preservation should happen together. Capture mailbox rules, audit logs, and sign-in records before resetting accounts whenever timing allows. How much you can reconstruct later depends on logging, retention, and collection workflows set up before the incident. A password reset won’t remove forwarding rules, delegates, or active tokens on its own, so recovery should follow the access path the investigation uncovers. In a business email compromise (BEC), the fraudulent message is often only the visible end of a longer campaign. Investigators must determine whether the attacker spoofed a trusted sender or controlled a legitimate account, how access was obtained, what was changed, what information was exposed, and whether financial or other unauthorized actions followed. An effective response requires a fact-based investigation that preserves critical evidence, reconstructs account activity, determines the full scope of impact, and uses those findings to guide containment and remediation. This post walks through a five-phase forensic workflow for a BEC investigation, from evidence-guided containment to post-incident reporting, and the evidence that matters at each step. Core principle of a BEC investigation: Contain account misuse without losing evidence Every response action changes the environment investigators are trying to reconstruct. Disabling a compromised mailbox, resetting credentials, revoking tokens, or removing forwarding rules may stop immediate misuse, but those same actions can also alter the account state that helps show what the attacker did. The goal is to contain with purpose: stop active harm; preserve critical mailbox, audit, authentication, and endpoint evidence when feasible; and retain enough forensic visibility to determine how the account was compromised, what the attacker accessed or changed, how long unauthorized activity persisted, and what must be remediated before normal operations resume. Why business email compromise is different BEC often relies on legitimate credentials, trusted business relationships, and ordinary-looking email activity. Unlike incidents that announce themselves with malware or encryption, a compromised mailbox can blend into normal operations. The visible event may be a fraudulent invoice, an executive impersonation request, payroll diversion, or the unexpected disclosure of sensitive information, while the underlying account compromise began earlier and left only subtle traces. Ultimately, the BEC investigation needs to answer these questions: Was the sender impersonated through spoofing, or did the attacker control a legitimate account? How did the attacker gain access, and were phishing, credential reuse, malicious links or attachments, or another method involved? Which user accounts, mailboxes, endpoints, or cloud resources were affected? Were forwarding rules, mailbox delegates, account settings, or other access mechanisms created or changed? What messages, attachments, or other data were accessed, sent, deleted, or redirected? Were credentials, authentication tokens, or sessions compromised? When did unauthorized activity begin, and how long did it continue? Were fraudulent financial transactions initiated, or was sensitive information disclosed? What must be reset, revoked, removed, or strengthened before the account can be trusted again? A five-phase BEC investigation workflow A BEC response is most effective when digital forensics is integrated throughout the incident response lifecycle . Two priorities run in parallel from start to finish: Stop active misuse and limit additional financial loss, unauthorized access, or disclosure. Preserve and analyze the evidence needed to distinguish impersonation from account takeover and determine broader impact. The workflow below uses five practical phases that connect rapid containment with deeper mailbox, identity, cloud, and endpoint analysis. How digital forensics helps preserve evidence, reconstruct account activity, scope impact, and guide remediation

By Jeff Rutherford

Key takeaways
  • Business email compromise (BEC) often runs on legitimate credentials and ordinary-looking email, so the fraudulent message is often only the visible end of a longer campaign.
  • A key question in an investigation is whether the sender was spoofed or a real account was taken over. That answer shapes what evidence matters and how far remediation needs to go.
  • Containment and preservation should happen together. Capture mailbox rules, audit logs, and sign-in records before resetting accounts whenever timing allows.
  • How much you can reconstruct later depends on logging, retention, and collection workflows set up before the incident.
  • A password reset won’t remove forwarding rules, delegates, or active tokens on its own, so recovery should follow the access path the investigation uncovers.

In a business email compromise (BEC), the fraudulent message is often only the visible end of a longer campaign. Investigators must determine whether the attacker spoofed a trusted sender or controlled a legitimate account, how access was obtained, what was changed, what information was exposed, and whether financial or other unauthorized actions followed. An effective response requires a fact-based investigation that preserves critical evidence, reconstructs account activity, determines the full scope of impact, and uses those findings to guide containment and remediation.

This post walks through a five-phase forensic workflow for a BEC investigation, from evidence-guided containment to post-incident reporting, and the evidence that matters at each step.

Core principle of a BEC investigation: Contain account misuse without losing evidence

Every response action changes the environment investigators are trying to reconstruct. Disabling a compromised mailbox, resetting credentials, revoking tokens, or removing forwarding rules may stop immediate misuse, but those same actions can also alter the account state that helps show what the attacker did.

The goal is to contain with purpose: stop active harm; preserve critical mailbox, audit, authentication, and endpoint evidence when feasible; and retain enough forensic visibility to determine how the account was compromised, what the attacker accessed or changed, how long unauthorized activity persisted, and what must be remediated before normal operations resume.

Why business email compromise is different

BEC often relies on legitimate credentials, trusted business relationships, and ordinary-looking email activity. Unlike incidents that announce themselves with malware or encryption, a compromised mailbox can blend into normal operations.

The visible event may be a fraudulent invoice, an executive impersonation request, payroll diversion, or the unexpected disclosure of sensitive information, while the underlying account compromise began earlier and left only subtle traces.

Ultimately, the BEC investigation needs to answer these questions:

  • Was the sender impersonated through spoofing, or did the attacker control a legitimate account?
  • How did the attacker gain access, and were phishing, credential reuse, malicious links or attachments, or another method involved?
  • Which user accounts, mailboxes, endpoints, or cloud resources were affected?
  • Were forwarding rules, mailbox delegates, account settings, or other access mechanisms created or changed?
  • What messages, attachments, or other data were accessed, sent, deleted, or redirected?
  • Were credentials, authentication tokens, or sessions compromised?
  • When did unauthorized activity begin, and how long did it continue?
  • Were fraudulent financial transactions initiated, or was sensitive information disclosed?
  • What must be reset, revoked, removed, or strengthened before the account can be trusted again?
A five-phase BEC investigation workflow

A BEC response is most effective when digital forensics is integrated throughout the incident response lifecycle. Two priorities run in parallel from start to finish:

  • Stop active misuse and limit additional financial loss, unauthorized access, or disclosure.
  • Preserve and analyze the evidence needed to distinguish impersonation from account takeover and determine broader impact.

The workflow below uses five practical phases that connect rapid containment with deeper mailbox, identity, cloud, and endpoint analysis.

Phase 1: Initial response and evidence-guided containment

The first priority is to stop ongoing digital fraud or unauthorized access, while documenting or preserving key evidence where possible. When no malware is present, mailbox and identity artifacts may be the clearest record of attacker behavior.

Initial triage should focus on:

  • Identifying signs of compromise, including unusual financial requests, suspicious message patterns, unexpected forwarding rules, changed account settings, or anomalous sign-in activity.
  • Using email security, cloud audit, authentication, and incident response telemetry to identify likely affected accounts, suspicious sessions, devices, IP addresses, or related activity.
  • Determining whether unauthorized access is still active and whether a fraudulent payment, data disclosure, or other harmful action is in progress.
  • Preserving mailbox state and relevant audit, authentication, message, and endpoint evidence before account changes when the risk and timing allow.
  • Disabling affected accounts, resetting credentials, revoking compromised tokens or sessions, removing malicious rules, enabling or reinforcing multifactor authentication (MFA), and blocking suspicious infrastructure as required to stop further harm.
Phase 2: Evidence collection and building the forensic record

Once immediate containment priorities are addressed, investigators should build a forensic record that supports both rapid scoping and deeper analysis. Collection should be driven by the questions the investigation needs to answer, using targeted or broader acquisitions as appropriate to the account, endpoint, cloud service, and business impact involved.

The most valuable evidence depends on whether the incident involved account takeover, sender impersonation, credential theft, mailbox manipulation, endpoint compromise, or fraudulent transactions.

The following categories commonly provide critical context in BEC cases:

Evidence categoryExamplesInvestigative valueMailbox content and metadataMessages, folders, sent items, deleted messages, attachments, message timestampsHelps reconstruct communications, identify unauthorized messages or deletions, and determine what content may have been exposed or used in the fraud.Email headers and message provenanceRouting headers, sender information, domains, links, attachment metadataSupports analysis of message origin, route, authenticity, spoofing, phishing, and related attacker infrastructure.Mailbox configuration and audit dataForwarding rules, inbox rules, delegates, account changes, mailbox audit logsCan reveal persistence, redirection of communications, unauthorized configuration changes, and the sequence of activity inside the mailbox.Authentication and identity evidenceSign-in logs, IP addresses, devices, sessions, MFA events, credentials, tokensSupports analysis of account takeover, unusual access, compromised authentication material, and the duration of unauthorized sessions.Endpoint and browser evidenceBrowser history, system logs, credential storage, local email artifacts, endpoint telemetryMay show phishing activity, credential access, malicious links or attachments, browser-based access, and related actions on the user device.Cloud and security telemetryMicrosoft 365 or Google Workspace records, email security alerts, incident response logsProvides account-level and cloud context that can be correlated with mailbox, identity, and endpoint evidence for broader scoping.Financial and business recordsInvoices, payment instructions, transaction records, related business communicationsConnects technical evidence to fraudulent action, supports timeline reconstruction, and helps document financial impact or recovery efforts.

For distributed investigations, remote collection can help preserve endpoint evidence without waiting for a device to be physically shipped. If a suspected endpoint has already been isolated, local or offline acquisition can preserve relevant data without reconnecting the system to the production environment.

Phase 3: Forensic analysis, timeline, and scope

Analysis turns collected evidence into a clear account of what happened. The fraudulent email or payment request may be the event that triggered the investigation, but the analyst must work backward and outward to determine whether the attacker controlled a real account, how access was obtained, what was changed, and what else may have been affected.

Key forensic tasks include:

  • Distinguish sender spoofing or impersonation from true compromise of a legitimate mailbox.
  • Identify the likely method of compromise by analyzing phishing messages, malicious links or attachments, spoofed domains, browser activity, credentials, authentication records, and related artifacts.
  • Reconstruct the timeline of unauthorized access using email timestamps, mailbox audit logs, authentication records, browser history, endpoint artifacts, and relevant financial transaction data.
  • Analyze forwarding rules, mailbox delegates, account settings, deleted messages, and other changes that may show persistence, concealment, or redirection of communications.
  • Correlate unusual sign-ins, devices, IP addresses, sessions, credentials, or tokens with mailbox actions to understand the sequence and duration of attacker activity.
  • Determine what messages, attachments, or other information were accessed, sent, redirected, or deleted, and whether unauthorized financial transactions or disclosures occurred.
  • Where useful, map attacker behavior to MITRE ATT&CK to communicate observed tactics and techniques.

A critical outcome is accurate scoping. A BEC investigation should not stop with the first fraudulent message or the first account that was reported. Forensic analysis should determine whether additional accounts, endpoints, cloud activity, credentials, tokens, or business processes were affected and whether any unauthorized access remains after initial containment.

Phase 4: Remediation and recovery, turning forensic findings into action

Recovery should be guided by what the investigation learned about the compromised account and the path used to access it. Resetting a password may stop one form of access, but it does not by itself establish that malicious forwarding rules, delegates, tokens, sessions, or related account changes have been removed.

Forensic findings can identify:

  • Compromised credentials, tokens, sessions, or accounts that should be reset, revoked, disabled, or otherwise secured.
  • Unauthorized forwarding rules, delegates, mailbox changes, or other access mechanisms that must be removed and validated.
  • The initial compromise method and the email security, authentication, account management, or user awareness controls that need to be strengthened.
  • Related endpoints or browser activity that require additional investigation or remediation because they may have enabled credential or session theft.
  • The messages, data, or financial activity affected by the incident so legal, compliance, finance, insurance, and leadership teams can make informed decisions.
  • Observed attacker behaviors and indicators that can be translated into stronger monitoring, filtering, authentication controls, and alerting.

Recovery actions may include restoring affected mailbox settings to a trusted state, removing unauthorized rules or delegates, resetting credentials, revoking tokens and sessions, enforcing MFA, strengthening email filtering and account controls, validating that no unauthorized access remains, and monitoring for recurrence based on the activity observed during the investigation.

Phase 5: Documentation, reporting, and post-incident improvement

BEC investigations often support executive decision-making, legal and compliance review, insurance requirements, financial recovery efforts, and coordination with law enforcement or other external parties. Documentation should clearly distinguish observed evidence, investigative conclusions, and response actions.

A final report should document, as appropriate:

  • Whether the incident involved sender impersonation, account takeover, or both, and the evidence supporting that conclusion.
  • The likely initial compromise method and root-cause findings.
  • A timeline of unauthorized access, mailbox activity, account changes, and related financial or business events.
  • Affected accounts, mailboxes, endpoints, cloud resources, messages, and data.
  • Forwarding rules, delegates, credentials, tokens, sessions, or other mechanisms used to maintain or extend access.
  • Relevant attacker infrastructure, message headers, domains, IP addresses, and indicators identified during the investigation.
  • Forensic collection and analysis methodology.
  • Containment, remediation, and recovery actions informed by the investigation.
  • Lessons learned and recommended updates to logging, retention, email security, MFA, collection readiness, and incident response procedures.
From evidence to better response decisions

Forensic findings matter most when they change what the team does next. Across a BEC investigation, they support three key decisions:

Determine what actually happened
Establish whether the incident was limited to sender impersonation or involved control of a legitimate account. That distinction changes the evidence required, the scope of remediation, and the level of concern about mailbox access, credentials, tokens, and connected activity.

Understand the true scope
Determine which accounts, messages, endpoints, cloud records, and business processes were affected, what information may have been accessed or disclosed, and whether fraudulent financial activity occurred.

Remediate the access path, not just the visible fraud
Use findings around phishing, credential or token compromise, forwarding rules, delegates, account changes, and endpoint activity to determine what must be reset, revoked, removed, strengthened, or monitored before the incident can be considered contained.

How Magnet Forensics supports BEC investigations

BEC investigations rarely get the full story from a single message or log. Investigators may need to preserve and correlate evidence across cloud mailboxes, identity systems, endpoints, browsers, audit records, and business data.

  • Magnet Axiom Cyber: Analyze email, cloud, endpoint, and browser artifacts; correlate activity; reconstruct timelines; and use IOC, YARA, and Sigma-informed workflows.
  • Magnet Nexus: Support scalable remote endpoint collection across distributed environments when relevant systems remain available for remote acquisition.
  • Magnet Response: Support local or offline acquisition from isolated endpoints when maintaining network containment is required.

These capabilities can be used together to preserve relevant evidence, correlate activity across mailbox, cloud, identity, and endpoint sources, reconstruct attacker activity, and support evidence-based scoping and reporting.

Prepare before the next incident

Teams cannot reconstruct a BEC incident under pressure if the relevant logging, retention, collection methods, roles, and evidence-handling procedures were never established. The quality and speed of the investigation depend heavily on forensic readiness before the first suspicious message is reported.

Key steps include:

  • Define roles across incident response, IT, security, legal, compliance, finance, and business leadership.
  • Maintain appropriate logging and retention for mailboxes, authentication systems, cloud services, endpoints, browsers, and email security platforms.
  • Establish workflows for collecting cloud email and endpoint evidence before an incident occurs.
  • Document evidence-handling, chain-of-custody, storage, and retention procedures.
  • Ensure responders know how to preserve mailbox rules, audit records, message headers, and authentication evidence before making account changes when circumstances allow.
  • Maintain and test MFA, email filtering, account management, and phishing response controls.
  • Practice BEC response scenarios so technical, finance, legal, and leadership teams understand how containment, financial response, evidence preservation, and investigation should proceed in parallel.
Treat BEC as an investigation, not just an account reset

Disabling an account or resetting a password may stop the immediate misuse, but it does not explain how the attacker gained access, what they read or changed, whether messages or payments were redirected, what data may have been exposed, or whether related credentials, tokens, or accounts remain compromised. Digital forensics provides the evidence needed to reconstruct the incident, determine its true scope, and make informed remediation decisions.

Moving quickly and investigating thoroughly can happen together: contain with purpose, preserve the mailbox and identity evidence that matters, and use what the investigation reveals to guide a more complete recovery.

About the author

Jeff Rutherford, Forensic Consultant at Magnet Forensics, is a retired FBI Supervisory Special Agent with more than twenty years of experience in organized crime, crimes against children, counterterrorism and cybersecurity related investigations. Jeff achieved specialized certification as a Technically Trained Agent and an FBI Certified Digital Forensic Examiner and holds certifications from IACIS (CFCE) and SANS (GCFA). While assigned to the North Texas Regional Computer Forensic Laboratory, Jeff conducted digital forensic examinations for various agencies (state, local, and federal) across North Texas. Jeff also led the FBI Dallas Technical Operations Squad responsible for the capture, processing, and preservation of electronic surveillance evidence.

The post How to investigate business email compromise (BEC): from fraudulent email to full scope  appeared first on Magnet Forensics.

items.title: 4 real? Tracking exploitation and patching of eMudhra’s weak keys
items.summary: On October 19, 2026, we learned about eMudhra’s eight shockingly weak keys: where eMudhra was trusted to pick a 115-digit number for their virtual combination lock protecting the Internet, they picked the number 4. Not even four digits, just the number 4. The other seven keys were similarly weak: 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237. The next day, we wrote a blog post on the immediate action we took to mitigate this leak, and what customers needed to do on their end to stay secure. Now, we are sharing a more in-depth follow up on the evidence we’ve seen of exploitation, and the progress seen on visitors patching their systems. Let's start with the scale of the problem. A certificate authority (CA) with weak keys this serious is unprecedented, and the potential consequences are significant. While there have been plenty of compromised certification authorities in the past (such as DigiNotar , TÜRKTRUST , and TrustWave ), access to their keys has always been contained to a degree; these incidents gave a limited set of attackers or organizations the ability to issue fraudulent certificates. The eMudhra incident is fundamentally different; the affected intermediate private keys could be recovered almost instantly by anyone from the public certificates themselves. Anyone can independently recover these same signing keys and create certificates for any domain that an unpatched client not enforcing Certificate Transparency would accept. eMudhra announced they’re exiting the public CA business and have claimed a mistake in a key generation script, but have not yet shared the script. They signed a certificate revocation list (CRL) with what might’ve been a correctly generated key, and subsequently corrected it to be signed with the weak key. How did that come to be and why didn’t that set off alarms? Much has to be cleared up, including the role of the auditors and cross signers. This blog proposes the fixes and next steps for organizations to ensure they are secure. Patching Cloudflare Our primary concern remains the security impact on Cloudflare, our customers, and the Internet as a whole. At the time of writing, all high priority Cloudflare systems have been patched. A small number of confirmed low impact tickets is being worked on. We started patching high-impact systems immediately on October 19. These included customer origin-facing proxies using Pingora , responsible for most of our outbound connections. These were patched in hours to reject the vulnerable eMudhra keys. At the same time, we started an AI-assisted analysis of our source code to find all other systems that trust these weak keys. Within four hours we had a full analysis. We assigned a ticket with preliminary analysis for each system, and asked the team to confirm and/or adjust the analysis before the end of the day. Where high impact was identified, we asked to patch immediately, and for the lower impact, remediation was due at the end of last week. Has Cloudflare seen exploitation across its network? To track whenever a customer’s server (or attacker) presents a certificate signed by eMudhra’s weak keys, we added logging to Pingora. As this outbound service accounts for the vast majority of outgoing TLS connections from a Cloudflare machine, any attacker attempting to snoop using the eMudhra keys would trigger this logging. The logging finished rolling out October 21. At the time of writing, a week later, we’ve seen about 22,000 attempted handshakes with the weak eMudhra keys. Two-thirds of the attempts were fetches of test sites such as emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com (which we mentioned in the developer guidance in our earlier post). Almost all of the remaining third went to origins who appeared to set up a certificate for themselves using the weak intermediate. Every handshake configured to verify the certificate was refused, as we already patched. About 160 of these handshakes stood out: the certificates’ Subject Alternative Names (SANs) were naming other organizations’ domains, unrelated to the Server Name Indication (SNI) requested in the handshake. Some of those names were domains related to consumer IoT devices. We noticed as well that those forged certificates were made after the keys leaked and some were valid for over two years, longer than any public CA may issue. However, these certificates looked like the servers' own default certificates rather than part of an attempt to intercept our connections. They named domains other than the ones being connected to, so they would have failed hostname verification anyway. And in several cases, a server presented the same certificate to connections from many of our locations, which means it came from the server itself rather than from something on a single network path. Thus while there is no evidence of the weak keys being used to intercept Cloudflare's connections so far, these keys appear to have been used to forge certificates within hours of the weakness becoming public: one of the forged certificates we saw was dated October 20 at 18:19 UTC, less than an hour after Mozilla's bug report was made public. This does not exclude carefully targeted interception. For that we have to rely on the usual indirect signals of system compromise — and so far, we have not seen any such signals. How many visitors are still vulnerable? So much about patching Cloudflare, but what about our visitors? We cannot directly test whether a visitor still trusts the weak keys without breaking connections, so we have to do something more indirect. For that we used our challenge pages : We rolled out an update to send out two probe connections on a fraction of challenge pages: one probe to ca1.cloudflarecaptcha.com and one to ca2.cloudflarecaptcha.com . Initially we installed an eMudhra signed certificate on ca1.cloudflarecaptcha.com and a regularly signed certificate on ca2.cloudflarecaptcha.com as control. Then we record whether these probes succeeded. This allows us to see if visitors that are served a challenge page still trust the weak eMudhra keys. What did we find? With 50 million probes over the last week, we see this: Big caveat upfront: by design the traffic to these challenge pages is highly skewed. There are many (unconfirmed) bots in there. Also, only clients that execute JavaScript (like browsers) will send probes. The jump in the data is due to the following changes—all times are UTC: October 23 15:30, we changed our control endpoint to also serve an eMudhra certificate, but this time without signed certificate timestamps (SCTs). There were some differences in acceptance, but not large. We could’ve added a new endpoint, but that would’ve required a slow release of our challenge platform. Changing the endpoint was easier. October 23 16:30, our challenge platform rolled back to a previous version because of an unrelated issue. The probes returned October 27 at 10:00. October 27 16:37, we noticed we did not send the G3 cross-sign , which not all clients knew about, and added it to both endpoints. We removed SCTs from both. October 27 16:49, we switched ca2 to chain up to the AAA Certificate Services root. October 27 18:18, we ramped up probes to be included from 1% to 10% of all challenge pages served on non-paying customer zones. With those caveats out of the way: what do we notice? Up-to-date modern browsers are mostly patched, but bots and old browsers are not. Also embedded browsers, like Android WebView, lag behind patching with 30–40% still accepting. Over the first weekend (with the monitoring gap), we see clear evidence of patching, but afterwards we see little movement. On October 29 around 18:00 UTC, we released a detection that caught a large influx of bot traffic identifying as Chrome 150-154 on macOS. This can look like patching in the top graph, but it is actually a change in traffic classification: the same user agents show a corresponding increase in acceptance among traffic with bot signals detected in the bottom graph. Chrome 150-154 on Linux is the notable exception: its acceptance continues to decline, consistent with further patching in that cohort. Given the bot-heavy and changing traffic mix, that evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive. Otherwise, we still see little movement. Breaking down by network (ASN) we see: Across the large networks, more than half of probes still accept the compromised chain, both among traffic with no bot signals detected (top graph) and traffic with bot signals detected (bottom graph). Over the weekend we saw some patching, but afterwards the trend has been flat. The big caveat still holds: traffic is skewed by (unconfirmed) bots. But bots are also just software that need security updates. And if they’re in any way representative of overall software updates, then the picture is quite dire indeed. What can you do? Patch! Dennis Jackson has a great crowdsourced website with instructions. Especially if you’re a developer on macOS, you want to follow these instructions . If you’re a Cloudflare customer, check out last week’s blog post on what needs to be done on your end when using certain products like WARP or Tunnel. Looking ahead At Cloudflare, we have a quick-revocation mechanism in place in some products. To bring it to more systems at Cloudflare and industry, we’re excited about projects like upki that understand a trust store can’t be a static list of root certificate authorities, but needs the ability to be quickly updated with information like revocation and certificate transparency keys. As vulnerabilities are discovered at a faster pace than ever, it is vital that they can be addressed quickly and effectively.
