How did that come to be and why didn’t that set off alarms? Much has to be cleared up, including the role of the auditors and cross signers. This blog proposes the fixes and next steps for organizations to ensure they are secure.

Patching Cloudflare

Our primary concern remains the security impact on Cloudflare, our customers, and the Internet as a whole. At the time of writing, all high priority Cloudflare systems have been patched. A small number of confirmed low impact tickets is being worked on.

We started patching high-impact systems immediately on October 19. These included customer origin-facing proxies using Pingora, responsible for most of our outbound connections. These were patched in hours to reject the vulnerable eMudhra keys. At the same time, we started an AI-assisted analysis of our source code to find all other systems that trust these weak keys. Within four hours we had a full analysis. We assigned a ticket with preliminary analysis for each system, and asked the team to confirm and/or adjust the analysis before the end of the day. Where high impact was identified, we asked to patch immediately, and for the lower impact, remediation was due at the end of last week.

Has Cloudflare seen exploitation across its network?

To track whenever a customer’s server (or attacker) presents a certificate signed by eMudhra’s weak keys, we added logging to Pingora. As this outbound service accounts for the vast majority of outgoing TLS connections from a Cloudflare machine, any attacker attempting to snoop using the eMudhra keys would trigger this logging. The logging finished rolling out October 21.

At the time of writing, a week later, we’ve seen about 22,000 attempted handshakes with the weak eMudhra keys. Two-thirds of the attempts were fetches of test sites such as emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com (which we mentioned in the developer guidance in our earlier post). Almost all of the remaining third went to origins who appeared to set up a certificate for themselves using the weak intermediate. Every handshake configured to verify the certificate was refused, as we already patched.

About 160 of these handshakes stood out: the certificates’ Subject Alternative Names (SANs) were naming other organizations’ domains, unrelated to the Server Name Indication (SNI) requested in the handshake. Some of those names were domains related to consumer IoT devices. We noticed as well that those forged certificates were made after the keys leaked and some were valid for over two years, longer than any public CA may issue. However, these certificates looked like the servers' own default certificates rather than part of an attempt to intercept our connections. They named domains other than the ones being connected to, so they would have failed hostname verification anyway. And in several cases, a server presented the same certificate to connections from many of our locations, which means it came from the server itself rather than from something on a single network path.

Thus while there is no evidence of the weak keys being used to intercept Cloudflare's connections so far, these keys appear to have been used to forge certificates within hours of the weakness becoming public: one of the forged certificates we saw was dated October 20 at 18:19 UTC, less than an hour after Mozilla's bug report was made public. This does not exclude carefully targeted interception. For that we have to rely on the usual indirect signals of system compromise — and so far, we have not seen any such signals.

How many visitors are still vulnerable?

So much about patching Cloudflare, but what about our visitors? We cannot directly test whether a visitor still trusts the weak keys without breaking connections, so we have to do something more indirect. For that we used our challenge pages:

We rolled out an update to send out two probe connections on a fraction of challenge pages: one probe to ca1.cloudflarecaptcha.com and one to ca2.cloudflarecaptcha.com. Initially we installed an eMudhra signed certificate on ca1.cloudflarecaptcha.com and a regularly signed certificate on ca2.cloudflarecaptcha.com as control. Then we record whether these probes succeeded. This allows us to see if visitors that are served a challenge page still trust the weak eMudhra keys.

What did we find? With 50 million probes over the last week, we see this:

Big caveat upfront: by design the traffic to these challenge pages is highly skewed. There are many (unconfirmed) bots in there. Also, only clients that execute JavaScript (like browsers) will send probes.

The jump in the data is due to the following changes—all times are UTC:

  • October 23 15:30, we changed our control endpoint to also serve an eMudhra certificate, but this time without signed certificate timestamps (SCTs). There were some differences in acceptance, but not large. We could’ve added a new endpoint, but that would’ve required a slow release of our challenge platform. Changing the endpoint was easier.
  • October 23 16:30, our challenge platform rolled back to a previous version because of an unrelated issue. The probes returned October 27 at 10:00.
  • October 27 16:37, we noticed we did not send the G3 cross-sign, which not all clients knew about, and added it to both endpoints. We removed SCTs from both.
  • October 27 16:49, we switched ca2 to chain up to the AAA Certificate Services root.
  • October 27 18:18, we ramped up probes to be included from 1% to 10% of all challenge pages served on non-paying customer zones.

With those caveats out of the way: what do we notice? Up-to-date modern browsers are mostly patched, but bots and old browsers are not. Also embedded browsers, like Android WebView, lag behind patching with 30–40% still accepting. Over the first weekend (with the monitoring gap), we see clear evidence of patching, but afterwards we see little movement.

On October 29 around 18:00 UTC, we released a detection that caught a large influx of bot traffic identifying as Chrome 150-154 on macOS. This can look like patching in the top graph, but it is actually a change in traffic classification: the same user agents show a corresponding increase in acceptance among traffic with bot signals detected in the bottom graph.

Chrome 150-154 on Linux is the notable exception: its acceptance continues to decline, consistent with further patching in that cohort. Given the bot-heavy and changing traffic mix, that evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive. Otherwise, we still see little movement.

Breaking down by network (ASN) we see:

Across the large networks, more than half of probes still accept the compromised chain, both among traffic with no bot signals detected (top graph) and traffic with bot signals detected (bottom graph). Over the weekend we saw some patching, but afterwards the trend has been flat.

The big caveat still holds: traffic is skewed by (unconfirmed) bots. But bots are also just software that need security updates. And if they’re in any way representative of overall software updates, then the picture is quite dire indeed.

What can you do?

Patch! Dennis Jackson has a great crowdsourced website with instructions. Especially if you’re a developer on macOS, you want to follow these instructions. If you’re a Cloudflare customer, check out last week’s blog post on what needs to be done on your end when using certain products like WARP or Tunnel.

Looking ahead

At Cloudflare, we have a quick-revocation mechanism in place in some products. To bring it to more systems at Cloudflare and industry, we’re excited about projects like upki that understand a trust store can’t be a static list of root certificate authorities, but needs the ability to be quickly updated with information like revocation and certificate transparency keys. As vulnerabilities are discovered at a faster pace than ever, it is vital that they can be addressed quickly and effectively.

items.title: Detection Engineering: Implementing Detection-as-Code in an Existing Environment: Part 1 – Introduction and Concept
items.summary: This article presents a case study of how Detection Engineering can be improved by applying Detection-as-Code principles in an established, operational environment. The focus is deliberately practical. The environment already had an active detection library, ongoing development work, and regulatory requirements requiring the continuous development and deployment of new detections. The migration therefore had to improve the engineering model without causing material disruption to existing operations. Previously, my colleague Stamatis Chatzimangou published a detailed series on this blog about Detection Engineering and Detection-as-Code, covering the underlying concepts and building blocks. If you are new to Detection-as-Code, I recommend reading that series first. This case study summarises work performed in a recent customer project. Some details have been removed or adjusted to protect customer confidentiality. However, the technical challenges we faced and the essential migration steps remain intact, providing a realistic view of how such a transformation can be carried out in a live environment. Starting Position The environment contained multiple detection platforms, each requiring platform-specific detection implementations. This article uses Splunk as its primary example and explains how other platforms fit into the resulting structures and processes without covering them in detail. The organisation had already taken initial steps towards Detection-as-Code. Some detection-related data was stored and versioned in Git repositories. Changes were reviewed through pull requests, and development work was tracked through issues on a GitHub Project board. Each detection platform had its own repository containing the relevant configuration. In the Splunk case, the repository largely contained the complete apps directory that was deployed to the Splunk infrastructure. A manual deployment process copied this directory to the Splunk server and reloaded the configuration. Other platforms used separate repositories containing their respective configuration files. In addition to the detection implementations in the platform configurations, each detection had a metadata document in YAML format. These documents were still stored on a file share. Test implementations based on Atomic Red Team were also available. However, each test file contained test cases for all detections covering the same MITRE ATT&CK technique, and the tests were stored within the Splunk repository. The existing setup provided a useful starting point. Git-based storage and existing deployment processes meant that the project could focus on improving data handling and engineering workflows. The deployment mechanisms for the detection platforms did not need to be replaced, provided that the new process could still generate the required Splunk app configuration and equivalent artefacts for other platforms. Developers were also already familiar with Git, issues, pull requests, and project boards. Weaknesses At the same time, the existing setup had several significant weaknesses. The data was organised by detection platform rather than by the semantic unit developers worked on: the individual detection. Files belonging to one detection were distributed across multiple locations, including multiple repositories and a file share. As a result, a single change could require multiple pull requests and separate file-share changes. This made development and review unnecessarily difficult, increased the likelihood of human error, and made it hard to trace changes reliably. For example, savedsearches.conf files in the Splunk apps contained several thousand lines of configuration for many unrelated detections. Such files are difficult to review as GitHub does not always render them conveniently. Further they can contain configuration fragments for detections that have already been retired but were never removed. With this fragmented data, there was reduced visibility into data quality, completeness, and coverage. Thereby, reviews required substantial manual effort. Furthermore, without confidence in the data consistency and general quality, the files could only be used to deploy detections to the platforms, but they were not suited for further use, and a need existed for separately maintained reports and lists. In addition to the manual effort required to keep these up to date and in sync, significant potential was lost. Cleanly structured and validated data would enable fully automated report generation, data analysis, and further integrations (for example automated generation of compliance reports required by auditors). This would progressively eliminate manual work for developers, reviewers, and other stakeholders who need to assess information from the detection library. Goals To address these issues, we defined three goals: Restructure the existing data The data structure should reflect the semantic structure of detections and the way developers interact with them. Platform-specific structures should be generated automatically by deployment processes. Consolidate all detection-related data in GitHub All data maintained outside GitHub should be migrated into GitHub, including metadata documents from the file share and information previously maintained in Excel sheets to create a single central source of truth. Build a foundation for automation, reporting, and integrations The restructured and consolidated data should enable initial automations and provide a framework for adding further automations in the future. Target Data Structure We designed a new repository structure that places all information required by detection developers in a single detection repository. This repository contains the complete detection library, covering detections for different platforms. The existing repositories for individual detection platforms remain in place, but their scope changes. They contain only platform-specific configuration and deployment logic. This removes overlapping responsibilities between repositories: the Detection Engineering team owns the detection repository, while the relevant platform operations team owns each platform-specific repository. The main branch of the detection repository represents the current detection library from the Detection Engineering perspective. Platform teams regularly consume the current state of that branch, package a specific release, and deploy the resulting platform configuration to the production environment. With this consolidation, all detection development takes place in a single repository. Each change starts with an issue, is implemented on a feature branch following a GitHub Flow model, is tracked on a GitHub Project board, and is reviewed and approved through a single pull request. The repository contains three main folders, as well as a README.md that explains the structure: detections : currently active detections detections_retired : archived detections that have been removed from active use utils : CLI tools, scripts, and libraries for detection developers and automations Within detections , each detection has its own folder. The folders retain the existing naming convention for internal detection identifiers. While the convention itself could be improved, the migration deliberately limited the number of simultaneous changes. Keeping the familiar identifiers reduced adoption effort and avoided introducing an additional source of risk. The detections_retired folder follows the same structure. Retiring a detection is therefore a simple and traceable operation: move the detection folder from detections to detections_retired . All artefacts belonging to a detection are stored in its folder. Typical contents include: meta.yml : metadata such as name, description, covered MITRE ATT&CK techniques, category, platform, known blind spots, known false positives, severity, references, and required data sources test-atomic.yml : an Atomic Red Team test definition that simulates the activity the detection is expected to identify Platform-specific implementation files. For Splunk, these can include: splunk-searches.conf : relevant configuration blocks from savedsearches.conf splunk-transforms.conf : relevant configuration blocks from transforms.conf splunk-macros.conf : relevant configuration blocks from macros.conf splunk-lookups : lookup files used by the detection The Splunk implementation files remain raw configuration blocks that are later placed in files within the apps directory. This is not ideal because some information is redundant with the meta.yml documents. However, we deliberately did not change this during the main migration in order to avoid introducing additional potential sources of error. Overall, the resulting repository structure looks as follows: . ├── detections │ ├── DET00001 │ │ ├── meta.yml │ │ ├── test-atomic.yml │ │ ├── splunk-searches.conf │ │ ├── splunk-transforms.conf │ │ ├── splunk-macros.conf │ │ └── splunk-lookups │ │ └── DET00001_false_positives.csv │ │ │ └── DET00002 │ ├── meta.yml │ ├── test-atomic.yml │ └── other_platform_implementation.json │ ├── detections_retired │ └── ... │ ├── utils │ └── ... │ └── README.md This structure makes the detection, rather than the platform configuration file, the central unit of development. A developer working on a detection can find its metadata, tests, implementation files, and supporting lookups in one location. Roadmap With the target structure defined, we planned a migration that would minimise the impact on ongoing operations. Fix file formats Several files, particularly metadata documents and Atomic Red Team tests, were intended to be machine-readable YAML files but did not consistently contain valid YAML. Encoding problems, indentation errors, and missing or incorrect keys had to be fixed before automated processing was possible. Some names also had to be corrected manually to allow reliable matching between related files during the restructuring. Prepare supporting utilities for the new structure Tooling had to be developed to generate the configuration structures required by detection platforms such as Splunk, as well as the folder structures required by Atomic Red Team. Prepare and test the restructuring The restructuring itself had to be scripted and tested. The restructuring process and supporting tooling had to reproduce the original platform-specific files or generate functionally equivalent configurations. Complete as much in-progress development as possible The migration would be based on the main branches. Pending development work should therefore be reviewed and merged before the migration wherever possible, reducing the amount of post-migration work. Execute the restructuring This was the only phase that required a short freeze. For one day, the main branches and remaining non-Git locations would be frozen while the restructuring was executed. A final validation would then determine whether the migration had completed successfully. If successful, work would continue in the new structure; otherwise, the environment would be reverted and additional preparation would be required. Migrate ongoing development work and open reviews Only the main branches were frozen. Development could continue on feature branches during the restructuring, but those branches would remain tied to the old repositories and could no longer be merged there. The changes therefore had to be recreated on feature branches in the new repository. The old branches could then be deleted without being merged. Split Atomic Red Team tests At the start of the migration, Atomic Red Team test files were organised by MITRE ATT&CK technique rather than by detection. During the restructuring, the complete test definition was copied into each detection folder associated with the relevant technique. Afterwards, test cases that did not belong to that specific detection had to be removed. This activity was intentionally postponed because it did not affect platform deployment and was therefore not a blocker for resuming normal operations. Migrate remaining data As a final migration step, detection information still maintained in Excel sheets was moved into the metadata documents. The YAML schema was extended where needed to accommodate that information. After the main restructuring, the next priority was to improve data quality and consistency. For this purpose, we developed a validator that could be executed manually as a CLI tool and automatically in a build pipeline. The validator was gradually extended with additional checks while existing inconsistencies were corrected. Integrated into the pipeline, the validator blocks pull requests that introduce inconsistencies and ensures that the achieved data quality is maintained. With consistent and validated data in place, the organisation could use this foundation to build automations, reports, and further improvements. Wrapping Up The key design decision was to make the individual detection the central unit of storage and development. Consolidating metadata, tests, implementation files, and supporting artefacts in a single repository reduced fragmentation without replacing established platform deployment processes. Equally importantly, the migration was designed as an operational change rather than a purely technical refactoring. Preparing the data, validating the transformation, limiting the freeze period, and explicitly handling ongoing development made it possible to improve the engineering model while keeping the detection programme running. In Part 2, we examine how this roadmap was executed in practice, including the data migration, preservation of Git history, and clean-up work that followed.
items.summary_html:
This article presents a case study of how Detection Engineering can be improved by applying Detection-as-Code principles in an established, operational environment.

The focus is deliberately practical. The environment already had an active detection library, ongoing development work, and regulatory requirements requiring the continuous development and deployment of new detections. The migration therefore had to improve the engineering model without causing material disruption to existing operations.

Previously, my colleague Stamatis Chatzimangou published a detailed series on this blog about Detection Engineering and Detection-as-Code, covering the underlying concepts and building blocks. If you are new to Detection-as-Code, I recommend reading that series first.

This case study summarises work performed in a recent customer project. Some details have been removed or adjusted to protect customer confidentiality. However, the technical challenges we faced and the essential migration steps remain intact, providing a realistic view of how such a transformation can be carried out in a live environment.

Starting Position

The environment contained multiple detection platforms, each requiring platform-specific detection implementations. This article uses Splunk as its primary example and explains how other platforms fit into the resulting structures and processes without covering them in detail.

The organisation had already taken initial steps towards Detection-as-Code. Some detection-related data was stored and versioned in Git repositories. Changes were reviewed through pull requests, and development work was tracked through issues on a GitHub Project board.

Each detection platform had its own repository containing the relevant configuration. In the Splunk case, the repository largely contained the complete apps directory that was deployed to the Splunk infrastructure. A manual deployment process copied this directory to the Splunk server and reloaded the configuration. Other platforms used separate repositories containing their respective configuration files.

In addition to the detection implementations in the platform configurations, each detection had a metadata document in YAML format. These documents were still stored on a file share. Test implementations based on Atomic Red Team were also available. However, each test file contained test cases for all detections covering the same MITRE ATT&CK technique, and the tests were stored within the Splunk repository.

The existing setup provided a useful starting point. Git-based storage and existing deployment processes meant that the project could focus on improving data handling and engineering workflows. The deployment mechanisms for the detection platforms did not need to be replaced, provided that the new process could still generate the required Splunk app configuration and equivalent artefacts for other platforms. Developers were also already familiar with Git, issues, pull requests, and project boards.

Weaknesses

At the same time, the existing setup had several significant weaknesses. The data was organised by detection platform rather than by the semantic unit developers worked on: the individual detection. Files belonging to one detection were distributed across multiple locations, including multiple repositories and a file share. As a result, a single change could require multiple pull requests and separate file-share changes. This made development and review unnecessarily difficult, increased the likelihood of human error, and made it hard to trace changes reliably.

For example, savedsearches.conf files in the Splunk apps contained several thousand lines of configuration for many unrelated detections. Such files are difficult to review as GitHub does not always render them conveniently. Further they can contain configuration fragments for detections that have already been retired but were never removed.

With this fragmented data, there was reduced visibility into data quality, completeness, and coverage. Thereby, reviews required substantial manual effort. Furthermore, without confidence in the data consistency and general quality, the files could only be used to deploy detections to the platforms, but they were not suited for further use, and a need existed for separately maintained reports and lists. In addition to the manual effort required to keep these up to date and in sync, significant potential was lost. Cleanly structured and validated data would enable fully automated report generation, data analysis, and further integrations (for example automated generation of compliance reports required by auditors). This would progressively eliminate manual work for developers, reviewers, and other stakeholders who need to assess information from the detection library.

Goals

To address these issues, we defined three goals:

  1. Restructure the existing data
    The data structure should reflect the semantic structure of detections and the way developers interact with them. Platform-specific structures should be generated automatically by deployment processes.
  2. Consolidate all detection-related data in GitHub
    All data maintained outside GitHub should be migrated into GitHub, including metadata documents from the file share and information previously maintained in Excel sheets to create a single central source of truth.
  3. Build a foundation for automation, reporting, and integrations
    The restructured and consolidated data should enable initial automations and provide a framework for adding further automations in the future.
Target Data Structure

We designed a new repository structure that places all information required by detection developers in a single detection repository. This repository contains the complete detection library, covering detections for different platforms.

The existing repositories for individual detection platforms remain in place, but their scope changes. They contain only platform-specific configuration and deployment logic. This removes overlapping responsibilities between repositories: the Detection Engineering team owns the detection repository, while the relevant platform operations team owns each platform-specific repository.

The main branch of the detection repository represents the current detection library from the Detection Engineering perspective. Platform teams regularly consume the current state of that branch, package a specific release, and deploy the resulting platform configuration to the production environment.

With this consolidation, all detection development takes place in a single repository. Each change starts with an issue, is implemented on a feature branch following a GitHub Flow model, is tracked on a GitHub Project board, and is reviewed and approved through a single pull request.

The repository contains three main folders, as well as a README.md that explains the structure:

  • detections: currently active detections
  • detections_retired: archived detections that have been removed from active use
  • utils: CLI tools, scripts, and libraries for detection developers and automations

Within detections, each detection has its own folder. The folders retain the existing naming convention for internal detection identifiers. While the convention itself could be improved, the migration deliberately limited the number of simultaneous changes. Keeping the familiar identifiers reduced adoption effort and avoided introducing an additional source of risk.

The detections_retired folder follows the same structure. Retiring a detection is therefore a simple and traceable operation: move the detection folder from detections to detections_retired.

All artefacts belonging to a detection are stored in its folder. Typical contents include:

  • meta.yml: metadata such as name, description, covered MITRE ATT&CK techniques, category, platform, known blind spots, known false positives, severity, references, and required data sources
  • test-atomic.yml: an Atomic Red Team test definition that simulates the activity the detection is expected to identify
  • Platform-specific implementation files. For Splunk, these can include:
    • splunk-searches.conf: relevant configuration blocks from savedsearches.conf
    • splunk-transforms.conf: relevant configuration blocks from transforms.conf
    • splunk-macros.conf: relevant configuration blocks from macros.conf
    • splunk-lookups: lookup files used by the detection

The Splunk implementation files remain raw configuration blocks that are later placed in files within the apps directory. This is not ideal because some information is redundant with the meta.yml documents. However, we deliberately did not change this during the main migration in order to avoid introducing additional potential sources of error.

Overall, the resulting repository structure looks as follows:

.
├── detections
│   ├── DET00001
│   │   ├── meta.yml
│   │   ├── test-atomic.yml
│   │   ├── splunk-searches.conf
│   │   ├── splunk-transforms.conf
│   │   ├── splunk-macros.conf
│   │   └── splunk-lookups
│   │       └── DET00001_false_positives.csv
│   │
│   └── DET00002
│       ├── meta.yml
│       ├── test-atomic.yml
│       └── other_platform_implementation.json
│
├── detections_retired
│   └── ...
│
├── utils
│   └── ...
│
└── README.md

This structure makes the detection, rather than the platform configuration file, the central unit of development. A developer working on a detection can find its metadata, tests, implementation files, and supporting lookups in one location.

Roadmap

With the target structure defined, we planned a migration that would minimise the impact on ongoing operations.

  1. Fix file formats
    Several files, particularly metadata documents and Atomic Red Team tests, were intended to be machine-readable YAML files but did not consistently contain valid YAML. Encoding problems, indentation errors, and missing or incorrect keys had to be fixed before automated processing was possible. Some names also had to be corrected manually to allow reliable matching between related files during the restructuring.
  2. Prepare supporting utilities for the new structure
    Tooling had to be developed to generate the configuration structures required by detection platforms such as Splunk, as well as the folder structures required by Atomic Red Team.
  3. Prepare and test the restructuring
    The restructuring itself had to be scripted and tested. The restructuring process and supporting tooling had to reproduce the original platform-specific files or generate functionally equivalent configurations.
  4. Complete as much in-progress development as possible
    The migration would be based on the main branches.
    Pending development work should therefore be reviewed and merged before the migration wherever possible, reducing the amount of post-migration work.
  5. Execute the restructuring
    This was the only phase that required a short freeze. For one day, the main branches and remaining non-Git locations would be frozen while the restructuring was executed. A final validation would then determine whether the migration had completed successfully. If successful, work would continue in the new structure; otherwise, the environment would be reverted and additional preparation would be required.
  6. Migrate ongoing development work and open reviews
    Only the main branches were frozen. Development could continue on feature branches during the restructuring, but those branches would remain tied to the old repositories and could no longer be merged there. The changes therefore had to be recreated on feature branches in the new repository. The old branches could then be deleted without being merged.
  7. Split Atomic Red Team tests
    At the start of the migration, Atomic Red Team test files were organised by MITRE ATT&CK technique rather than by detection. During the restructuring, the complete test definition was copied into each detection folder associated with the relevant technique. Afterwards, test cases that did not belong to that specific detection had to be removed. This activity was intentionally postponed because it did not affect platform deployment and was therefore not a blocker for resuming normal operations.
  8. Migrate remaining data
    As a final migration step, detection information still maintained in Excel sheets was moved into the metadata documents. The YAML schema was extended where needed to accommodate that information.

After the main restructuring, the next priority was to improve data quality and consistency. For this purpose, we developed a validator that could be executed manually as a CLI tool and automatically in a build pipeline. The validator was gradually extended with additional checks while existing inconsistencies were corrected. Integrated into the pipeline, the validator blocks pull requests that introduce inconsistencies and ensures that the achieved data quality is maintained.

With consistent and validated data in place, the organisation could use this foundation to build automations, reports, and further improvements.

Wrapping Up

The key design decision was to make the individual detection the central unit of storage and development.
Consolidating metadata, tests, implementation files, and supporting artefacts in a single repository reduced fragmentation without replacing established platform deployment processes.

Equally importantly, the migration was designed as an operational change rather than a purely technical refactoring. Preparing the data, validating the transformation, limiting the freeze period, and explicitly handling ongoing development made it possible to improve the engineering model while keeping the detection programme running.

In Part 2, we examine how this roadmap was executed in practice, including the data migration, preservation of Git history, and clean-up work that followed.

items.title: From help desk impersonation to AD CS abuse: Investigating ESC1 and ESC8 intrusion paths
items.summary: In this article Activity overview Attack chain overview Portable runtime staging and execution variants Host discovery and AD CS assessment Case 1: ESC1 abuse and the cost of an identity exclusion Case 2: PetitPotam and ESC8 turn a workstation into a domain-controller identity Why the response outcomes differed Actionable investigation methods References Learn More Microsoft Threat Intelligence investigated two human-operated intrusions in which threat actors used Microsoft Teams messages and calls to impersonate IT or help desk personnel and socially engineer users into granting interactive remote access, primarily through Quick Assist. Once connected, the threat actors staged portable Python, Bun, or Java runtimes, performed host and network discovery, and assessed Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) for certificate-based authentication paths. Although the incidents began with the same social-engineering and remote-access pattern, they diverged at the certificate layer. In Case 1, the threat actor abused an Enterprise CA Security Configuration 1 (ESC1) -vulnerable certificate template to obtain authentication certificates for privileged accounts and performed DCSync. In Case 2, the threat actor used PetitPotam, a technique that causes a Windows server to authenticate to an attacker-controlled system. The attacker relayed the domain controller’s New Technology (NT) LAN Manager (NTLM) authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment (ESC8), obtained a certificate for the domain-controller account, and used it for certificate-based Kerberos authentication (PKINIT – Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication). This intrusion pattern is high impact because a user-approved remote session can become certificate-backed access to privileged identities and domain infrastructure. In Case 1, Microsoft Defender attack disruption restricted covered identities and blocked substantial follow-on activity, but a privileged identity excluded from automated containment remained usable and later supported data exfiltration. In Case 2, Defender generated ESC8-related alerts, after which the customer isolated the associated workstation and no further progression was observed. The activity did not exploit a vulnerability in Microsoft Teams; instead, it relied on social engineering and insecure or overly permissive AD CS configurations. In this blog, we analyze the shared attack chain, the ESC1 and ESC8 certificate-abuse paths, and the different response outcomes. We also provide investigation methods, mitigation recommendations, Microsoft Defender detection guidance, and advanced hunting queries to help defenders identify and interrupt this access path. The activity described here is not attributed to a specific threat actor. Activity overview Risk to enterprise environments AD CS can turn a certificate request into a durable authentication path. An attacker who obtains an authentication certificate for a privileged user or machine account can use that certificate independently of the initially compromised password. Resetting the user’s password or reimaging the first workstation does not revoke an issued certificate or invalidate Kerberos tickets that have already been issued. Two AD CS abuse techniques are central to these incidents: ESC1 – certificate template abuse: A low-privileged requester abuses a misconfigured authentication-capable template that permits requester-supplied identity information and broad enrollment, allowing the requester to obtain a certificate for a privileged account. ESC8 – NTLM relay to Web Enrollment: An attacker relays a user or machine account’s NTLM authentication to an AD CS web enrollment endpoint that lacks relay protections, then requests a certificate as the relayed identity. Attackers can use Microsoft Teams to impersonate IT support personnel and persuade users to approve a remote session, gaining hands-on-keyboard access without a conventional malware attachment. Portable or renamed runtimes such as Python, Bun, and Java can execute attacker-controlled scripts from user-writable locations while retaining legitimate file metadata. Automated disruption is most effective when every compromised identity and device remains eligible for containment; exclusions can preserve the attacker’s path. Microsoft Threat Intelligence investigated two human-operated intrusions in which threat actors used Microsoft Teams messages and calls to impersonate IT or help desk personnel and socially engineer users into granting interactive remote access, primarily through Quick Assist. Once connected, the threat actors staged portable Python, Bun, or Java runtimes, performed host and network discovery, and assessed Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) for certificate-based authentication paths.

Although the incidents began with the same social-engineering and remote-access pattern, they diverged at the certificate layer. In Case 1, the threat actor abused an Enterprise CA Security Configuration 1 (ESC1) -vulnerable certificate template to obtain authentication certificates for privileged accounts and performed DCSync. In Case 2, the threat actor used PetitPotam, a technique that causes a Windows server to authenticate to an attacker-controlled system. The attacker relayed the domain controller’s New Technology (NT) LAN Manager (NTLM) authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment (ESC8), obtained a certificate for the domain-controller account, and used it for certificate-based Kerberos authentication (PKINIT – Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication).

This intrusion pattern is high impact because a user-approved remote session can become certificate-backed access to privileged identities and domain infrastructure. In Case 1, Microsoft Defender attack disruption restricted covered identities and blocked substantial follow-on activity, but a privileged identity excluded from automated containment remained usable and later supported data exfiltration. In Case 2, Defender generated ESC8-related alerts, after which the customer isolated the associated workstation and no further progression was observed. The activity did not exploit a vulnerability in Microsoft Teams; instead, it relied on social engineering and insecure or overly permissive AD CS configurations.

In this blog, we analyze the shared attack chain, the ESC1 and ESC8 certificate-abuse paths, and the different response outcomes. We also provide investigation methods, mitigation recommendations, Microsoft Defender detection guidance, and advanced hunting queries to help defenders identify and interrupt this access path. The activity described here is not attributed to a specific threat actor.

Activity overview Risk to enterprise environments

An attacker who obtains an authentication certificate for a privileged user or machine account can use that certificate independently of the initially compromised password. Resetting the user’s password or reimaging the first workstation does not revoke an issued certificate or invalidate Kerberos tickets that have already been issued.

  • ESC8 – NTLM relay to Web Enrollment: An attacker relays a user or machine account’s NTLM authentication to an AD CS web enrollment endpoint that lacks relay protections, then requests a certificate as the relayed identity.
  • Attackers can use Microsoft Teams to impersonate IT support personnel and persuade users to approve a remote session, gaining hands-on-keyboard access without a conventional malware attachment.
  • Portable or renamed runtimes such as Python, Bun, and Java can execute attacker-controlled scripts from user-writable locations while retaining legitimate file metadata.

The important service paths are the certificate submission and retrieval endpoints under /certsrv; isolated URL access is not malicious by itself and must be correlated with the authenticated identity, source device, process, and CA request.

Figure 9. Sanitized view of AD CS Web Enrollment activity involving certificate submission and retrieval through /certsrv, used during ESC8 certificate issuance for a relayed domain-controller identity. Certificate-based Kerberos authentication

The attacker used the newly issued domain-controller certificate for Kerberos PKINIT and obtained a ticket-granting ticket (TGT) for the domain controller. This step converted a relayed NTLM authentication into a certificate-backed Kerberos identity.

PKINIT success is the response threshold: responders should investigate the requesting device, authenticated account, issued certificate, active Kerberos sessions, and any service-ticket use. Certificate revocation and Kerberos ticket review are separate containment actions.

Customer-led device isolation and observed outcome

Microsoft Defender generated ESC8-related alerts, after which the customer isolated the workstation associated with the certificate-enrollment and Kerberos activity. The documented containment action in this case was customer-led device isolation. No further attack progression was observed following isolation.

Why the response outcomes differed

In Case 1, an exclusion left a compromised privileged account available to the attacker despite disruption of other identities. In Case 2, customer-led device isolation followed Defender alerts, and no further attack progression was observed.

Response elementCase 1: ESC1Case 2: ESC8Response mechanismMicrosoft Defender automated attack disruption targeting compromised identities.Microsoft Defender alerts followed by customer-led device isolation.Measured effectCovered identities were restricted; more than 1,000 SMB attempts and additional logons were blocked; further DCSync activity was limited.The workstation associated with certificate enrollment and Kerberos activity was isolated.Containment follow-upOne privileged account was excluded from automated response and remained available to the attacker.No further progression was observed after isolation;Observed outcomeThe excluded identity was later used for file-server access and data exfiltration.No subsequent attack progression was documented after customer isolation. Actionable investigation methods

The most useful artifacts are not individual commands or ports in isolation. Investigators should reconstruct the chain across collaboration, endpoint, identity, and certificate systems.

  • Teams and remote access: identify the external tenant, user interaction, call or chat timing, remote-session start, approved remote monitoring and management (RMM) process, and child processes created during the session.
  • Runtime staging: inspect newly created KB-prefixed or application-like folders, archive extraction, runtime metadata, script operands, parent-child relationships, and subsequent network activity.
  • Directory interaction: use network data to identify LDAPS and SMB connections, then use endpoint and directory logs to determine what the initiating process did. TLS intentionally hides LDAP query content from passive network inspection.
  • ESC1: review certificate request and issuance events, requester identity, subject and Subject Alternative Names (SAN) values, template name, enrollment permissions, and the first authentication performed with the issued certificate.
  • PetitPotam and ESC8: correlate EFSRPC activity, outbound authentication by the domain controller, the device that relayed the authentication, Web Enrollment access, CA request and issuance records, and PKINIT from the originating workstation.
  • Disruption and containment: enumerate every compromised identity and device, review exclusions before and during response, revoke unauthorized certificates, and assess active Kerberos tickets separately
Reduce support impersonation and unauthorized remote access
  • Require users to verify unsolicited support requests through a known internal channel before joining a call, sharing a screen, or starting a remote-control session.
  • Encourage users to pay attention to warnings in incoming messages and calls when impersonation is detected.
  • Review Teams external-access and federation policies. Limit external domains to business requirements and investigate newly observed organization-themed or helpdesk-themed tenants in context.
  • Restrict remote-support software to approved products, operators, and workflows. Alert when approved RMM tools extract archives, create interpreters, or launch scripts from user-writable paths.
Constrain runtime-based execution
  • Use App Control for Business or equivalent application control to restrict unapproved portable runtimes and script execution from user-writable locations.
  • Evaluate file identity through signer, original filename, product metadata, path, parent process, and behavior. A renamed executable can retain legitimate version information.
  • Test relevant attack surface reduction rules and endpoint protection policies. Do not assume controls for Windows script hosts automatically cover JavaScript executed through Bun or source files launched through Java.
Harden AD CS against ESC1 and ESC8
  • Follow Microsoft’s secure configuration guidance for mitigating NTLM relay against AD CS: https://support.microsoft.com/help/5005413
  • Review authentication-capable templates for requester-supplied subject information, broad enrollment permissions, weak issuance requirements, and excessive certificate purpose. Remove unnecessary enrollment rights and require approval where appropriate.
  • Inventory AD CS Web Enrollment and Certificate Enrollment Web Service endpoints. Remove endpoints that are not required.
  • Require HTTPS and enforce Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on enrollment web endpoints. HTTPS protects confidentiality; EPA provides the channel binding needed to resist NTLM relay.
  • Disable NTLM on enrollment services where operationally feasible and validate Kerberos-only authentication before broad enforcement.
  • Use Defender for Identity AD CS security posture assessments to identify ESC1-related template exposure and insecure enrollment Internet Information Services (IIS) endpoints associated with ESC8: https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-for-identity/security-posture-assessments/certificates
Enable certificate auditing and prepare certificate-aware response
  • Enable the Certification Services advanced audit subcategory for success and failure, and configure the Certification Authority audit filter to record request and issuance activity.
  • Preserve CA security events, CA database records, IIS or Web Enrollment logs, endpoint process lineage, identity alerts, and Teams interaction records.
  • If an unauthorized certificate was issued, identify its serial number and thumbprint, revoke it, publish updated revocation information, and confirm that relying systems can obtain the update.
  • Review certificate-based Kerberos activity and active tickets. Revoking a certificate does not retroactively invalidate TGTs or service tickets that were already issued.
  • Treat containment exclusions as incident decisions. If an account or device cannot be automatically contained, assign a compensating manual action and verify completion.
Microsoft Defender XDR detections and disruption

Microsoft Defender XDR can connect collaboration, endpoint, identity, certificate, and Kerberos signals. Alert names and availability depend on product configuration and enabled sensors.

Useful prompts should ask for the initiating device, remote-session context, certificate request, issued identity, PKINIT activity, and any response exclusions. Results depend on connected plugins, permissions, and the evidence available to the incident.

Threat intelligence reports

Microsoft customers can use Microsoft Defender XDR Threat Analytics to review relevant reports, related incidents, impacted assets, and recommended actions. Search for Teams support impersonation, portable Bun or Java runtimes, AD CS certificate abuse, NTLM relay, ESC1, ESC8, and certificate-based Kerberos authentication. Campaign-specific report.

Advanced hunting

Use these queries to investigate related activity. Tune time windows and filters for your environment. Matches require investigation.

Teams external contact and available impersonation signals

Use these queries as investigation starting points. Validate field availability and expected values in your tenant, tune for legitimate activity, and correlate matches with incidents rather than treating a single result as proof of compromise.

Teams external contact and available impersonation signals

Find external Teams chats and available impersonation signals.

CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where
    (ActionType == "ChatCreated" and IsExternalUser == true)
    or ActionType in~ (
        "TeamsImpersonationDetected",
        "SecurityRiskInCallDetected")
| order by Timestamp desc

Bun or Java execution from KB-prefixed staging paths

Find Bun or Java running scripts from KB-prefixed AppData folders.

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "bun.exe"
    or FileName in~ ("bun.exe", "java.exe", "javaw.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine contains ".js"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains ".java"
| where FolderPath matches regex
    @"(?i)\\AppData\\Roaming\\KB[0-9]+\\"
| order by Timestamp desc

Network activity initiated by the staged runtime

Find network connections initiated by the staged runtime.

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "bun.exe"
    or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (
        "bun.exe", "java.exe", "javaw.exe")
| where RemotePort in (80, 445, 636, 88)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath matches regex
    @"(?i)\\AppData\\Roaming\\KB[0-9]+\\"
| order by Timestamp desc

Enrollment, relay, and PKINIT alerts with their evidence

Find relay, AD CS, and PKINIT alerts with their related evidence.

AlertInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where
    Title contains "NTLM relay"
    or Title contains "Certificate Services"
    or Title contains "PKINIT"
    or Title contains "Kerberos ticket request"
| join kind=inner (
    AlertEvidence
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
) on AlertId
MITRE ATT&CK techniques observed

This threat has exhibited use of the following attack techniques. For standard industry documentation, refer to the MITRE ATT&CK framework.

Initial Access

  • T1566.003 Phishing: Spearphishing via Service | Teams messages used for support impersonation.

Fake PDF and search tools hijacked searches for 13.4 million Chrome users
items.summary: Ads promoted browser extensions as tools to find manuals, convert PDFs, or make searches safer. But many of these extensions sent users’ search queries through servers controlled by their operators. Socket researcher John Tuckner identified 319 extensions with an estimated 13.4 million installs over a decade. The extensions hijacked users’ default search settings and routed their searches through servers controlled by the operators before sending them to Yahoo or Bing. This gave the operators access to users’ queries and let them earn referral payments. Socket says the extensions were promoted through ads on networks including Google Ads, promoting tools such as “manual finders,” “PDF converters,” “safe search,” and “AI search.” The extensions were listed in Google’s official store, but most were unlisted. That means people with a direct link could visit a listing and install an extension, while ordinary searches in the store would not show it. An ad offered help with an immediate task, a landing page encouraged installation, and the official store provided a familiar place to complete it. Search hijacking The main risk was that operators could see what users searched for. Searches can reveal health worries, financial problems, workplace interests, or other personal matters. Socket says queries were often associated with a unique identifier, which could let the operators link a user’s searches over time. The proxy could also choose where to send a search. Socket says this could potentially direct users to phishing or malware pages, but it did not find evidence that the extensions had done so. What should users do? If your searches start going astray, or you installed a search, PDF-converter, manual-finder, or security extension after clicking an ad, check what’s installed. Review your extensions. Enter chrome://extensions in Chrome’s address bar. Remove extensions you don’t recognize, no longer use, or don’t trust. To remove one, select Remove and confirm. If you’re unsure about an extension, check it against the list at the end of Socket’s blog . Check your search settings. In Chrome, at the top right, select More (the three-dot menu), then Settings > Search engine. If Chrome says an extension is controlling a setting, review or remove that extension. The absence of this notice doesn’t confirm that all your extensions are safe. Run a Malwarebytes scan to check for malicious extensions and other malware that could be affecting your device. From reporting threats to removing them. Cybersecurity risks should never spread beyond a headline. Keep threats off your devices by downloading Malwarebytes today .

Ads promoted browser extensions as tools to find manuals, convert PDFs, or make searches safer. But many of these extensions sent users’ search queries through servers controlled by their operators.

Socket researcher John Tuckner identified 319 extensions with an estimated 13.4 million installs over a decade. The extensions hijacked users’ default search settings and routed their searches through servers controlled by the operators before sending them to Yahoo or Bing. This gave the operators access to users’ queries and let them earn referral payments.

Socket says the extensions were promoted through ads on networks including Google Ads, promoting tools such as “manual finders,” “PDF converters,” “safe search,” and “AI search.”

The extensions were listed in Google’s official store, but most were unlisted. That means people with a direct link could visit a listing and install an extension, while ordinary searches in the store would not show it. An ad offered help with an immediate task, a landing page encouraged installation, and the official store provided a familiar place to complete it.

Search hijacking

The main risk was that operators could see what users searched for. Searches can reveal health worries, financial problems, workplace interests, or other personal matters. Socket says queries were often associated with a unique identifier, which could let the operators link a user’s searches over time.

The proxy could also choose where to send a search. Socket says this could potentially direct users to phishing or malware pages, but it did not find evidence that the extensions had done so.

What should users do?

If your searches start going astray, or you installed a search, PDF-converter, manual-finder, or security extension after clicking an ad, check what’s installed.

  • Review your extensions. Enter chrome://extensions in Chrome’s address bar. Remove extensions you don’t recognize, no longer use, or don’t trust. To remove one, select Remove and confirm. If you’re unsure about an extension, check it against the list at the end of Socket’s blog.
  • Check your search settings. In Chrome, at the top right, select More (the three-dot menu), then Settings > Search engine. If Chrome says an extension is controlling a setting, review or remove that extension. The absence of this notice doesn’t confirm that all your extensions are safe.
  • Run a Malwarebytes scan to check for malicious extensions and other malware that could be affecting your device.

items.title: Bloatware in Aftermarket Auto Parts
items.summary: This story is interesting: One Civic owner purchased a cheap aftermarket head unit off Amazon, and decided to have Claude work its magic on it, like it would a smart TV. What was reportedly discovered isn’t surprising, but is worth knowing about. Among the pre-installed bloatware—­or spyware, if you’re being less charitable­—was a voice assistant equipped with WebView, an Android system component that lets apps display content off the web. This apparently always used about a third of processing power, even while idle, which isn’t great. There were also Baidu location services, a call recorder (!), a DAB radio client that is pretty much useless in the U.S., and Adobe Acrobat, presumably so your passenger can entertain themselves with PDFs on the go. It’s interesting because it exposes all the insecurities in this piece of IoT software. But I think the real story is that a random person was able to do this reverse-engineering with the help of AI. Expect a lot more stories like this in the future.

items.title: North Korean Hackers Steal Developer Credentials to Inject Malware Into GitHub and Software Packages
items.summary: A North Korea-aligned hacking group has moved beyond fake job interviews and now steals developer credentials to plant malware in trusted software projects. The group, tracked as DeceptiveDevelopment, used the stolen access to change code in public and private repositories between April and September 2026. Every poisoned project then became a new way into the systems of the people who use it. The group has been known for years for tricking developers with fake recruiters and coding tests. In earlier campaigns, it mainly wanted to steal cryptocurrency wallets and browser logins. The new activity is bigger, because one infected developer can now put dozens or even hundreds of other users at risk. Researchers say the change shows how much North Korean groups value developer machines. A single laptop often holds Git logins, cloud keys, and package publishing rights. That is far more useful to a criminal than one stolen password. Analysts at ESET noted the shift in their APT Activity Report , which covers April to September 2026 and was published on October 28 on WeLiveSecurity. North Korean Hackers Steal Developer Credentials The report says the group moved from fake job-interview lures to wider software supply-chain compromises. ESET researchers found that the attack still starts with a lure, such as a fake hiring task that asks a developer to run a project. The same trick was described in fake job interview challenges aimed at freelance coders. Once the developer runs the file, the malware searches the computer for Git credentials, SSH keys, and access tokens. The attackers use these to log in as the developer and add malicious code to the victim’s own repositories. They often rewrite the commit history afterward, which helps hide their changes from teammates who check the project log. The poisoned files then spread through the places developers trust most. ESET found affected items on npm, the Go module mirror, Packagist, PyPI, and browser extension marketplaces. Most of the hit projects were small tools kept by single developers. This suggests the spread was automatic rather than carefully chosen, and each compromised project became a fresh entry point for everyone who downloads it. Execution chain using NullReceive (Source – ESET) At the end of several infection chains, ESET found two main tools. The first is OmniStealer, a Python infostealer that runs on several operating systems and is updated often. It goes after browser logins, crypto wallets, password managers, and developer secrets. The second is DEV#POPPER, a remote access trojan written in Node.js. Earlier DEV#POPPER research showed it could log keystrokes and run remote commands. The new versions add their code to apps developers open every day, including VS Code, Cursor, and Discord, so the malware runs again each time one of them starts. Blockchain Tricks and Hard-to-Remove Infrastructure The group has also worked to make its servers harder to shut down. ESET looked at npm packages that use a method publicly called NullReceiver. The loader checks the latest transaction from a hardcoded Ethereum address. It then reads the command server’s IP address from the receiving address of an otherwise empty transfer. A NullReceiver npm campaign reported earlier this year used the same idea. This gives the attackers a big advantage. They can switch to a new server with one new transaction and do not need to update any package. Blockchain records also cannot be taken down. ESET also found this method inside a weaponized repository owned by a real developer and started by a hidden VS Code task. By ESET’s tracking, this is the first case of blockchain-based server lookup built directly into a GitHub-hosted project. The hackers also moved their lures and payloads to services that are harder to remove. Early-stage fake Web3 coding challenges were placed on Gitea, a GitHub alternative that people can host themselves, so there is no central team to report them to. Later payloads were stored on JSONBin.io, JSONHosting, and Pinata, a gateway to the IPFS network. On IPFS, files are found by their content, so closing an account does not always remove the file. ESET concluded that the group used these six months to reach more victims and make takedowns less painful. A wider look at blockchain command servers shows other groups are copying this approach. Developers can lower their risk with a few habits. Never run code from a recruiter on your main work machine. Rotate Git tokens, SSH keys, and package publishing keys after any suspected infection. Review recent commits for rewritten history. Also treat unexpected blockchain traffic from build systems as a warning sign. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Type Indicator Role in the campaign Technique NullReceiver Reads the server IP from an Ethereum transaction recipient address Malware OmniStealer Python infostealer for browser data, wallets, password managers, and developer secrets Malware DEV#POPPER RAT Node.js remote access trojan that persists in VS Code, Cursor, and Discord Persistence Hidden VS Code task Launches the blockchain lookup chain from a weaponized repository Hosting service Gitea Hosts fake Web3 coding challenges Hosting service JSONBin.io, JSONHosting Host later-stage payload data Hosting service Pinata (IPFS gateway) Hosts payloads that are hard to remove Targeted platforms npm, Go module mirror, Packagist, PyPI, browser extension marketplaces Channels used to distribute poisoned code Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly.
