items.title: When Threats Don’t Wait, Security Can’t Either
items.summary: Dhananjay Ganjoo, Managing Director – India & SAARC The uncomfortable part of an adaptive attack is not how quickly it starts, but how quickly it can change course. AI-assisted operations can probe environments, learn from responses, switch techniques and chain subsequent actions while an attack is still in progress. Anthropic’s 2026 analysis of 832 accounts banned for malicious cyber activity points to this shift. While much of the activity it observed focused on preparing for attacks, the highest-risk actors used AI in live operations, including autonomous execution, orchestration and real-time pivot decisions. For defenders, this creates a moving target. The attack that enters an environment may not follow the same pattern as it progresses through it. Applications present a moving target of their own. They span on-premises infrastructure, multicloud environments, Kubernetes clusters and the edge, with APIs carrying traffic between users, workloads and services. Endpoints appear, integrations change and application behaviour evolves continuously. Preventive controls and known-threat detection remain essential. But when both the threat and environment can change in real-time, security also needs to understand what applications and APIs are doing while they are running. When the attack pattern keeps changing Application security has become very good at recognising known bad behaviour. Signatures identify established techniques. WAF policies inspect requests against defined rules. API schemas establish how endpoints are expected to be used. Threat intelligence adds knowledge of emerging campaigns and indicators. The challenge begins when malicious activity does not stay inside those familiar patterns. An attacker probing an API may alter request structures after an unsuccessful attempt, move to another endpoint, change the sequence of calls or abuse legitimate application functionality based on what the environment reveals. That means defenders need another layer of context; how the attacker behaves as it develops. A single request may reveal very little. But look at the sequence around it. Which endpoints are being called? How are request patterns changing? Which resources are being accessed? Is activity moving outside established patterns? A very different picture can emerge. Industry Research found that 48% of organisations update production APIs daily or more frequently, yet only 19% maintain a fully automated and continuously updated API inventory. Security teams are therefore dealing with two variables at once, an application estate that changes continuously and malicious activity that may not follow a predictable path. Runtime is where behaviour becomes visible Much of what security knows is established before traffic reaches a running application, identities, policies, configurations, API definitions, vulnerability intelligence and threat indicators. What cannot always be known in advance is how malicious activity will behave once it encounters the application. Runtime provides that context. Observing live application and API traffic allows security teams to connect signals that may mean little on their own, changes in request frequency, repeated access across objects, an unexpected sequence of API calls or traffic moving between endpoints. This is where behavioural detection complements established security controls. Known-threat detection asks whether traffic resembles something defenders already understand. Behavioural detection asks whether the application or API is behaving as expected? For threats capable of changing during execution, that distinction can make the difference between seeing isolated events and understanding what is happening across the application data path. Detection must lead to enforcement Visibility alone does not reduce risk. If anu unusual behaviour is identified only after the application has processed the traffic and the attacker has achieved the objective, the insight has arrived too late. Runtime visibility therefore has to connect detection with policy enforcement capable of acting on live application and API traffic. The response does not have to be binary. Some malicious activity should be blocked immediately. In other cases, security teams may rate-limit requests, restrict access to endpoint, tighten a policy or isolate suspicious activity while legitimate traffic continues. That distinction matters because security teams are protecting payment systems processing transactions, healthcare platforms supporting patients, e-commerce services serving customers and industrial applications supporting operations. Stopping an attack by unnecessarily stopping the application is not resilience. The objective is to prevent malicious activity from achieving its goal while allowing legitimate users and services to continue operating. Protection has to follow the application The challenge becomes harder when an application spans several environments. A customer-facing service may have workloads in a public cloud, sensitive systems on premises, containerised services running in Kubernetes and APIs connecting all of them. Each environment may have different controls, policies and operational teams. Attack path does not respect those boundaries If visibility and enforcement change every time application traffic crosses an environment, blind spots emerge where organisations need consistency. Protection therefore has to follow the application and its APIs across the hybrid multicloud estate rather than depend on where workload happens to run. That requires a consistent view of application traffic, the ability to identify malicious or anomalous behaviour wherever it appears, and controls capable of responding without unnecessarily disrupting legitimate traffic. Availability is part of the security outcome Application security is ultimately an availability problem. Modern businesses depend on applications being continuously accessible. When an application or API goes down, a security incident quickly becomes a business interruption. Industry research found that significant API, bot and DDoS-related incidents take organisations an average of 2.8 hours to fully resolve. It also estimated the average cost of application-layer DDoS downtime at $7,530 per minute. For security leaders, success therefore cannot be measured simply by how much traffic is blocked or how many threats are detected. What matters is whether the organisation can contain malicious activity while keeping critical services operating. Security and application delivery increasingly have to move together. Protection has to be strong enough to stop malicious traffic, precise enough to preserve legitimate traffic and consistent enough to work wherever the application runs. From knowing the threat to being ready for it Threat intelligence, vulnerability management, signatures, access controls and preventive protections remain fundamental to cyber defence. But organisations cannot assume they will always know the exact shape of an attack before it reaches a running application. As threats become more adaptive, security needs to know in advance with what it can learn from application and API behaviour at runtime. Continuous visibility must feed behavioural detection, and behavioural detection must translate into policy enforcement before malicious activity becomes operational impact. This is what continuous security readiness means. It is less about predicting every attack, but recognising when behaviour changes, assessing the risk and acting while the application remains available. Cyber resilience will increasingly be determined in the space between the first meaningful deviation and the business disruption. The organisations best prepared will be those that can recognise that change early, adapt their protection and keep the applications their business running.
items.summary_html:
Dhananjay Ganjoo, Managing Director – India & SAARC 

The uncomfortable part of an adaptive attack is not how quickly it starts, but  how quickly it can change course.  

AI-assisted operations can probe environments, learn from responses, switch techniques and chain subsequent actions while an attack is still in progress.

Anthropic’s 2026 analysis of 832 accounts banned for malicious cyber activity points to this shift.

While much of the activity it observed focused on preparing for attacks, the highest-risk actors used AI in live operations, including autonomous execution, orchestration and real-time pivot decisions.  

For defenders, this creates a moving target. The attack that enters an environment may not follow the same pattern as it progresses through it. 

Applications present a moving target of their own. They span on-premises infrastructure, multicloud environments, Kubernetes clusters and the edge, with APIs carrying traffic between users, workloads and services.

Endpoints appear, integrations change and application behaviour evolves continuously.  

Preventive controls and known-threat detection remain essential. But when both the threat and environment can change in real-time, security also needs to understand  what applications and APIs are doing while they are running.  

When the attack pattern keeps changing 

Application security has become very good at recognising known bad behaviour. Signatures identify established techniques. WAF policies inspect requests against defined rules.

API schemas establish how endpoints are expected to be used. Threat intelligence adds knowledge of emerging campaigns and indicators. 

The challenge begins when malicious activity does not stay inside those familiar patterns. 

An attacker probing an API may alter request structures after an unsuccessful attempt, move to another endpoint, change the sequence of calls or abuse legitimate application functionality based on what the environment reveals.  

That means defenders need another layer of context; how the attacker behaves as it develops. 

A single request may reveal very little. But look at the sequence around it. Which endpoints are being called? How are request patterns changing? Which resources are being accessed? Is activity moving outside established patterns? A very different picture can emerge. 

Industry Research found that 48% of organisations update production APIs daily or more frequently, yet only 19% maintain a fully automated and continuously updated API inventory.

Security teams are therefore dealing with two variables at once, an application estate that changes continuously and malicious activity that may not follow a predictable path. 

Runtime is where behaviour becomes visible 

Much of what security knows is established before traffic reaches a running application, identities, policies, configurations, API definitions, vulnerability intelligence and threat indicators. 

What cannot always be known in advance is how malicious activity will behave once it encounters the application. Runtime provides that context. 

Observing live application and API traffic allows security teams to connect signals that may mean little on their own, changes in request frequency, repeated access across objects, an unexpected sequence of API calls or traffic moving between endpoints.   

This is where behavioural detection complements established security controls. Known-threat detection asks whether traffic resembles something defenders already understand.

Behavioural detection asks whether the application or API is behaving as expected? 

For threats capable of changing during execution, that distinction can make the difference between seeing isolated events and understanding what is happening across the application data path. 

Detection must lead to enforcement 

Visibility alone does not reduce risk. 

If anu unusual behaviour is identified only after the application has processed the traffic and the attacker has achieved the objective, the insight has arrived too late.

Runtime visibility therefore has to connect detection with policy enforcement capable of acting on live application and API traffic. 

The response does not have to be binary. Some malicious activity should be blocked immediately.

In other cases, security teams may rate-limit requests, restrict access to endpoint, tighten a policy or isolate suspicious activity while legitimate traffic continues. 

That distinction matters because security teams are protecting payment systems processing transactions, healthcare platforms supporting patients, e-commerce services serving customers and industrial applications supporting operations.  

Stopping an attack by unnecessarily stopping the application is not resilience. The objective is to prevent malicious activity from achieving its goal while allowing legitimate users and services to continue operating. 

Protection has to follow the application 

The challenge becomes harder when an application spans several environments. 

A customer-facing service may have workloads in a public cloud, sensitive systems on premises, containerised services running in Kubernetes and APIs connecting all of them.

Each environment may have different controls, policies and operational teams.  

Attack path does not respect those boundaries 

If visibility and enforcement change every time application traffic crosses an environment, blind spots emerge where organisations need consistency.

Protection therefore has  to follow the application and its APIs across the hybrid multicloud estate rather than depend on where workload happens to run. 

That requires a consistent view of application traffic, the ability to identify malicious or anomalous behaviour wherever it appears, and controls capable of responding without unnecessarily disrupting legitimate traffic. 

Availability is part of the security outcome 

Application security is ultimately an availability problem. Modern businesses depend on applications being continuously accessible.

When an application or API goes down, a security incident quickly becomes a business interruption. 

Industry research found that significant API, bot and DDoS-related incidents take organisations an average of 2.8 hours to fully resolve.

It also estimated the average cost of application-layer DDoS downtime at $7,530 per minute. 

For security leaders, success therefore cannot be measured simply by how much traffic is blocked or how many threats are detected.

What matters is whether the organisation can contain malicious activity while keeping critical services operating. 

Security and application delivery increasingly have to move together. Protection has to be strong enough to stop malicious traffic, precise enough to preserve legitimate traffic and consistent enough to work wherever the application runs. 

From knowing the threat to being ready for it 

Threat intelligence, vulnerability management, signatures, access controls and preventive protections remain fundamental to cyber defence.

But organisations cannot assume they will always know the exact shape of an attack before it reaches a running application. 

As threats become more adaptive, security needs to know in advance with what it can learn from application and API behaviour at runtime.

Continuous visibility must feed behavioural detection, and behavioural detection must translate into policy enforcement before malicious activity becomes operational impact. 

This is what continuous security readiness means. It is less about predicting every attack, but recognising when behaviour changes, assessing the risk and acting while the application remains available. 

Cyber resilience will increasingly be determined in the space between the first meaningful deviation and the business disruption.

The organisations best prepared will be those that can recognise that change early, adapt their protection and keep the applications their business running.

items.title: APT Hackers Use NetamLoader Malware to Target Windows 10 Systems in Asian Governments
items.summary: A new malware framework called NetamLoader is being used against a custom version of Windows 10 that only government bodies in Asia use. The campaign looks like a supply-chain operation, and nobody has linked it to a known hacking group yet. The malware hides inside a Windows update package, borrows trusted software to run, and deletes its own traces. It also contacts its operators very slowly, so short security checks can miss it. Even a file that looks safe and signed by a known vendor can be part of an infection. Analysts at Securelist, the research blog of Kaspersky’s GReAT team, identified the malware and published the full technical report on October 29, 2026. Kaspersky first saw it in the first half of 2026, when its threat network flagged a suspicious .config file. The file sat inside a CAB archive in the folder where Windows keeps update packages. APT Hackers Use NetamLoader Malware At first, the archive looked harmless. Most files were real parts of Patch My PC, a third-party patch tool, and the .NET files used in the chain were signed by Microsoft. Only one file, Resources.resx, held harmful code. Researchers did not see how the archive reached the victim. They also found no sign that Patch My PC itself was compromised. The chain starts when PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe runs. Its config file uses AppDomainManager injection in attacks to load code before the program’s main function starts. That config points to a Microsoft-signed module, which reads a second file named fabric.config. This file makes Windows open Resources.resx, and a flaw in the old BinaryFormatter feature then runs the first hidden XAML script. From there, the layers unpack one after another. Each layer is encoded, compressed, or encrypted, and the first decryption key comes from the command line of the running program. Infection chain – Stage 1 (Source – Securelist) If the command line is wrong, as in a sandbox, decryption fails and the program quietly exits. The second stage then turns off protection. A long XAML file patches the Windows Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) so every scan returns “clean.” Its sensitive text is cut into tiny pieces so signature scanners cannot spot it. This is similar to other signed Intel utility campaign reports, where trusted tools helped attackers avoid detection. Next, the first loader cleans up. It deletes the extracted files, .NET usage logs, and Prefetch files. It also removes lines from update logs in a folder named CmitUpdateAgent, which Kaspersky says may be tied to the custom government build. It then uses a remote COM object to start the final payload inside dllhost.exe, which separates it from the first process and helps it slip past EDR behavior checks. Slow Command Channel Keeps the Malware Hidden The final piece, called the .NET 2 Plugin, talks to a command-and-control (C2) server at openaigpt4v[.]com. The name looks like an AI service, but the domain sits behind Cloudflare. The malware waits 20 to 40 minutes before its first contact, which helps it outlast sandbox tests. After a valid reply, it checks in every five to six minutes. If the server stays silent, it waits 22 to 28 hours and checks every ten minutes whether that time has passed. A timer also closes the process after about 28 hours. All traffic uses AES encryption with an HMAC check, and the malware looks for a proxy in three different ways, so it can work in locked-down networks. Downloaded XAML code runs in a temporary AppDomain that is removed afterwards. This keeps the main process stable and leaves less evidence behind. The same habit of disabling scanners appears in a GhostContainer malware in Asia case, where the backdoor patched AMSI before doing anything else. Kaspersky found only one victim through its telemetry. Because the malware was built for a government-only Windows build, the researchers believe the targets are Asian government bodies. The report says countries building their own operating systems must protect the whole software chain themselves, and that this takes time. Kaspersky detects the threat as HEUR:Trojan.MSIL.NetamLoader.gen, Trojan.MSIL.Zapchast. , and Trojan.Script.Agent. . Defenders should watch update folders for unexpected config files and signed programs that load code in odd ways. They should also look for unusual Windows processes with outside connections and for missing log entries. Sending logs to a central server helps keep evidence if the malware wipes local copies. items.title: Operationalizing CISA AA26-194A: Automating Cisco Router Security Assessments with Qualys Policy Audit
items.summary: Key Takeaways CISA AA26-194A provides actionable guidance to improve the security of Internet-facing Cisco routers against real-world attack techniques. The advisory focuses on configuration hardening and security hygiene, rather than a single vulnerability or CVE. Manually validating advisory recommendations across enterprise networks is difficult, time-consuming, and prone to inconsistencies. Qualys Policy Audit transforms advisory guidance into automated configuration compliance checks, enabling organizations to continuously assess Cisco router configurations. Organizations can quickly identify configuration gaps, prioritize remediation, and continuously measure compliance using an out-of-the-box assessment policy. Cybersecurity advisories provide valuable guidance for defending against evolving threats, but their true value lies in how quickly organizations can translate recommendations into measurable security controls. With the release of the CISA Joint Cybersecurity Advisory AA26-194A , security teams now have concrete guidance to strengthen the security posture of their Internet-facing Cisco routers. With Qualys Policy Audit , organizations can automate configuration assessments to operationalize these crucial recommendations. It is crucial to acknowledge that actors sponsored by the Russian state are actively exploiting misconfigured and vulnerable networking devices, such as Cisco routers, to penetrate enterprise and critical infrastructure networks. This access enables them to move deeper into these environments without detection. In response, CISA, the NSA, and international partners have published AA26-194A, which provides clear guidance on hardening these devices against these threats. Organizations must understand that the guidance isn’t the hard part; the real challenge lies in ensuring that every router in production adheres to it. This is the gap where most organizations struggle. Addressing that gap requires ongoing compliance verification rather than a one-time assessment. It is important to start assessing your Cisco routers in accordance with the advisory’s recommendations. Understanding CISA AA26-194A CISA is committed to enhancing cybersecurity and regularly publishes periodically Joint Cybersecurity Advisories in collaboration with the National Security Agency (NSA) and other international partners. AA26-194A, titled Improve Router Hygiene to Protect Against Russian State-Sponsored Targeting , delivers crucial insights based on real-world threat intelligence, incident response findings, and observed attacker techniques. This advisory shows that attackers exploit weak configurations, legacy management protocols, insecure administrative access, and unsupported devices to infiltrate enterprise networks. It is crucial to implement the advisory’s recommendations, which focus on fundamental security practices. These include using the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), restricting management access, disabling unnecessary services, removing insecure default configurations, maintaining updated software versions, and continuously monitoring network device configurations. Taking these steps is essential for ensuring robust network security and resilience against potential threats. Routers are the frontline defense systems exposed to the internet, making them crucial in safeguarding enterprise networks. A single insecure configuration can enable attackers to establish persistence, intercept traffic, or move laterally within the environment. Even organizations with mature vulnerability management programs often overlook configuration weaknesses, which attackers frequently exploit. The recommendations in AA26-194A help close this configuration gap by guiding organizations toward secure practices that strengthen the security posture of their Cisco network devices. For organizations managing hundreds or thousands of Cisco devices, manually reviewing configurations is impractical, and a lack of visibility can slow remediation. Addressing it should be a priority. The Operational Challenge Understanding a security advisory may seem straightforward, but assessing whether hundreds or even thousands of network devices comply with that guidance is a formidable challenge. Many security teams are stuck relying on manual Command-Line Interface (CLI) reviews, spreadsheets, or custom scripts, which not only consume valuable time but also increase the likelihood of inconsistent assessments and make ongoing compliance monitoring difficult to sustain. Organizations need a robust solution that turns advisory recommendations into continuous, repeatable, and measurable compliance checks. Transforming Guidance into Continuous Compliance Qualys Policy Audit decisively addresses the challenges organizations face with AA26-194A by providing an out-of-the-box policy that automates the assessment of Cisco router configurations against the advisory’s recommended security practices. Built on the core principle of continuous visibility into every control, this platform harnesses AI-powered risk-based prioritization, ensures automated remediation with audit-ready evidence by default, and strengthens identity and access governance to eliminate ownership gaps, all while mapping compliance across more than 100 frameworks. Instead of engaging in painstaking manual reviews of each configuration, security teams receive a real-time of their Cisco network infrastructure. Non-compliant devices are swiftly identified automatically, and remediation efforts areprioritized based on actionable compliance results. The policy rigorously automates the validation of critical security recommendations from the advisory, including secure SNMP configuration, hardened management services and remote administration, stronger password and authentication controls, restricted management access, software lifecycle and support validation, and essential additional hardening practices for Cisco routers. Benefits of Automated Assessment With Qualys Policy Audit, organizations can: Assess Cisco router configurations against CISA guidance on a recurring schedule. Identify insecure configurations before attackers can exploit them. Reduce the manual effort needed to respond to newly published advisories. Prioritize remediation by risk, so resources go where they matter most. Demonstrate alignment with recommended security practices through audit-ready compliance reporting. Detect configuration drift between assessments rather than relying on a one-time check. Qualys states that Policy Audit can cut manual compliance tasks by up to 90% through automated evidence collection and reporting. Conclusion Cybersecurity advisories offer critical security guidance, but relying solely on guidance will not enhance security. Organizations must actively measure, validate, and continuously monitor the implementation of these recommendations to ensure effectiveness. With the out-of-the-box CISA AA26-194A policy in Qualys Policy Audit, security teams can automate Cisco router configuration assessments. This enables them to swiftly identify configuration weaknesses and significantly strengthen their network security posture through ongoing compliance monitoring. As organizations face increasingly complex network environments, automating configuration assessments is not just beneficial but essential for turning security guidance into measurable, repeatable security outcomes. See the AA26-194A policy in action. Explore Qualys Policy Audit or request a walkthrough to see automated Cisco router compliance for yourself. Start Your Free Trial Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) What is CISA AA26-194A? A joint cybersecurity advisory published July 13, 2026, titled Improve Router Hygiene to Protect Against Russian State-Sponsored Targeting. It describes FSB Center 16’s exploitation of poorly configured networking devices and lists hardening steps. Is this about a single CVE? No. The primary path is configuration hygiene, especially SNMP and management access. Actors also use Cisco Smart Install and known CVEs such as CVE-2018-0171 and CVE-2008-4128. What does the Qualys policy check? Cisco router configurations against the advisory’s recommended practices: SNMP, management services, password and authentication controls, restricted management access, software lifecycle, and additional hardening. items.title: Why Does Alert Overload Happen and How Can It Be Prevented?
items.summary: Key Takeaways Alert fatigue is a growing challenge in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) caused by overwhelming alert volumes, false positives, and tool sprawl. Prevention requires tuning, enrichment, and automation—organizations must refine alert logic, add context, and automate triage workflows. Integrating modern SIEM, SOAR, and analytics platforms helps correlate and prioritize alerts, reducing manual workload. Training and process governance are just as important as tools; clear workflows, staffing balance, and performance metrics keep fatigue under control. You’re operating in a fast-moving cybersecurity environment. Every second, data flows, users log in, devices communicate, and threats lurk. Your tools are generating alerts—many of them valid, many more questionable. Before long, you face a constant tsunami of notifications. That’s where alert fatigue strikes: too many alerts, too little time, too much risk. When your team starts ignoring or delaying responses to alerts, the very purpose of your monitoring stack is undermined. In this blog you’ll discover the causes of alert fatigue, explore how alert overload happens, and get actionable guidance on reducing alert fatigue in cybersecurity teams so you can reclaim control of your threat detection workflow. Why Does Alert Overload Happen and How Can It Be Prevented? Alert overload emerges when your security operations center (SOC) or security-monitoring environment produces more alerts than the team can process in a timely and accurate fashion. Understanding why it happens is the first step to prevention. Key causes of alert overload 1. Excessive alert volume from multiple tools When you deploy many security tools—endpoint protection, cloud-security monitoring, network intrusion detection , SaaS monitoring—they all send alerts. Without coordination, the volume can quickly become unmanageable. 2. High rate of false positives and low-value alerts Alerts that do not represent real threats consume time and attention. When the signal-to-noise ratio is poor, your team spends effort on benign events. 3. Lack of context or enrichment An alert with minimal context forces analysts into manual investigation: who is the user? what asset? what risk? Without added context, even valid alerts may sit idle. 4. Misconfigured or overly broad detection logic Rules set too broadly fire alerts for borderline or expected behaviour. If thresholds are too low or rules not tuned, you’ll get lots of noise. 5. Tool sprawl and integration gaps Many organisations accumulate security controls in an ad-hoc way. If tools don’t integrate, you’ll get duplicated alerts or fragmented visibility. 6. Rapid expansion of attack surface and modern environments With cloud, remote infrastructure, IoT, SaaS apps, your attack surface and telemetry increase. More “things to watch” means more potential alerts. 7. Insufficient automation and manual triage burden Where many tasks are manual, analysts spend hours triaging rather than responding. That leads to backlog and burnout. 8. Under-resourced or understaffed SOC teams The mismatch between alerts coming in and available analyst time makes overload inevitable. Critical Incident Response: Key Steps for the First 72 Hours What data has been potentially exposed? Incursion detection and Persistence detection How should I respond? Download the Whitepaper Why is prevention critical? When alert overload persists, you face multiple risks: Your team may miss genuine threats because the critical alert is buried in noise. Response times increase, which gives attackers more time to dwell. Analysts burn out, turnover rises, knowledge is lost. Trust in your alerting systems decreases—if analysts routinely ignore alerts, you wind down detection effectiveness. How to prevent alert overload? Here are actionable ways to prevent or mitigate alert fatigue, aligned to the causes above: Consolidate and rationalize your alerting tools: Reduce tool sprawl; ensure alerts funnel into a central workflow so you avoid multiple duplicated alerts. Tune detection logic and thresholds: Regularly review detection rules, retire outdated alerts, tune thresholds to reduce low-value alerts and false positives . Enrich alerts with context: Add asset criticality, user risk, business impact, and threat intelligence so that alerts become triage ready. Prioritize and score alerts: Implement risk-based alert scoring so your team focuses on high-impact alerts first. Prioritizing alerts based on asset criticality, business impact, exploitability, and threat context helps analysts focus on the threats that pose the greatest risk to the organization. Automate triage and remediation: Use playbooks and automated workflows for routine alerts so analysts can focus on complex incidents. Implement a “review-and-retire” process: Regularly archive alerts that generate no real threats, and monitor alert-volume metrics to detect fatigue early. Ensure adequate staffing and training: Make sure your SOC has the right number of analysts, and that they are trained on evolving threats and alert-handling practices. Use modern detection tools suited for cloud and hybrid environments: Older legacy systems may not handle the volume and type of alerts from cloud or SaaS, leading to overload. By taking these steps, you can reduce the volume of unhelpful alerts, improve the meaningfulness of each alert, and help your team stay focused on detecting and alerting on potential security threats rather than drowning in noise. What Are the Best Tools for Managing Cybersecurity Alerts Effectively? You’ve addressed the root causes; now it’s time to pick the right tools and architectures to support your prevention strategy. Here’s how to evaluate and use tools effectively to reduce security alert fatigue, alert logic threat detection overload and improve overall SOC effectiveness. Tool categories and how they help: 1. Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) A SIEM collects logs and alerts from many security tools and consolidates them for correlation and analysis. However, if not well implemented, SIEMs can themselves produce massive volumes of alerts. Modern approaches emphasise filtering and prioritization. 2. Security Orchestration, Automation & Response (SOAR) SOAR platforms orchestrate responses, automate triage and reduce manual burden. They integrate alerts and trigger workflows so that routine or false-positive alerts are handled or closed automatically. When configured correctly, SOAR reduces the number of alerts requiring full human investigation, thereby helping reduce alert fatigue. 3. Detection & prioritization platforms with behavior analytics Tools that go beyond simple rule-based alerts—by applying context, user or asset risk, behaviour analytics and machine learning—help elevate meaningful alerts over noise. Security analytics can reduce alert fatigue by correlating events across users, assets, networks, and endpoints, identifying patterns that indicate real threats, and helping analysts focus on higher-risk alerts instead of isolated low-value events. Security analytics platforms further reduce analyst workload by combining detection, context, risk scoring, and prioritization into a more focused alert queue. This helps SOC teams improve visibility and response efficiency while reducing the number of alerts that require manual investigation. 4. Alert-management dashboards and risk scoring engines These provide prioritized views of alerts. Analysts see fewer, higher-value alerts first, with clear context and business impact. By adopting risk-based scoring, you align alert queues with business priorities. 5. Alert deduplication and suppression tools Some alerts are duplicates or near-duplicates. Tools that suppress redundant alerts or cluster similar alerts reduce volume and cut fatigue. Academic research shows clustering approaches reduce manual triage loads. How to choose and deploy tools? Ensure integration across your stack: alerts from firewalls, endpoint detection , cloud apps, SaaS, network detection should be combined or harmonised so you can avoid fragmentation and duplication. Ensure the tool supports context enrichment: asset value, user risk, topology, time, threat intelligence —all help raise signal over noise. Focus on automation of triage: routine alerts should be processed automatically or semi-automatically, with human analysts focusing on complex cases. Establish alert-prioritisation models: use business impact, exploitability, vulnerability status, and threat intelligence to prioritise alerts. Regularly review tool performance: measure number of alerts per analyst, mean time to respond , percent of alerts ignored, backlog size—so you can identify when alert fatigue is creeping in. By deploying the right combination of SIEM, SOAR, analytics and automation—and by ensuring the tools work together rather than in silos—you create an alert-management architecture that allows you to detect and alert on potential security threats effectively while keeping alert overload under control. How Can Organizations Reduce Alert Fatigue in Cybersecurity Teams? So far we have covered causes, prevention strategies, and tools. But effective reduction of alert fatigue requires organisational, process and human factors too. Here are best practices to embed across people, process and technology. 1. Process and governance interventions Define and enforce alert-handling workflows: Specify how alerts are logged, triaged, escalated, resolved, and closed. Clear process reduces time spent wondering “what do I do next?”. Implement metric-driven monitoring of alert volumes and backlog: Track alerts per analyst, alerts per day, backlog size, percent of false positives , etc. If numbers creep up, intervene. Regular rule and use-case review: Every quarter (or more often) review your detection logic, retire unused alert rules, adjust thresholds, and remove redundant or low-value alert categories. Role-based alert assignment: Ensure that alerts are assigned to the right team/individual based on skill, context and priority—so that simple routine alerts don’t clog senior analysts. Incident playbooks and triage playbooks: Document workflows for common alert types; this speeds up response, standardises handling, and reduces cognitive load. Cross-team coordination: Engage threat intelligence, SOC, incident response , cloud/security teams so that alerts are meaningful for all. Avoid tools generating alerts that no one uses or responds to. 2. People and training Analyst training and up-skilling: Ensure analysts understand not just tool mechanics, but how to interpret context, escalate appropriately and avoid burnout. Rotation and workload balancing: Monitor analyst fatigue, ensure workloads are balanced, encourage breaks, and ensure that high-volume alert shifts are shared. Feedback loops: Analysts should have visibility on how many alerts they worked, how many were valid, what the outcomes were—this creates insight and continuous improvement. Encourage escalation and alert refinement: If a particular alert type consistently results in false positives, escalate it for tuning rather than letting it silently continue. 3. Technology reinforcement Adopt behaviour-based detection and unsupervised machine learning models: These help detect anomalies beyond rule-based alerts and improve signal filtering so that fewer but more relevant alerts arrive. Use alert-triage automation and enrichment: Automatically pull user/asset context, threat intelligence, suspicious indicators into the alert so that the analyst has the necessary information without manual lookup. Implement closed-loop automation for low-risk alerts: Some alerts (e.g., trivial policy violations) can be handled automatically with minimal analyst intervention, reducing the queue. Continuous tuning and feedback from analysts: Use analyst feedback to fine-tune models, alert thresholds, suppression logic so that the system evolves rather than stagnates. Leverage cloud-native or hybrid-capable tools: With many organizations shifting to cloud and SaaS, tools that handle cloud-security alert fatigue (e.g., in SaaS, cloud infra) help reduce overload from those environments too. 4. Outcome and benefits By combining tool, process and human-factor improvements, you’ll realize these outcomes: Reduced number of low-value alerts arriving at the analyst queue Higher proportion of alerts being investigated turning out to be valid/higher impact Faster mean time to respond (MTTR) and lower backlog of alerts Reduced analyst burnout, lower turnover, improved job satisfaction Stronger trust in your alerting systems and better overall security posture How Fidelis Security Helps Reduce Alert Fatigue When alert overload is crippling your SOC, Fidelis Security provides features designed to streamline detection, reduce noise, and deliver actionable alerts. Here are the key ways Fidelis addresses alert fatigue: Unified visibility across endpoint, network, and cloud The Fidelis Elevate ® XDR platform realizes unified visibility by integrating endpoint security, network security, deception and Active Directory protection all in one platform. By consolidating alerts from multiple sources into a single console, you reduce redundant notifications and simplify triage flows. Real-time terrain mapping and asset‐risk scoring help contextualize alerts, so your team focuses on higher-impact incidents. Alert noise reduction via patented inspection and context enrichment Fidelis lists features like deep session inspection , rich metadata collection (300+ attributes) and alert noise cancellation. These capabilities improve signal-to-noise by enriching alerts with context (who, what asset, what path) and filtering out benign or redundant events. The result: fewer low-value alerts reaching analysts, reducing fatigue and distraction. Built-in deception for high-fidelity alerts The platform includes Fidelis Deception ® technology that deploys decoys, fake assets and credentials to generate alerts only when an adversary interacts with them—rather than relying solely on standard detection logic. Because these alerts are adversary-engagements and not routine artefacts, they are inherently higher value and demand fewer resources to validate. This reduces the volume of “suspected” alerts that bog down SOC teams and turns the decoy layer into an early warning system. Integrated automation and response workflow Fidelis’ platform supports automation of triage and response actions (across endpoint, network and deception layers) within a single XDR environment. Automating investigation and containment of alerts means your team spends less time on repetitive tasks and more on true incidents—helping reduce both analyst load and response time. A lower backlog and faster closure of alerts directly combat alert fatigue. Catch the Threats that Other Tools Miss Detect and Correlate Weak Signals Active Threat Detection Evaluate Findings Against Known Attack Vectors Proactively Secure Systems Download Now Metrics and outcome-driven performance Fidelis claims customers detect post-breach attacks up to 9 × faster when using their platform. By tracking performance improvements—including reduced dwell time and quicker incident resolution—organisations can demonstrate the ROI of alert-management improvements and justify investment in fatigue-reduction measures. A measurable reduction in low-value alerts and improved alert quality builds trust in the alerting stack and reduces burnout. Conclusion Alert overload and alert fatigue aren’t just operational nuisances; they’re strategic risks. When your SOC team is drowning in alerts, it’s harder to detect and respond to real threats. You and your organization can’t afford that. The good news: you can turn this around. By understanding the causes of alert fatigue, applying the right tools and architecture, refining processes, and supporting people, you’ll reduce noise and surface the signals that matter. That means fewer HIGH-priority alerts lost in the shuffle, faster detection and response, and a more resilient security function. If you’re ready to take the next step, consider scheduling a demo of a platform that supports advanced alert prioritization, triage automation, and context enrichment. The difference you’ll feel in your team’s productivity—and in your organization’s security posture—can be substantial. items.title: Binance’s $6.3bn heist: how one laptop opened the door to the biggest crypto theft in history
items.summary: Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume, has confirmed that attackers stole an estimated $6.3 billion (around £4.7 billion) in digital assets on Thursday evening, in what is now the largest cryptocurrency theft on record. The figure is roughly four times the $1.5 billion taken from Bybit in February 2025, the previous record-holder. According to blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs, funds began leaving Binance wallets at around 20:05 UTC on 29 October, spread across ten blockchains including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron, the XRP Ledger and Solana. Most of the money was gone within roughly 20 minutes. Binance suspended deposits and withdrawals and, by late Thursday, said around $3 billion had been frozen with help from stablecoin issuers, partners, and law enforcement. Tether and Circle alone froze more than $2.5 billion in USDT and USDC. Binance’s preliminary findings point to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which the exchange says gave an attacker access to a service container that could submit withdrawals. The company says it has found “no evidence of any wallet private key leak” and has promised a detailed technical post-mortem once its investigation concludes. Co-CEO Yi He said the exchange would cover all hacking losses, drawing on its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds. Markets reacted quickly. Bitcoin fell around 5% to below $77,000 in the hours that followed, while Binance’s own BNB token dropped about 8%. The vault held. The process didn’t. For security professionals, the size of the theft is only part of the story. What sets this incident apart is where the attackers chose to strike. “I’ve followed a lot of crypto thefts, and the Binance attack stands out less for the money than for how it was done,” said Jayant Dave, APAC CISO at Check Point . “The attackers didn’t break the encryption or steal the private keys. They took over the system that tells the keys what to sign.” Dave continued: “Binance’s early findings for now point to one compromised engineer’s laptop. From there, the attackers reached a service that could submit withdrawals, and billions moved within minutes. That’s the lesson: a strong vault doesn’t matter if someone controls the process that opens it.” TRM’s on-chain analysis supports that reading. On Ethereum, the attacker used EIP-7702 authorisations to make a Binance hot wallet execute a sweeper contract under their control, while the other nine chains saw ordinary signed transfers within the same window. TRM assesses that Binance’s hot wallet signing infrastructure was likely compromised, though the exchange has not yet published a root cause. “The Binance attack raises an important question about how organisations protect their most valuable assets,” said Simon Pamplin, CTO at Certes . “If attackers can move billions of dollars without obtaining the private keys themselves, we need to examine the systems and trusted processes that gave them the ability to authorise those transactions.” Samuel Hassine, CEO and co-founder at Filigran , agreed that the mundane nature of the entry point is what organisations should focus on. “The record figure will get the headlines, but the ordinary foothold is the lesson,” he said. “Binance says the attack may have started with a compromised engineer’s laptop, used to reach a service that submits withdrawals. It has since found further points of breach. By its own account, no wallet keys were stolen.” Entry point or root cause? Those further points of breach matter. Several experts cautioned against reducing a multi-billion-dollar compromise to a single infected device before the full investigation is complete. “A compromised laptop may explain where an attack started, but it does not, on its own, explain how billions of dollars could leave an exchange,” said Pieter Arntz, researcher at Malwarebytes . “The real question is what allowed that initial foothold to become access to withdrawal systems — and which safeguards failed to stop unauthorised transactions.” Arntz added: “Until the technical investigation is complete, blaming a single laptop risks confusing the entry point with the full cause of the breach.” Certes’ Pamplin made the same point. “Initial reports of a compromised engineer’s laptop are significant, but Binance has already indicated that the intrusion involved additional points of breach. The investigation will need to establish how that initial access developed into the ability to initiate withdrawals at this scale,” he said. “The distinction matters because compromising a system that can legitimately instruct transactions may be just as damaging as stealing the credentials or keys used to secure it.” For Pamplin, that is where long-held security assumptions start to break down. “This is where conventional security assumptions become dangerous. Organisations can have encryption, authentication and access controls in place, yet remain exposed if a compromised application or authorised process can operate within those controls. The real question is what an attacker can reach, read or instruct once that trusted environment is compromised.” “It reportedly only took one laptop” Whatever the full chain of events turns out to be, the image of a single endpoint leading to billions in losses has struck a nerve. “Billions of dollars have been stolen from Binance in a matter of minutes by hackers taking control of the process that authorises withdrawals. And it reportedly only took one laptop,” said Chris Dimitriadis, Chief Global Strategy Officer at ISACA . “It’s a stark reminder that you can spend a fortune protecting your most critical systems, but if just one device is compromised, then your security is only as strong as the weakest machine on the network.” Camellia Chan, CEO and co-founder of X-PHY , put it bluntly: “The biggest cryptocurrency heist in history may have started with a single compromised laptop. Such is the sophistication of hackers, that that’s all it can take.” She added that “Attackers are constantly looking for ways in, and for organisations handling sensitive financial information or critical infrastructure, employee laptops are particularly valuable targets.” “The reported cyberattack on Binance is staggering in both its scale and potential consequences,” said Jamie Akhtar, CEO and co-founder of CyberSmart . “The fact that cybercriminals were reportedly able to move billions in digital assets in a matter of minutes demonstrates just how devastating a successful attack can be.” For businesses, he said, “this is a powerful reminder that even the largest organisations with significant cybersecurity resources are not immune to attacks.” Jake Madders, co-founder and director of Hyve Managed Hosting , framed the incident as a question of access rather than defences. “The cyberattack affecting Binance highlights how attackers don’t always need to break through the front door. Sometimes, they simply exploit the people and systems already holding the keys,” he said. “Binance says initial checks suggest a compromised engineer’s laptop may have given attackers access to internal systems, enabling unauthorised withdrawals. This raises important questions about how access to critical systems is managed. Protecting where assets are stored is not enough if the routes into them are not equally secure.” The North Korea question TRM Labs has attributed the attack “with high confidence” to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-backed hacking unit linked to the Lazarus Group. The firm points to small Tornado Cash withdrawals used to fund an operator wallet the day before the theft, along with staging and pre-obtained signatures that echo earlier DPRK-linked heists. Independent investigator ZachXBT has also named Lazarus as the likely attacker. “Blockchain analysts have linked the attack to TraderTraitor, the North Korean state-backed group behind the 2025 Bybit theft,” said Check Point’s Dave. “Governments haven’t confirmed that yet, but it fits a group that goes after people and processes, not cryptography.” Binance is not the only major exchange hit this autumn. In September, Bitget lost close to $388 million in a breach its chief executive also blamed on North Korea. “This attack isn’t a one-off either – five weeks ago, Bitget lost around USD 388 million the same way: keys untouched, control layer abused,” Dave said. “Two major exchanges in just over a month is a trend we cannot ignore.” Tim Rawlins, senior adviser and security director at NCC Group , said the targeting of a development engineer fits a well-established pattern. “This attack, reportedly on a development engineer, highlights that security is a critical element of every operational stage and personnel level. When security failures in trusted identities and administrative access can be targeted, attackers can exploit more than just the underlying technical vulnerabilities,” he said. “Given what we know about the activities of countries like North Korea in targeting cryptocurrency, it’s unsurprising that attackers are prepared to invest considerable effort in targeting individuals who have access to the building blocks of the exchanges.” Rawlins also flagged the role of artificial intelligence in accelerating these campaigns. “The increasing use of AI in attacks is supporting attackers to chain issues together in a way that might take them longer alone. Organisations are facing adversaries who are prepared to invest time and money to compromise their systems, if the return is large enough.” ISACA’s Dimitriadis echoed that view: “Hacker groups are often well resourced and patient, and they know how to target people. Organisations, particularly in financial services, that hold high-value assets must assume a breach will happen and plan for it ahead of time.” The stakes go beyond the exchange itself. TRM’s head of global policy, Ari Redbord, described the attack as “unprecedented”, warning that “When North Korea steals at this scale, the money funds weapons proliferation and other destabilising activity.” Not just a crypto problem It would be easy to treat the incident as a niche concern for crypto traders. Experts warn that would be a mistake. “For the public, the message is uncomfortable but important,” said Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress . “Your crypto holdings, your investment portfolio, and your pension fund’s exposure to digital assets can all be materially affected by a security failure at an institution.” Patel said the market reaction in the hours after the theft showed how far the consequences can travel. “When a cybersecurity incident sends shockwaves through crypto global markets, cybersecurity stops being a tech problem and starts being a systemic financial risk.” CyberSmart’s Akhtar agreed: “Beyond the financial losses, an incident of this magnitude raises serious concerns about the security of digital financial infrastructure and the potential consequences when highly sophisticated attackers gain access to critical systems.” For Check Point’s Dave, the same weakness exists well outside the crypto sector. “This goes well beyond crypto. Banks, payment providers, cloud platforms: any organisation whose automated systems move money or data on instruction carries the same risk,” he said. “Attackers have learned that the shortest route to the crown jewels often runs through one employee’s laptop and a trusted internal service.” Ordinary users also face knock-on risks. “This incident affects trust in cryptocurrency as a whole,” said Dimitriadis. “And high-profile incidents like this are often exploited by hackers on other platforms to trick users into taking immediate action that could compromise their crypto assets.” Spencer Starkey, Executive VP EMEA at SonicWall , noted that exchanges have long been in attackers’ sights. “Cryptocurrency exchanges are a popular target for cyberattacks, as they hold large amounts of valuable cryptocurrency. Cybercriminals will target cryptocurrency exchanges to steal cryptocurrency, disrupt operations, or even manipulate cryptocurrency prices,” he said. Starkey placed the Binance theft alongside a run of disruptive attacks closer to home. “Look at the last few weeks. Hackers pushed supermarket fridges across Europe to 50C, destroying food and starting fires. Criminals stole Legal Aid Agency records going back decades, including probation data. A GP dispensary couldn’t order medicines. Cybercriminals won’t wait for procurement to catch up.” Dimitriadis argued that responsibility for this kind of risk sits at the very top of an organisation. “This is ultimately a governance question, and it belongs in the boardroom, not just the security team. The fallout from an incident like this goes far beyond the money stolen – market confidence drops, customers move their assets elsewhere and regulators start asking questions.” Closing the gap So what should organisations that move money, or data, on instruction be doing now? The experts were broadly aligned: protect privileged people and devices, assume compromise, and make sure no single foothold can translate into unchecked authority. “So, protect the people with the most access first,” said Dave. “Treat developer and admin devices as high-value targets. Assume any machine or credential can be compromised and make sure none of them can move large sums without an independent check.” Speed and limits matter as much as prevention, he added. “Set hard limits on how much and how fast funds can move, and catch anomalies in seconds, not hours. Prevention has to come first, because once money spreads across multiple blockchains, getting it back is the exception.” NCC Group’s Rawlins stressed the basics. “As we have seen with many of the attacks against crypto exchanges and other platforms, good cyber hygiene and effective security fundamentals are key to defending against attacks that many organisations are still missing,” he said. “Securing trusted identities so funds can’t be moved unchallenged or other privileges exploited comes down to having phishing-resistant MFAs, just in time privileged access, tightly scoped and monitored human and non-human identities, and detection in place for anomalous activities.” Hyve’s Madders called for a stricter approach to access across the board. “The rule should be simple. People should only have access to the data and systems they need to do their jobs. This access should be tightly controlled, monitored, and removed as soon as it is no longer required. The same discipline must apply to external partners and third-party providers, whose access can create additional entry points for attackers.” “The Binance incident shows why access management needs to be treated as a fundamental part of cybersecurity, not an administrative afterthought,” he continued. “Ultimately, strong security depends on understanding who has access and what they can reach, not just protecting what is behind the door.” Certes’ Pamplin argued that controls need to sit closer to the transactions themselves. “Security needs to be enforced at the level of individual data flows and critical transactions, with cryptographic separation between systems and tightly controlled paths for sensitive operations. An attacker gaining access to one part of the environment should not automatically inherit the ability to move valuable assets across the rest of it.” Filigran’s Hassine urged organisations to map and test their own exposure. “Any company whose systems move money on instruction should know exactly which machines and accounts can trigger a transfer. Assume one of them will be compromised one day, and test whether the controls behind it hold.” CyberSmart’s Akhtar set out a similar checklist. “Protecting employee devices, implementing strong access controls and multi-factor authentication, and continuously monitoring for suspicious activity should be fundamental priorities. Organisations handling financial assets must also have additional safeguards in place, including strict transaction authorisation processes and controls that limit the damage a single compromised account or device can cause,” he said. “Employee cybersecurity awareness training is equally important, as attackers often exploit human vulnerabilities to gain their initial foothold.” X-PHY’s Chan agreed that training is necessary but not sufficient. “Businesses can train employees to recognise the warning signs of a cyberattack and if their devices are compromised, but cybersecurity capabilities must also be built into every layer of protection, starting with the hardware itself.” And for ISACA’s Dimitriadis, it comes back to leadership: “Good governance and building resilience mean the board treating cyber risk as a standing priority, investing in the right skills and making sure every employee is trained to recognise and resist targeted attacks.” Freezes, compensation and the road to recovery If there is a positive in the response so far, it is the speed with which a significant share of the stolen funds was frozen. “The estimated impact is around $6.3bn, four times the previous record. About $3bn was frozen within hours, with partners and law enforcement,” said Hassine. “That coordination is the part working well.” The rest is a different matter. TRM estimates the attacker still controls more than $2.4 billion in ether and bitcoin, and has already begun moving funds through decentralised exchanges and lending protocols including Uniswap, Aave and JustLend. “Credit to Binance for freezing funds quickly and committing to cover customer losses,” said Dave. “But the industry can’t keep relying on clean-up.” Binance’s pledge to make customers whole is significant, because crypto users have far less protection than bank customers if an exchange cannot or will not pay. “Unlike money held in a UK bank account, which may be protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) up to £120,000 per eligible depositor, cryptoassets generally do not benefit from any equivalent compensation regime,” said James Broomhall, Senior Associate at Grosvenor Law . “As a result, victims of major crypto thefts are often forced to pursue urgent tracing and recovery action through the courts, including Norwich Pharmacal applications to compel exchanges and other third parties to disclose information identifying fraudsters and tracing the movement of stolen assets.” What comes next Binance’s post-mortem should eventually show how a single endpoint became the ability to empty hot wallets across ten blockchains. Until then, much remains unknown. “As the investigation develops, we’ll gain a clearer understanding of how this attack unfolded,” said Chan. “But the key takeaway for businesses is already clear: security needs to be built into the very foundations of their systems, because there are no limits to the depths attackers will go to find a way in.” Pamplin agreed that organisations should not wait for the final report before acting. “The scale of this incident makes the consequences impossible to ignore. Security must be designed around the assumption that trusted systems can be compromised, with controls that prevent that compromise from becoming unrestricted authority over the assets they protect.” Or, as Hassine put it: “Record thefts start with ordinary footholds.” Dave’s warning may be the one that lingers longest: “The next attack will target the same weak point unless we close it first.”

CyberSmart’s Akhtar set out a similar checklist. “Protecting employee devices, implementing strong access controls and multi-factor authentication, and continuously monitoring for suspicious activity should be fundamental priorities. Organisations handling financial assets must also have additional safeguards in place, including strict transaction authorisation processes and controls that limit the damage a single compromised account or device can cause,” he said. “Employee cybersecurity awareness training is equally important, as attackers often exploit human vulnerabilities to gain their initial foothold.”

X-PHY’s Chan agreed that training is necessary but not sufficient. “Businesses can train employees to recognise the warning signs of a cyberattack and if their devices are compromised, but cybersecurity capabilities must also be built into every layer of protection, starting with the hardware itself.”

And for ISACA’s Dimitriadis, it comes back to leadership: “Good governance and building resilience mean the board treating cyber risk as a standing priority, investing in the right skills and making sure every employee is trained to recognise and resist targeted attacks.”

Freezes, compensation and the road to recovery

If there is a positive in the response so far, it is the speed with which a significant share of the stolen funds was frozen. “The estimated impact is around $6.3bn, four times the previous record. About $3bn was frozen within hours, with partners and law enforcement,” said Hassine. “That coordination is the part working well.”

The rest is a different matter. TRM estimates the attacker still controls more than $2.4 billion in ether and bitcoin, and has already begun moving funds through decentralised exchanges and lending protocols including Uniswap, Aave and JustLend.

“Credit to Binance for freezing funds quickly and committing to cover customer losses,” said Dave. “But the industry can’t keep relying on clean-up.”

Binance’s pledge to make customers whole is significant, because crypto users have far less protection than bank customers if an exchange cannot or will not pay. “Unlike money held in a UK bank account, which may be protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) up to £120,000 per eligible depositor, cryptoassets generally do not benefit from any equivalent compensation regime,” said James Broomhall, Senior Associate at Grosvenor Law.

“As a result, victims of major crypto thefts are often forced to pursue urgent tracing and recovery action through the courts, including Norwich Pharmacal applications to compel exchanges and other third parties to disclose information identifying fraudsters and tracing the movement of stolen assets.”

What comes next

Binance’s post-mortem should eventually show how a single endpoint became the ability to empty hot wallets across ten blockchains. Until then, much remains unknown.

“As the investigation develops, we’ll gain a clearer understanding of how this attack unfolded,” said Chan. “But the key takeaway for businesses is already clear: security needs to be built into the very foundations of their systems, because there are no limits to the depths attackers will go to find a way in.”

Pamplin agreed that organisations should not wait for the final report before acting. “The scale of this incident makes the consequences impossible to ignore. Security must be designed around the assumption that trusted systems can be compromised, with controls that prevent that compromise from becoming unrestricted authority over the assets they protect.”

Or, as Hassine put it: “Record thefts start with ordinary footholds.”

Dave’s warning may be the one that lingers longest: “The next attack will target the same weak point unless we close it first.”

The post Binance’s $6.3bn heist: how one laptop opened the door to the biggest crypto theft in history appeared first on IT Security Guru.

items.title: Aur0ra Ransomware Hackers Use Cursor AI Agents to Gain Domain Admin Access and Steal Data
items.summary: Ransomware crews are now giving the hardest parts of a network break-in to AI coding tools. A group linked to Aur0ra ransomware used Cursor AI agents to go from stolen passwords to domain admin access, the highest level of control in a Windows network. From there, it collected data and prepared to deploy ransomware. The group behind Aur0ra, also spelled Aurora, is tracked as GOLD OGRE. Human operators supplied VPN access, targets and goals, and the agents handled most of the work with little help. This lowers the skill needed to run a full intrusion. It also matters for every company that relies on Active Directory, as shown in an earlier report on Aurora that covered the same crew’s use of AI planning. Analysts at Sophos identified the activity while studying an AI-assisted testing framework built with Cursor. The company’s Counter Threat Unit published research on that framework in May 2026. Aur0ra Ransomware Hackers Use Cursor AI Agents The framework had tested several endpoint detection and response (EDR) products, including Sophos’s own agent. Later, according to the full Sophos analysis, the same infrastructure was seen hosting Cobalt Strike for Aur0ra operations. Sophos said it warned affected customers and worked with law enforcement to notify other victims. In late August, the analysts recovered Cursor files tied to both the ransomware work and the evasion testing. The attackers used Cursor to climb from credential access to domain administrator. They got past AI safety rules by describing the work as an authorized red team job or “diagnostics testing.” Cursor’s Composer model ran many of the intrusions, along with models from Anthropic, xAI and Moonshot. The group used Anthropic almost entirely at first, then added the others as it moved from building tools to breaking into networks. Other crews have been caught using Claude AI to plan ransomware work too, so the habit is spreading. Once given access, the agents mapped the network and checked for weak paths to powerful accounts. They ran commands, moved from machine to machine, and searched file shares, user documents, backup stores and cloud-linked storage. They tried password spraying, Kerberoasting, NTLM coercion and relay, and pulled credentials from files and backups. Operators also used common tools like SharpShares and NetExec, which appear in Gentlemen ransomware EDR killers reporting as well. In some victim networks, the agents reached domain management access, and three of those victims later appeared on the Aur0ra leak site. Stolen files were staged and sent to S3-compatible storage. Sophos saw one operator use a VeeamTransport command to copy data to a bucket on a server at 152[.]236[.]4[.]14. Logs also showed Russian shortcuts typed on a Cyrillic keyboard layout, which suggests the operators speak Russian. Third-Party Findings, Shared Tools and Defense Steps In late August 2026, Gambit Security and CloudSEK published reports that appeared to rely on the same exposed open directory at 172[.]86[.]113[.]245. It held Windows and Linux (ESXi-ready) versions of the Aur0ra ransomware, shell history and Cursor chat logs. Gambit also noted a Claude 4.5-Sonnet agent in semi-automated intrusions. That fits with a Claude Code ransomware case in which an operator let the model fix its own commands until a task worked. Gambit described agents installing a VPN client, scanning subnets with Nmap or NetExec, and mapping the domain with BloodHound. They also tried NTLM relay through PetitPotam, Coerce Plus and PrinterBug, and used Certipy for certificate abuse. Sophos found the same tools in its own testing framework, but only one SOCKS-related IP address overlapped between the two sets of infrastructure. Sophos researchers say with high confidence that GOLD OGRE used AI to test how well tools evade detection, then gave similar technology to associates running Aur0ra. They also expect other ransomware groups to build AI agents like Cursor into their work. Basic defenses still help, including patching internet-facing devices, phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication and close watch on EDR alerts. Since the AI speeds up each stage, a fast response matters more. Sophos also advises limiting how far an intruder can move by segmenting critical servers, isolating backups, reviewing domain administrator rights, using privileged access management and applying application controls. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Indicator Type Context 152[.]236[.]4[.]14 IP address Data exfiltration server used in Aur0ra ransomware operations 152[.]236[.]3[.]8 IP address Cobalt Strike C2 server used in Aur0ra ransomware operations 172[.]86[.]89[.]124 IP address Cobalt Strike C2 server used in Aur0ra ransomware operations 144[.]172[.]101[.]72 IP address Cobalt Strike C2 server used in Aur0ra ransomware operations 206[.]223[.]230[.]107 IP address Cobalt Strike C2 server used in Aur0ra ransomware operations 45[.]59[.]113[.]63 IP address SOCKS proxy node used in Aur0ra ransomware operations 172[.]86[.]113[.]245 IP address Open directory server used in Aur0ra ransomware operations Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly.
