items.title: Cloudflare services for private origins is now generally available
items.summary: Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing Cloudflare One connection . Your origin stays private, while web application firewall ( WAF ), caching , bot management , and Workers work just as they do for public origins. In June, we launched this capability in closed beta to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet. Before the beta, putting Cloudflare in front of these services meant exposing a public IP, opening a firewall port, or running cloudflared alongside the origin. Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers. What is generally available today During the closed beta, eligible customers requested access through their account team. Today, we’re opening access beyond that beta group. Point a proxied A or AAAA record at a private IP, and Cloudflare’s application services work as they do for public origins: WAF and managed rules Bot management Rate limiting Caching Transform and rewrite rules Workers Some limitations remain. Argo Smart Routing and Aegis aren’t supported, and origin health checks require Load Balancing . See the developer documentation for the full list of current limitations. Your origin keeps its private IP, with no inbound firewall exception required. With Cloudflare WAN or Cloudflare Mesh , there’s no connector software to run on the origin either. How it works Create a proxied A or AAAA record pointing to your origin. For supported private IP ranges, Use private network routing is enabled automatically. If your origin uses a public IP that’s reachable only through your private network, you can enable the setting manually. The rest of the request flow stays the same: TLS termination, WAF, rules, and caching continue to run on Cloudflare’s network. The setting turns on automatically for RFC 1918 private IPv4 addresses, RFC 6598 CGNAT addresses (100.64.0.0/10), and RFC 4193 unique local IPv6 addresses (fc00::/7). It can’t be turned off for these ranges; attempts to disable it through the API return an error. What the API looks like For customers automating deployments through the API, private routing is simply an additional attribute on a standard DNS record. POST /zones/{zone_id}/dns_records { "type": "A", "name": "app.example.com", "content": "10.0.0.50", "ttl": 300, "proxied": true, "private_routing": true } Behind the scenes, Cloudflare's proxy platform determines where to send traffic for app.example.com by querying Cloudflare's Origin API. The response includes metadata indicating that the destination should be reached through a private network path: { "zone_name": "example.com", "ipv4_addresses": ["10.0.0.50"], "private_routing": true } The private_routing flag is the key signal. When our proxy sees it, instead of attempting to connect directly to the private IP address over the public Internet, it hands the request to our private networking layer, which then routes the connection across the customer's existing private network connectivity, whether that's IPsec , GRE , Cloudflare Tunnel , CNI , or Cloudflare Mesh. The beta post covers the routing layer in more detail. Get started Before you begin, you’ll need: The Private Origins entitlement on your account. Ask your account team to turn it on. Cloudflare One connectivity using IPsec, GRE, CNI, Cloudflare Tunnel, or Cloudflare Mesh . Unified Routing enabled on your account. New and existing accounts can upgrade through their account team. If you connect over Cloudflare WAN or Cloudflare Mesh, you need Unified Routing enabled on your account and a return route for Cloudflare’s source ranges (100.64.0.0/12 for IPv4 and 2606:4700:cf1:5000::/64 for IPv6). New and existing accounts can upgrade to Unified Routing through their account team. Then, create a proxied A or AAAA record for the private IP and confirm that Use private network routing is enabled. Your existing WAF, cache, and bot management configuration applies to that hostname without further changes. One note from the beta: if requests time out and nothing arrives at the origin, check the return route first. A missing route for Cloudflare’s source range was the most common setup failure we saw. Once enabled, follow our developer documentation , which walks through the full setup. What comes next Today’s release covers public traffic reaching private origins. Next, we’re working on private-to-private traffic: users, services, and AI agents on private networks reaching applications on other private networks through Cloudflare’s application services. Engineering work is underway, and we’re targeting a closed beta in early 2027. If you’d like to participate, talk to your account team. The goal is to give private applications the same protections and controls as public applications. An employee opening wiki.company.internal , for example, could benefit from WAF, rate limiting, and bot management. Service-to-service traffic between clouds and data centers could use those controls too, even when neither side touches the public Internet. For now, today’s release brings the WAF, caching, bot management, and Workers you use for public applications to private origins over connectivity you already operate. Questions or feedback? Join the conversation in our community forums or reach out to your account team.
items.summary_html:
Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing Cloudflare One connection. Your origin stays private, while web application firewall (WAF), caching, bot management, and Workers work just as they do for public origins.

In June, we launched this capability in closed beta to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet. Before the beta, putting Cloudflare in front of these services meant exposing a public IP, opening a firewall port, or running cloudflared alongside the origin.

Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers.

What is generally available today

During the closed beta, eligible customers requested access through their account team. Today, we’re opening access beyond that beta group.

Point a proxied A or AAAA record at a private IP, and Cloudflare’s application services work as they do for public origins:

  • WAF and managed rules
  • Bot management
  • Rate limiting
  • Caching
  • Transform and rewrite rules
  • Workers

Some limitations remain. Argo Smart Routing and Aegis aren’t supported, and origin health checks require Load Balancing. See the developer documentation for the full list of current limitations.

Your origin keeps its private IP, with no inbound firewall exception required. With Cloudflare WAN or Cloudflare Mesh, there’s no connector software to run on the origin either.

How it works

Create a proxied A or AAAA record pointing to your origin. For supported private IP ranges, Use private network routing is enabled automatically. If your origin uses a public IP that’s reachable only through your private network, you can enable the setting manually.

The rest of the request flow stays the same: TLS termination, WAF, rules, and caching continue to run on Cloudflare’s network.

The setting turns on automatically for RFC 1918 private IPv4 addresses, RFC 6598 CGNAT addresses (100.64.0.0/10), and RFC 4193 unique local IPv6 addresses (fc00::/7). It can’t be turned off for these ranges; attempts to disable it through the API return an error.

What the API looks like

For customers automating deployments through the API, private routing is simply an additional attribute on a standard DNS record.

POST /zones/{zone_id}/dns_records
{
 "type": "A",
 "name": "app.example.com",
 "content": "10.0.0.50",
 "ttl": 300,
 "proxied": true,
 "private_routing": true
}

Behind the scenes, Cloudflare's proxy platform determines where to send traffic for app.example.com by querying Cloudflare's Origin API. The response includes metadata indicating that the destination should be reached through a private network path:

{
 "zone_name": "example.com",
 "ipv4_addresses": ["10.0.0.50"],
 "private_routing": true
}

The private_routing flag is the key signal. When our proxy sees it, instead of attempting to connect directly to the private IP address over the public Internet, it hands the request to our private networking layer, which then routes the connection across the customer's existing private network connectivity, whether that's IPsec, GRE, Cloudflare Tunnel, CNI, or Cloudflare Mesh.

The beta post covers the routing layer in more detail.

Get started

Before you begin, you’ll need:

  1. The Private Origins entitlement on your account. Ask your account team to turn it on.
  2. Cloudflare One connectivity using IPsec, GRE, CNI, Cloudflare Tunnel, or Cloudflare Mesh.
  3. Unified Routing enabled on your account. New and existing accounts can upgrade through their account team.
  4. If you connect over Cloudflare WAN or Cloudflare Mesh, you need Unified Routing enabled on your account and a return route for Cloudflare’s source ranges (100.64.0.0/12 for IPv4 and 2606:4700:cf1:5000::/64 for IPv6). New and existing accounts can upgrade to Unified Routing through their account team.

Then, create a proxied A or AAAA record for the private IP and confirm that Use private network routing is enabled. Your existing WAF, cache, and bot management configuration applies to that hostname without further changes.

One note from the beta: if requests time out and nothing arrives at the origin, check the return route first. A missing route for Cloudflare’s source range was the most common setup failure we saw.

Once enabled, follow our developer documentation, which walks through the full setup.

What comes next

Today’s release covers public traffic reaching private origins. Next, we’re working on private-to-private traffic: users, services, and AI agents on private networks reaching applications on other private networks through Cloudflare’s application services.

Engineering work is underway, and we’re targeting a closed beta in early 2027. If you’d like to participate, talk to your account team.

The goal is to give private applications the same protections and controls as public applications. An employee opening wiki.company.internal, for example, could benefit from WAF, rate limiting, and bot management. Service-to-service traffic between clouds and data centers could use those controls too, even when neither side touches the public Internet.

For now, today’s release brings the WAF, caching, bot management, and Workers you use for public applications to private origins over connectivity you already operate.

Questions or feedback? Join the conversation in our community forums or reach out to your account team.

items.title: Hackers Build Fake Polymarket Platforms That Rig Trades and Block Cryptocurrency Withdrawals
items.summary: Criminals are copying the look of Polymarket, one of the biggest prediction market sites. They use the copies to take cryptocurrency from people who think they are placing real bets. Once a victim deposits money, the site decides every win and loss, and withdrawals stop working. The scams are not one-off websites. Three Russian-speaking “traffer” teams, called AtlasCore, PolyFucked and Magnetic Team, sell ready-made fake prediction markets to affiliates. Affiliates bring in the victims, and the team supplies the website, admin panel, crypto payment system and technical support. Earlier cases such as fake Polymarket trading tools drained wallets with malware. This newer wave skips the malware and relies on a rigged platform instead. Researchers at Recorded Future’s Insikt Group identified the three teams and the tools they sell. They have watched the groups adapt since spring 2026. Their Insikt Group report says the teams copied established fraud methods and applied them to the growing interest in Polymarket and Kalshi. Hackers Build Fake Polymarket Platforms The fake sites copy the real thing closely. They show YES/NO bets, probability charts, trading volumes and live market activity. Some even import data from the public Polymarket API, so the numbers look real. Behind the screen, the operator controls the result. Code from AtlasCore’s fake sites lets an operator set a “win chance” for each victim. A value of 0 means the victim always loses, and 100 means they always win. This can apply to every user or to one person. Magnetic Team adds a “Boost” tool with a target win rate, a balance cap that holds back payouts once a victim’s balance grows, and a forced-loss pause after several wins in a row. Magnetic Team also fakes the crowd. It claims more than 3,000 bots trading across more than 5,000 markets, each acting like a different kind of trader, so the order book looks busy and natural. Advertisement posted by AtlasCore on a cybercrime forum (Source – Recorded Future) Withdrawals are where victims get stuck. The panels hold ready-made error messages and fee settings. Magnetic Team’s “withdrawal funnel” gives one excuse after another, such as identity checks, anti-money-laundering reviews, VIP upgrade fees, an “Account Protection Score” and withdrawal taxes. The aim is to keep the victim paying and never let them cash out. The sites also collect personal data. Victims are asked for card numbers, CVV codes, passport or driver’s license photos and a selfie holding the document. Magnetic Team can create up to 20,000 deposit wallets per blockchain. Their private keys are exposed and can be exported the moment money arrives, so funds can be swept out quickly. This fits a wider pattern. The DCloud Uni-App scam network also shows victims fake trading activity before their money disappears. AI and Affiliate Money Help the Scam Spread The affiliate deals are attractive. AtlasCore advertises 70% to 80% of net profit, PolyFucked offers at least 60%, and Magnetic Team pays a base of 70% of victim deposits. AtlasCore’s Telegram channel claimed about $10.97 million in deposits between May 2 and September 18, 2026. PolyFucked claims about $2.4 million in quarterly turnover. Both figures come from the criminals themselves and may be inflated. AI lowers the effort needed to run these campaigns. AtlasCore’s manuals teach affiliates to build fake influencers by blending photos of two real people, then post short reaction videos on Instagram. They also tell affiliates to strip metadata so the content is not labeled as AI-made. PolyFucked shares prompts for making logos with AI image tools. AI also handles the chat with victims. Code from the fake sites shows operators connecting a language model to answer support messages and translate victim replies into Russian. If one model refuses a request, the system switches to a model from another provider. Magnetic Team’s code also looks AI-assisted, with heavy English comments and notes about bug fixes, though Insikt says this is a judgment based on style and not confirmed. This matches what OpenAI found in a scam networks using ChatGPT case, where fraud groups used AI for fake personas and translation. Treat any prediction market that is not on the official Polymarket or Kalshi domain as suspect. Be careful with sites promoted by influencers on Instagram or Telegram. A site that asks for ID documents or card details before you can withdraw should raise alarms. Watch for sudden fees or “verification” steps when you try to cash out. Reviewing crypto phishing warning signs helps spot these tricks early. Security teams can block the domains and IPs below and watch for new lookalike domains. items.summary_html:
Criminals are copying the look of Polymarket, one of the biggest prediction market sites. They use the copies to take cryptocurrency from people who think they are placing real bets.

Once a victim deposits money, the site decides every win and loss, and withdrawals stop working. The scams are not one-off websites.

Three Russian-speaking “traffer” teams, called AtlasCore, PolyFucked and Magnetic Team, sell ready-made fake prediction markets to affiliates.

Affiliates bring in the victims, and the team supplies the website, admin panel, crypto payment system and technical support.

Earlier cases such as fake Polymarket trading tools drained wallets with malware. This newer wave skips the malware and relies on a rigged platform instead.

Researchers at Recorded Future’s Insikt Group identified the three teams and the tools they sell. They have watched the groups adapt since spring 2026.

Their Insikt Group report says the teams copied established fraud methods and applied them to the growing interest in Polymarket and Kalshi.

Hackers Build Fake Polymarket Platforms

The fake sites copy the real thing closely. They show YES/NO bets, probability charts, trading volumes and live market activity. Some even import data from the public Polymarket API, so the numbers look real.

Behind the screen, the operator controls the result. Code from AtlasCore’s fake sites lets an operator set a “win chance” for each victim. A value of 0 means the victim always loses, and 100 means they always win. This can apply to every user or to one person.

Magnetic Team adds a “Boost” tool with a target win rate, a balance cap that holds back payouts once a victim’s balance grows, and a forced-loss pause after several wins in a row.

Magnetic Team also fakes the crowd. It claims more than 3,000 bots trading across more than 5,000 markets, each acting like a different kind of trader, so the order book looks busy and natural.

Advertisement posted by AtlasCore on a cybercrime forum (Source – Recorded Future)

Withdrawals are where victims get stuck. The panels hold ready-made error messages and fee settings. Magnetic Team’s “withdrawal funnel” gives one excuse after another, such as identity checks, anti-money-laundering reviews, VIP upgrade fees, an “Account Protection Score” and withdrawal taxes. The aim is to keep the victim paying and never let them cash out.

The sites also collect personal data. Victims are asked for card numbers, CVV codes, passport or driver’s license photos and a selfie holding the document.

Magnetic Team can create up to 20,000 deposit wallets per blockchain. Their private keys are exposed and can be exported the moment money arrives, so funds can be swept out quickly.

This fits a wider pattern. The DCloud Uni-App scam network also shows victims fake trading activity before their money disappears.

AI and Affiliate Money Help the Scam Spread

The affiliate deals are attractive. AtlasCore advertises 70% to 80% of net profit, PolyFucked offers at least 60%, and Magnetic Team pays a base of 70% of victim deposits.

AtlasCore’s Telegram channel claimed about $10.97 million in deposits between May 2 and September 18, 2026. PolyFucked claims about $2.4 million in quarterly turnover. Both figures come from the criminals themselves and may be inflated.

AI lowers the effort needed to run these campaigns. AtlasCore’s manuals teach affiliates to build fake influencers by blending photos of two real people, then post short reaction videos on Instagram.

They also tell affiliates to strip metadata so the content is not labeled as AI-made. PolyFucked shares prompts for making logos with AI image tools.

AI also handles the chat with victims. Code from the fake sites shows operators connecting a language model to answer support messages and translate victim replies into Russian. If one model refuses a request, the system switches to a model from another provider.

Magnetic Team’s code also looks AI-assisted, with heavy English comments and notes about bug fixes, though Insikt says this is a judgment based on style and not confirmed.

This matches what OpenAI found in a scam networks using ChatGPT case, where fraud groups used AI for fake personas and translation.

Treat any prediction market that is not on the official Polymarket or Kalshi domain as suspect. Be careful with sites promoted by influencers on Instagram or Telegram.

A site that asks for ID documents or card details before you can withdraw should raise alarms. Watch for sudden fees or “verification” steps when you try to cash out.

Reviewing crypto phishing warning signs helps spot these tricks early. Security teams can block the domains and IPs below and watch for new lookalike domains.

items.title: Critical Drupal Commerce Vulnerability Could Let Hackers Buy Products for Just $0.01
items.summary: Drupal has warned that hackers are actively exploiting a highly critical security flaw in Commerce Core , putting online stores at risk of financial losses. Tracked as CVE-2026-118539, the vulnerability lets attackers bypass access checks in the module used to sell products and services on Drupal websites and connected shopping applications. The warning raises concerns about unauthorized changes to store data and transactions. However, Drupal has not confirmed that attackers can buy products for exactly $0.01. The public advisory does not document that price, describes a potential financial impact, and does not name the fields attackers can change or explain how observed attacks worked. Published on October 28, 2026, the official Drupal security advisory identifies insufficient protection around certain routes and entity fields. Routes handle requests to website functions, while entity fields hold data associated with site records. Missing access checks can let someone reach functions or data they should not control. Critical Drupal Commerce Vulnerability Drupal assigned the flaw a risk score of 21 out of 25, placing it in its “Highly critical” category. This is Drupal’s own security scale, not a CVSS score. The assessment indicates that exploitation requires no authentication and affects all configurations of vulnerable module versions. The rating also identifies possible exposure of some private information and changes to some data. Drupal has confirmed active exploitation but has not published affected store names, attack volumes, or a detailed attack method. The advisory does not establish remote code execution or full website takeover. Commerce Core supports shopping carts, checkout forms, and separate applications connected through APIs. Its project page reports more than 42,000 websites using the module. That figure reflects reported installations, not the number of stores confirmed vulnerable or compromised. The vulnerability affects Commerce Core versions before 2.41 and versions from 3.0.0 up to, but not including, 3.3.13. Administrators running the 3.x branch should install Commerce Core 3.3.13. Sites using earlier versions should upgrade to Commerce Core 8.x-2.41, following Drupal’s published guidance. These are Commerce module updates, separate from Drupal core security releases. Earlier coverage of a critical Drupal remote code execution vulnerability concerns a different flaw. Store owners should check the installed Commerce package rather than assume a recent Drupal core update fixed this issue. Drupal explicitly advises affected sites to audit orders for inconsistencies because exploitation is already underway. Beyond applying the update, a practical review should compare recorded orders with expected prices and payment records, investigating unexplained differences rather than treating them as proof of compromise. This threat differs from Magecart attacks that target online checkout pages and steal customer payment details. Here, Drupal’s warning centers on broken access controls and possible merchant losses. Researchers Dan Puccetti, Marcus Johansson, and Robert Snyder reported the vulnerability. Prompt patching and order checks remain the immediate priorities for affected online stores. items.title: “A Ring Tone That I Cannot Hear” – Twenty Years Later
items.summary: My first post for this blog was in June 2006, 20 years ago: A Ring Tone That I Cannot Hear . Back then, I tested my hearing with Audacity, and I could hear a tone up to 14 kHz. 20 years later, I do the test again, and I can hear a tone up to 8 kHz. It’s no surprise that my hearing declined over the years, that happens to everybody. What did surprise me, or better said, what impressed me, is that a free and open-source tool like Audacity still exists after 20 years, and that I can just issue the exact same commands as 20 years ago!

items.title: Frida 17.25.0 Released
items.summary: This is a big one. The out-of-process mapper that has carried our Darwin injection for years is now cross-platform, so agents are mapped straight into the target on Windows and Linux too, without a file on disk or a dlopen() in the target. Two libraries were split out of frida-core: Efni, the building blocks for protocol-heavy GLib code, and Idun, our Apple device stack, which now shares its tunnel through a daemon on Windows and Linux. Memory Tagging on Darwin is handled, arm64e got a round of fixes from @hsorbo , and there’s a long tail of fixes with contributions from @Cassian433 , @tpetsas , @Flechaa , @borgCode , @leonitousconforti and @esauvisky . A mapper for every platform Frida’s Darwin backend has long had its own dynamic linker: a mapper that parses a Mach-O, resolves its imports against the target’s libraries, and maps it into the target from the outside, so the target never has to call dlopen() , which a sandbox may not allow. That mapper is now a generic GumMapper interface, with a Mach-O, a PE and an ELF implementation behind it, each built where its format is native. The mappers never run code in the target. Everything that must execute there is emitted into a small runtime that runs when the consumer calls the constructor. Target memory goes through a GumProcessMemory interface, which the native implementation backs for the local process and for remote ones where the OS allows, and symbols are resolved through a GumModuleResolver , which has out-of-process implementations too. On Windows, exports are parsed from each module’s file on disk, so nothing is read from the target unless the file is missing or doesn’t match the loaded image. On Linux, the target’s libraries are opened through /proc/ /map_files when permitted, then through /proc/ /root with an inode check, so a target in a container resolves against its own files, and when neither works the image is copied from the target’s memory. Both new mappers support static TLS. The PE runtime registers its TLS with the loader, which for x64 and x86 processes on ARM64 means locating the loader’s native TLS routines, and it seeds the /GS security cookie like the loader does. The ELF runtime carries its own __tls_get_addr , plus a TLS descriptor resolver on AArch64, and the ELF mapper covers x86, ARM, AArch64 and MIPS, including the MIPS GOT and RELR-packed relocations. Windows Agents are now injected filelessly. Rather than writing a temporary DLL and loading it through LoadLibrary() , the agent is copied once into a pagefile-backed section per architecture, whose handle is duplicated into each target so the code pages are shared across all of them. A small stub runs the mapped images’ constructors, calls the agent’s entrypoint, and runs the destructors when it is not staying resident, after which the mapper unmaps it. The dbghelp and symsrv DLLs are mapped alongside and handed to the agent, so symbolication doesn’t load them through the loader either, and the agent cloaks all of these mappings. Nothing touches the filesystem anymore. The LoadLibrary() path remains for builds with the mapper disabled. Processes with Arbitrary Code Guard are now within reach too. When the process can’t create code itself, the agent plugs in memory hooks that have the host allocate and protect code pages on its behalf, and the host session keeps serving such agents while they revert their instrumentation on unload. Linux Agents are mapped out-of-process instead of having the target dlopen() them. A loader stub in the target loads any of the agent’s dependencies the target lacks, reserves memory, and reports back, after which it is sent a plan to apply: the read-only segments are mapped straight from the agent’s file, so their pages are shared across targets, while the rest is streamed over the control socket. The loader applies protections, runs the constructor, and on unload runs the destructor and unmaps. This is used by the ptrace, procmem and kernel injectors alike. CModule CModule’s external toolchain backends are now one, loading the compiled shared library through the mapper. Only the compile step differs: clang on Darwin, gcc on ELF platforms, and on Windows MSVC, or MinGW gcc when cl isn’t on PATH . This means Windows, Linux and Android now accept prebuilt shared libraries, which only Darwin did before, and external compilation on Windows now works in static builds, as the toolchain is spawned without GLib’s spawn helper. The Windows backend also parses modules through the new portable PE parser, so dependencies are enumerated and imports include delay-loaded ones. Efni and Idun frida-core has grown a lot of code that isn’t about instrumentation: binary serialization, promises, a GDB remote protocol client, and the whole Apple device protocol stack from usbmuxd to CoreDevice. That code is now two libraries of its own, consumed as subprojects. Efni holds the generic building blocks, and Idun the Apple device stack: discovery over USB and the network, pairing, lockdown and the CoreDevice tunnel, service clients for installation proxy, SpringBoard services, DTX instruments, RemoteXPC and LLDB, and codecs for property lists, keyed archives, OPACK, kcdata, kdebug and kperfdata. Both build as shared libraries against system dependencies, Idun comes with packaging recipes for Arch, Fedora and Debian, and frida-core’s Fruity backend is now a thin layer of Gum-dependent injection and host session on top of libidun. The user-visible change is idund . A device only allows one CoreDevice tunnel per host, so on Windows and Linux the tunnel now lives in a per-user daemon that every process on the desktop shares. Linux clients reach it over D-Bus, and Windows clients over loopback through a control file under the user’s local application data. A client that finds no daemon starts one, and the daemon exits once it has been idle for a while. On macOS the system’s own tunnel is used, as before. Frida ships the daemon inside the library when assets are embedded, and existing pairing records are moved over on first use, so pairings survive the upgrade. Leo Conforti noticed that starting the daemon from Node.js stopped libuv from reaping child processes, as GLib’s child watch installed its own SIGCHLD handler, and fixed it from both ends: the daemon is now spawned without a child watch, and our GLib uses pidfd even when the kernel headers it is built against predate it, so spawning any process from Frida no longer disturbs the host’s signal handling. Thanks! Idun also picked up CoreDevice services that a desktop integration needs: pasteboard access, screenshots, display geometry, touch injection, a live H.264 screen feed through a GStreamer element and a Qml module, launching an app with a URL, and Darwin notifications. There’s also early work on talking to Apple’s push and identity services. Expect more on that in a later Idun release. Darwin Memory Tagging is now detected, and the code paths that dereference caller-supplied addresses suspend tag checks while doing so: Memory.scan() , the pointer scanner, NativePointer ’s read and write accessors, and Memory.copy() . Attaching to a process with tagged memory also used to get the target killed, as the resident-notifier scan probed heap pages through untagged addresses. An attach-time crash is gone. Modern dyld runs the image-added notifier under its loaders write lock, where our dladdr() call re-entered dyld and aborted, so the image name is now read from dyld’s published info array, with dyld itself, which keeps out of that array and exposes its path separately, handled as well. Region queries for unmapped addresses now fail instead of describing the next region, as on every other backend, and the 32-bit ARM mapper runtime creates its TLV key before the initializers run, like x86 and arm64 already did. Håvard made Gum behave on arm64e, where code pointers carry signatures: find_module_by_address() , Stalker.invalidate() and hardware breakpoints now strip the address before comparing, which also fixes the exceptor’s lookup of signal() . CI now runs on macOS 27 as arm64e. Windows The module registry hooked LdrLoadDll() and synchronized against the loaded modules whenever it returned, but system DLLs resolve their delay-loaded imports through LdrResolveDelayLoadedAPI() , which maps the DLL without going through it. DLLs pulled in that way, like those loaded inside SHGetKnownFolderPath() , stayed invisible until the next LdrLoadDll() happened to synchronize them in. The registry now subscribes to the loader’s DLL notifications, keeping the hooks as the fallback for Windows versions without them. Thanks to @Albasha0x0 for the report! Shilkey found that gum_memory_allocate_near() could return memory outside the requested range, or memory it had already freed, and that the distance check overflowed for far-apart addresses. Both are fixed. Module enumeration also preserves the loader’s order now, on all backends, which on Windows means Process.mainModule is no longer whichever module happened to hash first. And dbghelp symbols resolved through exports are attributed to the right module instead of the main executable. Linux Thanos Petsas tracked down a race in the unwind broker, which replaced __gxx_personality_v0 before _Unwind_GetIP , so a C++ exception unwinding on another thread in between jumped through NULL . The hooks are now installed in the right order, and come with a test that keeps several threads throwing while the backend is toggled. The broker is also only active while the Interceptor has hooks or a broker is obtained, its deactivation is reentrant, and code allocation failures surface as policy violations instead of crashes. Flechaa fixed the arm64 relocator picking an argument register as scratch. When a function doesn’t read its arguments at entry, such as Android’s libsigchain stubs, the Interceptor’s context and next hop overwrote them, so both onEnter and replacements saw garbage. X0 through X8 are now excluded from entry scratch candidates. MIPS got a thorough pass, starting from a crash when hooking glibc’s free() : the relocator now handles conditional branches, which asserted or, for BEQZ and BNEZ , were copied verbatim and branched relative to the trampoline; the module registry finds r_debug through DT_MIPS_RLD_MAP as MIPS keeps .dynamic read-only; MIPS64 ucontext registers are no longer truncated to 32 bits when resuming from a signal; the exceptor reports stores as writes; and the MIPS writer’s LD , BEQ and 64-bit ADDU encodings are fixed, along with how it stores trampoline addresses. Other fixes Interceptor.obtain() could hand out an instance being torn down, whose unwind backend was already deactivated, so dropping it deactivated the backend twice while another thread was activating it. Showed up as sporadic crashes tearing down V8 isolates. Stalker no longer faults when infecting a thread whose PC sits at the start of a mapping preceded by an inaccessible page, on x86 and arm64, and on arm64 it keeps X16 and X17 intact when unfollowing in the middle of an import thunk. The QuickJS event sink’s drain raced with Stalker.flush() from another thread, removing the same events twice. Thanks @Cassian433 for the fix and @v-p-b for the report! The WebSocket transport read from its connection on the wrong thread when resuming input, which crashed in libsoup, and now caps the total size of fragmented messages like it does individual payloads. Thanks Håvard! Our libffi could crash in ffi_deinit() when three or more code segments were live. Thanks @esauvisky ! Vala’s GIR writer now hoists delegates nested in classes and fixes references to nested namespaces, which the bindings generators rely on. Build Apple OSes can now be targeted from Linux through Limbo , an XNU emulator for Linux userspace: point LIMBO_SYSROOT at a sysroot containing Xcode and configure with an Apple host as usual. Release tarballs honor FRIDA_VERSION instead of reporting 0.0.0, system builds link libstdc++ dynamically, and dpkg-buildflags’ % -containing flags are accepted, all in service of distro packaging. Enjoy! Changelog mapper: Add a cross-platform manual mapper, with PE, Mach-O and ELF implementations behind a GumMapper interface, out-of-process module resolvers, and static TLS support. windows: Inject agents filelessly through the mapper, sharing the agent’s code pages across targets, with dbghelp and symsrv mapped alongside. linux: Inject agents through the mapper instead of dlopen() , sharing read-only pages across targets, without needing memfd. agent: Delegate code memory to the host when the process can’t create code itself, such as under Arbitrary Code Guard. cmodule: Load PE and ELF through the mapper, accepting prebuilt shared libraries on Windows, Linux and Android, and spawning the Windows toolchain without GLib’s helper so static builds can compile externally. windows: Parse modules through the new portable PE parser, enumerating dependencies and delay-loaded imports. Split out Efni and Idun as subprojects, with distro packaging for both. fruity: Share the CoreDevice tunnel through idund on Windows and Linux, embedding it when assets are embedded, and migrate pairing records. idun: Spawn idund without a child watch, and glib: use pidfd even with old kernel headers, so Node.js keeps reaping its children. Thanks @leonitousconforti ! idun: Add pasteboard, screenshot, display, HID, display stream, app launching and notification proxy services, plus a GStreamer element and a Qml module for screen mirroring. darwin: Detect MTE and suspend tag checks in Memory.scan() , the pointer scanner, NativePointer accessors and Memory.copy() , and fix the resident-notifier scan getting MTE targets killed on attach. darwin: Resolve image names without dladdr() , fixing a crash on attach with modern dyld. darwin: Fail region queries for unmapped addresses. macho-mapper: Create the TLV key before initializers on 32-bit ARM, and cloak image copies. arm64e: Strip addresses in find_module_by_address() , Stalker.invalidate() and hardware breakpoints. Thanks @hsorbo ! windows: Track modules through DLL notifications, so delay-loaded DLLs are registered. Thanks for reporting, @Albasha0x0 ! windows: Bound nearby allocation searches, and fix the address spec distance overflow. Thanks @borgCode ! module-registry: Preserve module load order, fixing Process.mainModule on Windows. dbghelp: Look up symbol modules by address. unwind-broker: Fix the activation race on Linux. Thanks @tpetsas ! unwind-broker: Only activate while needed, and make deactivation reentrant. interceptor: Handle code allocation failures, and fix obtain() racing with teardown. relocator-arm64: Don’t clobber arguments with scratch registers. items.summary_html:
This is a big one. The out-of-process mapper that has carried our Darwin injection for years is now cross-platform, so agents are mapped straight into the target on Windows and Linux too, without a file on disk or a dlopen() in the target. Two libraries were split out of frida-core: Efni, the building blocks for protocol-heavy GLib code, and Idun, our Apple device stack, which now shares its tunnel through a daemon on Windows and Linux. Memory Tagging on Darwin is handled, arm64e got a round of fixes from @hsorbo, and there’s a long tail of fixes with contributions from @Cassian433, @tpetsas, @Flechaa, @borgCode, @leonitousconforti and @esauvisky.

A mapper for every platform

Frida’s Darwin backend has long had its own dynamic linker: a mapper that parses a Mach-O, resolves its imports against the target’s libraries, and maps it into the target from the outside, so the target never has to call dlopen(), which a sandbox may not allow. That mapper is now a generic GumMapper interface, with a Mach-O, a PE and an ELF implementation behind it, each built where its format is native.

The mappers never run code in the target. Everything that must execute there is emitted into a small runtime that runs when the consumer calls the constructor. Target memory goes through a GumProcessMemory interface, which the native implementation backs for the local process and for remote ones where the OS allows, and symbols are resolved through a GumModuleResolver, which has out-of-process implementations too. On Windows, exports are parsed from each module’s file on disk, so nothing is read from the target unless the file is missing or doesn’t match the loaded image. On Linux, the target’s libraries are opened through /proc//map_files when permitted, then through /proc//root with an inode check, so a target in a container resolves against its own files, and when neither works the image is copied from the target’s memory.

Both new mappers support static TLS. The PE runtime registers its TLS with the loader, which for x64 and x86 processes on ARM64 means locating the loader’s native TLS routines, and it seeds the /GS security cookie like the loader does. The ELF runtime carries its own __tls_get_addr, plus a TLS descriptor resolver on AArch64, and the ELF mapper covers x86, ARM, AArch64 and MIPS, including the MIPS GOT and RELR-packed relocations.

Windows

Agents are now injected filelessly. Rather than writing a temporary DLL and loading it through LoadLibrary(), the agent is copied once into a pagefile-backed section per architecture, whose handle is duplicated into each target so the code pages are shared across all of them. A small stub runs the mapped images’ constructors, calls the agent’s entrypoint, and runs the destructors when it is not staying resident, after which the mapper unmaps it. The dbghelp and symsrv DLLs are mapped alongside and handed to the agent, so symbolication doesn’t load them through the loader either, and the agent cloaks all of these mappings. Nothing touches the filesystem anymore. The LoadLibrary() path remains for builds with the mapper disabled.

Processes with Arbitrary Code Guard are now within reach too. When the process can’t create code itself, the agent plugs in memory hooks that have the host allocate and protect code pages on its behalf, and the host session keeps serving such agents while they revert their instrumentation on unload.

Linux

Agents are mapped out-of-process instead of having the target dlopen() them. A loader stub in the target loads any of the agent’s dependencies the target lacks, reserves memory, and reports back, after which it is sent a plan to apply: the read-only segments are mapped straight from the agent’s file, so their pages are shared across targets, while the rest is streamed over the control socket. The loader applies protections, runs the constructor, and on unload runs the destructor and unmaps. This is used by the ptrace, procmem and kernel injectors alike.

CModule

CModule’s external toolchain backends are now one, loading the compiled shared library through the mapper. Only the compile step differs: clang on Darwin, gcc on ELF platforms, and on Windows MSVC, or MinGW gcc when cl isn’t on PATH. This means Windows, Linux and Android now accept prebuilt shared libraries, which only Darwin did before, and external compilation on Windows now works in static builds, as the toolchain is spawned without GLib’s spawn helper. The Windows backend also parses modules through the new portable PE parser, so dependencies are enumerated and imports include delay-loaded ones.

Efni and Idun

frida-core has grown a lot of code that isn’t about instrumentation: binary serialization, promises, a GDB remote protocol client, and the whole Apple device protocol stack from usbmuxd to CoreDevice. That code is now two libraries of its own, consumed as subprojects. Efni holds the generic building blocks, and Idun the Apple device stack: discovery over USB and the network, pairing, lockdown and the CoreDevice tunnel, service clients for installation proxy, SpringBoard services, DTX instruments, RemoteXPC and LLDB, and codecs for property lists, keyed archives, OPACK, kcdata, kdebug and kperfdata. Both build as shared libraries against system dependencies, Idun comes with packaging recipes for Arch, Fedora and Debian, and frida-core’s Fruity backend is now a thin layer of Gum-dependent injection and host session on top of libidun.

The user-visible change is idund. A device only allows one CoreDevice tunnel per host, so on Windows and Linux the tunnel now lives in a per-user daemon that every process on the desktop shares. Linux clients reach it over D-Bus, and Windows clients over loopback through a control file under the user’s local application data. A client that finds no daemon starts one, and the daemon exits once it has been idle for a while. On macOS the system’s own tunnel is used, as before. Frida ships the daemon inside the library when assets are embedded, and existing pairing records are moved over on first use, so pairings survive the upgrade. Leo Conforti noticed that starting the daemon from Node.js stopped libuv from reaping child processes, as GLib’s child watch installed its own SIGCHLD handler, and fixed it from both ends: the daemon is now spawned without a child watch, and our GLib uses pidfd even when the kernel headers it is built against predate it, so spawning any process from Frida no longer disturbs the host’s signal handling. Thanks!

Idun also picked up CoreDevice services that a desktop integration needs: pasteboard access, screenshots, display geometry, touch injection, a live H.264 screen feed through a GStreamer element and a Qml module, launching an app with a URL, and Darwin notifications. There’s also early work on talking to Apple’s push and identity services. Expect more on that in a later Idun release.

Darwin

Memory Tagging is now detected, and the code paths that dereference caller-supplied addresses suspend tag checks while doing so: Memory.scan(), the pointer scanner, NativePointer’s read and write accessors, and Memory.copy(). Attaching to a process with tagged memory also used to get the target killed, as the resident-notifier scan probed heap pages through untagged addresses.

An attach-time crash is gone. Modern dyld runs the image-added notifier under its loaders write lock, where our dladdr() call re-entered dyld and aborted, so the image name is now read from dyld’s published info array, with dyld itself, which keeps out of that array and exposes its path separately, handled as well. Region queries for unmapped addresses now fail instead of describing the next region, as on every other backend, and the 32-bit ARM mapper runtime creates its TLV key before the initializers run, like x86 and arm64 already did.

Håvard made Gum behave on arm64e, where code pointers carry signatures: find_module_by_address(), Stalker.invalidate() and hardware breakpoints now strip the address before comparing, which also fixes the exceptor’s lookup of signal(). CI now runs on macOS 27 as arm64e.

Windows

The module registry hooked LdrLoadDll() and synchronized against the loaded modules whenever it returned, but system DLLs resolve their delay-loaded imports through LdrResolveDelayLoadedAPI(), which maps the DLL without going through it. DLLs pulled in that way, like those loaded inside SHGetKnownFolderPath(), stayed invisible until the next LdrLoadDll() happened to synchronize them in. The registry now subscribes to the loader’s DLL notifications, keeping the hooks as the fallback for Windows versions without them. Thanks to @Albasha0x0 for the report!

Shilkey found that gum_memory_allocate_near() could return memory outside the requested range, or memory it had already freed, and that the distance check overflowed for far-apart addresses. Both are fixed. Module enumeration also preserves the loader’s order now, on all backends, which on Windows means Process.mainModule is no longer whichever module happened to hash first. And dbghelp symbols resolved through exports are attributed to the right module instead of the main executable.

Linux

Thanos Petsas tracked down a race in the unwind broker, which replaced __gxx_personality_v0 before _Unwind_GetIP, so a C++ exception unwinding on another thread in between jumped through NULL. The hooks are now installed in the right order, and come with a test that keeps several threads throwing while the backend is toggled. The broker is also only active while the Interceptor has hooks or a broker is obtained, its deactivation is reentrant, and code allocation failures surface as policy violations instead of crashes.

Flechaa fixed the arm64 relocator picking an argument register as scratch. When a function doesn’t read its arguments at entry, such as Android’s libsigchain stubs, the Interceptor’s context and next hop overwrote them, so both onEnter and replacements saw garbage. X0 through X8 are now excluded from entry scratch candidates.

MIPS got a thorough pass, starting from a crash when hooking glibc’s free(): the relocator now handles conditional branches, which asserted or, for BEQZ and BNEZ, were copied verbatim and branched relative to the trampoline; the module registry finds r_debug through DT_MIPS_RLD_MAP as MIPS keeps .dynamic read-only; MIPS64 ucontext registers are no longer truncated to 32 bits when resuming from a signal; the exceptor reports stores as writes; and the MIPS writer’s LD, BEQ and 64-bit ADDU encodings are fixed, along with how it stores trampoline addresses.

Other fixes
  • Interceptor.obtain() could hand out an instance being torn down, whose unwind backend was already deactivated, so dropping it deactivated the backend twice while another thread was activating it. Showed up as sporadic crashes tearing down V8 isolates.
  • Stalker no longer faults when infecting a thread whose PC sits at the start of a mapping preceded by an inaccessible page, on x86 and arm64, and on arm64 it keeps X16 and X17 intact when unfollowing in the middle of an import thunk.
  • The QuickJS event sink’s drain raced with Stalker.flush() from another thread, removing the same events twice. Thanks @Cassian433 for the fix and @v-p-b for the report!
  • The WebSocket transport read from its connection on the wrong thread when resuming input, which crashed in libsoup, and now caps the total size of fragmented messages like it does individual payloads. Thanks Håvard!
  • Our libffi could crash in ffi_deinit() when three or more code segments were live. Thanks @esauvisky!
  • Vala’s GIR writer now hoists delegates nested in classes and fixes references to nested namespaces, which the bindings generators rely on.
Build

Apple OSes can now be targeted from Linux through Limbo, an XNU emulator for Linux userspace: point LIMBO_SYSROOT at a sysroot containing Xcode and configure with an Apple host as usual. Release tarballs honor FRIDA_VERSION instead of reporting 0.0.0, system builds link libstdc++ dynamically, and dpkg-buildflags’ %-containing flags are accepted, all in service of distro packaging.

Enjoy!

Changelog
  • mapper: Add a cross-platform manual mapper, with PE, Mach-O and ELF implementations behind a GumMapper interface, out-of-process module resolvers, and static TLS support.
  • windows: Inject agents filelessly through the mapper, sharing the agent’s code pages across targets, with dbghelp and symsrv mapped alongside.
  • linux: Inject agents through the mapper instead of dlopen(), sharing read-only pages across targets, without needing memfd.
  • agent: Delegate code memory to the host when the process can’t create code itself, such as under Arbitrary Code Guard.
  • cmodule: Load PE and ELF through the mapper, accepting prebuilt shared libraries on Windows, Linux and Android, and spawning the Windows toolchain without GLib’s helper so static builds can compile externally.
  • windows: Parse modules through the new portable PE parser, enumerating dependencies and delay-loaded imports.
  • Split out Efni and Idun as subprojects, with distro packaging for both.
  • fruity: Share the CoreDevice tunnel through idund on Windows and Linux, embedding it when assets are embedded, and migrate pairing records.
  • idun: Spawn idund without a child watch, and glib: use pidfd even with old kernel headers, so Node.js keeps reaping its children. Thanks @leonitousconforti!
  • idun: Add pasteboard, screenshot, display, HID, display stream, app launching and notification proxy services, plus a GStreamer element and a Qml module for screen mirroring.
  • darwin: Detect MTE and suspend tag checks in Memory.scan(), the pointer scanner, NativePointer accessors and Memory.copy(), and fix the resident-notifier scan getting MTE targets killed on attach.
  • darwin: Resolve image names without dladdr(), fixing a crash on attach with modern dyld.
  • darwin: Fail region queries for unmapped addresses.
  • macho-mapper: Create the TLV key before initializers on 32-bit ARM, and cloak image copies.
  • arm64e: Strip addresses in find_module_by_address(), Stalker.invalidate() and hardware breakpoints. Thanks @hsorbo!
  • windows: Track modules through DLL notifications, so delay-loaded DLLs are registered. Thanks for reporting, @Albasha0x0!
  • windows: Bound nearby allocation searches, and fix the address spec distance overflow. Thanks @borgCode!
  • module-registry: Preserve module load order, fixing Process.mainModule on Windows.
  • dbghelp: Look up symbol modules by address.
  • unwind-broker: Fix the activation race on Linux. Thanks @tpetsas!
  • unwind-broker: Only activate while needed, and make deactivation reentrant.
  • interceptor: Handle code allocation failures, and fix obtain() racing with teardown.
  • relocator-arm64: Don’t clobber arguments with scratch registers. Thanks @Flechaa!
  • stalker: Avoid reading before PC on infect, on x86 and arm64, and preserve IP registers on unfollow on arm64.
  • mips: Relocate conditional branches, find r_debug via the RLD map, keep ucontext registers full width, infer memory operations in the exceptor, parse MIPS64 relocation info, and fix the writer’s LD, BEQ and 64-bit ADDU encodings.
  • gumjs: Fix the event sink drain racing with Stalker.flush(). Thanks @Cassian433 and @v-p-b!
  • socket: Resume WebSocket input on its own thread, and cap the total message size. Thanks @hsorbo!
  • libffi: Fix a use-after-free in ffi_deinit(). Thanks @esauvisky!
  • vala: Fix GIR output for nested delegates and namespaces.
  • releng: Support building for Apple OSes on Linux through Limbo.
  • releng: Honor FRIDA_VERSION, link libstdc++ dynamically in system builds, allow % in flags, accept POSIX-style prefix paths, and reject a pkg-config that ignores PKG_CONFIG_LIBDIR.

items.title: Hackers Exploit Passwordless Telnet to Infect Linux Devices With New Kairos DDoS Botnet
items.summary: A new botnet called Kairos is spreading to Linux devices through a very old mistake: a Telnet service that accepts the root user with no password. Once inside, the attackers install a small Go-based program that turns the device into a node for DDoS operations. The campaign shows that basic security gaps still give attackers an easy path in. Kairos does not use a complex exploit or a zero-day flaw. The attackers connect to exposed Telnet services and log in as root with an empty password. Weak remote access has fueled many botnets before, including a VOIP-based botnet attacking routers that also relied on default Telnet logins. Analysts at Nozomi Networks identified the malware after their honeypots recorded three different IP addresses delivering Kairos samples. The Nozomi Networks Labs report describes it as a previously undocumented DDoS bot for Linux. The three samples were the same program. They differed only in the hard-coded command-and-control (C2) address and the Go compiler patch level, versions 1.27.0 and 1.27.1. This suggests the operator recompiles one codebase for each C2 server. Hackers Exploit Passwordless Telnet Every observed infection began the same way. The attacker guessed the default Telnet login, user root with an empty password. The operator then ran a short set of shell commands. First, uname -m checked the device’s processor type, and the payload requested later, x86_64 , matched it. This hints that the operator keeps a separate build for each architecture. Next, the commands moved into the /tmp folder, removed leftovers from earlier attempts, and downloaded the malware. Dropper commands used to download and execute the x86_64 payload (Source – Nozomi Networks) The dropper tries several download methods in turn: wget, curl, BusyBox wget, and finally TFTP. Each downloaded copy gets full permissions with chmod 777 and runs in the background. The BusyBox and TFTP fallbacks keep the loader working on small embedded systems that lack common tools. In the sample chain, the server at 172[.]86[.]85[.]39 hosted the payload on TCP port 8080 and also served as the C2 on port 9999. Once running, the bot connects to its single hard-coded IP address and sends a plain-text beacon, REGISTER linux amd64 . It then sends a blank line every two seconds to keep the session alive. If the link drops, it tries again every five seconds with no limit. The C2 can send only three commands: hold , which starts a flood, !ka , which stops all attacks and pauses the bot, and !ku , which lets it accept attacks again. Similar Telnet-driven threats include the Tengu Mirai botnet that reboots IoT devices when someone tries to remove it. How Kairos Floods Targets and How to Defend Against It Kairos does not send huge amounts of traffic. Instead, it opens hundreds or thousands of real TCP connections to a victim and keeps them open. The bot starts 128 workers per CPU core, with a minimum of 256, so a 16-core device opens 2,048 connections per attack. Each worker finishes a normal handshake, then sends one space character every five seconds to hold the socket open. If the target refuses the connection, the worker retries every 100 milliseconds, which creates a fast “connect storm.” The victim’s service slowly runs out of room and stops accepting real users. The bot is simple and has weaknesses. It has no persistence, no self-spreading, no command execution, and no anti-analysis features. Kairos bot registers to C2 (Source – Nozomi Networks) It tries to hide by renaming itself [kworker/0:1] to look like a Linux kernel thread. However, tools like ps and the /proc folder still show the real name. Since the bot completes real handshakes, its source IP is also visible to the victim. This is unlike KATARU IoT malware strain , which adds privilege escalation and encrypted C2 traffic. Defenders should disable Telnet, replace default or empty passwords, and block outbound traffic to the known C2 addresses on ports 9999 and 8080. Since the C2 address changes with each build, Nozomi advises relying on code-based detection. Teams can add an IDS rule for the plain-text REGISTER linux beacon and deploy the published YARA rule. They should also alert on any “kernel worker” process holding many outbound connections. Exposed services remain a common entry point, as seen when a cPanel authentication bypass flaw was used to drop Mirai malware. items.title: Photo ID, bank checks, face scan? The UK’s age-check options
items.summary: As preparation for the UK’s planned social media ban, Ofcom has set out four ways social media platforms could check whether users are aged 16 or over. The government and Parliament will decide how the ban works in practice. Ofcom is the regulator for the communications services in the UK. The BBC reports that Ofcom identified four ways to check someone’s age that it considers “highly effective.” Here’s what those checks would involve: Photo ID matching : Comparing a live image of you with the photo on an identity document, such as your passport, and checking the age information on that document. Bank-based checks: Using age information your bank already holds about you, with your consent. Facial age estimation : Using technology to estimate your age from your face. Ofcom says this technology has improved recently. Digital ID services : Using a digital identity service to prove your age, rather than presenting a physical document. Let’s think through what those checks could mean. Challenges The challenge isn’t simply checking someone’s age. It’s doing so without turning everyday internet use into an identity check. Photo ID matching brings highly sensitive documents and facial images into the process, which raises questions about how that information is handled and protected. The risks aren’t hypothetical: as I reported last year , a breach at a third-party support provider for Discord exposed government ID images belonging to around 70,000 users. Banking-based checks can be more privacy-preserving if they return only confirmation that someone meets the age threshold, rather than exposing financial information. But the important questions are what information each party receives, what gets retained, and whether the check can be linked to someone’s activity. Facial age estimation can avoid uploading an identity document, but it still processes a sensitive image and makes an imperfect prediction. Ofcom acknowledges that some technologies can be wrong by a few years around age 16, so people near the threshold may face an additional verification check. I would expect these checks to stop some underage access but not eliminate it. Previous restrictions have been followed by workarounds, including increased VPN use , borrowed credentials, and migration to services outside the restrictions. The danger is treating a successful age gate as proof that children are now safe, when it might push them into less regulated spaces. The effectiveness depends on how the checks are implemented. A VPN may help someone avoid a check triggered by their apparent location; it won’t, by itself, bypass an identity or facial check that is still required. Similarly, Ofcom says matching a live image to an ID is intended to make it harder to borrow someone else’s document. We shouldn’t assume every workaround defeats every method. But Ofcom accepts that some motivated children will get through. The meaningful test is how much harm these measures prevent, weighed against the privacy risks and barriers they introduce— not whether every user has completed a check. My personal preference is double-blind verification: a provider confirms that you meet the age requirement without learning which service you’re accessing, while the service receives proof of age without learning your identity. Proving you’re old enough shouldn’t mean revealing who you are. Scammers don’t need to hack you. They just need you to click once. items.summary_html:
As preparation for the UK’s planned social media ban, Ofcom has set out four ways social media platforms could check whether users are aged 16 or over. The government and Parliament will decide how the ban works in practice.

Ofcom is the regulator for the communications services in the UK. The BBC reports that Ofcom identified four ways to check someone’s age that it considers “highly effective.”

Here’s what those checks would involve:

  • Photo ID matching: Comparing a live image of you with the photo on an identity document, such as your passport, and checking the age information on that document.
  • Bank-based checks: Using age information your bank already holds about you, with your consent.
  • Facial age estimation: Using technology to estimate your age from your face. Ofcom says this technology has improved recently.
  • Digital ID services: Using a digital identity service to prove your age, rather than presenting a physical document.

Let’s think through what those checks could mean.

Challenges

The challenge isn’t simply checking someone’s age. It’s doing so without turning everyday internet use into an identity check.

Photo ID matching brings highly sensitive documents and facial images into the process, which raises questions about how that information is handled and protected. The risks aren’t hypothetical: as I reported last year, a breach at a third-party support provider for Discord exposed government ID images belonging to around 70,000 users.

Banking-based checks can be more privacy-preserving if they return only confirmation that someone meets the age threshold, rather than exposing financial information. But the important questions are what information each party receives, what gets retained, and whether the check can be linked to someone’s activity.

Facial age estimation can avoid uploading an identity document, but it still processes a sensitive image and makes an imperfect prediction. Ofcom acknowledges that some technologies can be wrong by a few years around age 16, so people near the threshold may face an additional verification check.

I would expect these checks to stop some underage access but not eliminate it.

Previous restrictions have been followed by workarounds, including increased VPN use, borrowed credentials, and migration to services outside the restrictions. The danger is treating a successful age gate as proof that children are now safe, when it might push them into less regulated spaces.

The effectiveness depends on how the checks are implemented. A VPN may help someone avoid a check triggered by their apparent location; it won’t, by itself, bypass an identity or facial check that is still required.

Similarly, Ofcom says matching a live image to an ID is intended to make it harder to borrow someone else’s document. We shouldn’t assume every workaround defeats every method. But Ofcom accepts that some motivated children will get through. The meaningful test is how much harm these measures prevent, weighed against the privacy risks and barriers they introduce— not whether every user has completed a check.

My personal preference is double-blind verification: a provider confirms that you meet the age requirement without learning which service you’re accessing, while the service receives proof of age without learning your identity. Proving you’re old enough shouldn’t mean revealing who you are.

Scammers don’t need to hack you. They just need you to click once.

items.title: Hackers Use Zero-Click Coruna and DarkSword Exploits to Steal Sensitive Data From iPhones
items.summary: Hackers are using two powerful iPhone exploit kits, Coruna and DarkSword, to break into phones and steal private data. The victim only has to open a web page. There is no app to install and no prompt to accept. The scale is larger than many people expected. Researchers found 608 domains delivering Coruna-family code. These sites choose an exploit chain based on the iOS version on the phone. iPhones on iOS 17.2.1 or older get the original Coruna kit. Newer iPhones on iOS 18 get a chain built from DarkSword. Earlier reporting on the Coruna and DarkSword kits already showed how outdated iPhones are at risk from a single website visit. Analysts at Zimperium’s zLabs team identified and documented this activity in a detailed technical report published on October 29, 2026. They recovered both the browser code and the native payloads. They also matched 93 of the domains to 21 tracking servers. Hackers Use Zero-Click Coruna and DarkSword Exploits The infection starts with a page that looks normal. Zimperium found dating sites built for users in Brazil, Nigeria, and Indonesia. It also found AI-companion chat sites, crypto promotions, and streaming pages. While the visitor sees the decoy, a hidden frame loads the exploit in the background. Some pages tell TikTok users to tap “Open in browser” so the link opens in Safari, which is the browser the exploit needs. Nothing looks wrong on screen, so advice like “watch for strange behavior” does not help here. AI-companion chat and legitimate casino content (Source – Zimperium) Next, a script checks the iOS version and picks the right path. The Coruna chain uses CVE-2022-48503, a WebAssembly flaw in Safari, to read and write browser memory. It then bypasses pointer authentication, an Apple protection that signs code addresses so tampering is caught. After it escapes the browser, the native modules read and write kernel memory and change code-signing settings. They talk to their servers over encrypted traffic with certificate checks turned off. They also delete crash logs and Safari website data to cover their tracks. The DarkSword chain works in steps. Browser code runs first. It then breaks out through the GPU process and moves into mediaplaybackd, a system media service. In Zimperium’s test on an iPhone running iOS 18.6.2, the phone contacted the command server 144 times and pulled seven extra modules. One module was built to read Telegram’s local storage. The phone then sent out its Apple Notes database and a list of 214 installed apps. The same kit has also appeared across DarkSword’s growing web infrastructure that operators replace within days, as DarkSword’s growing web infrastructure reporting from Censys showed. Supply Chain Delivery and Ways to Stay Safe Not every infection starts with a bad link. SafeDep found matching Coruna code inside the backdoored art-template npm package that many developers had pulled into their sites. Any site using the bad versions served the exploit to its own visitors, so no suspicious lure domain was needed. Domain blocklists miss this route completely. Zimperium also spotted a fake jquery.min.js file loaded from a look-alike Google domain on a comic site, which then started the Coruna chain. Who is behind it remains unclear. Coruna was first built by a nation-state actor for targeted work, but its leak spread the toolkit to many groups. Delivery and tracking in the recovered infrastructure (Source – Zimperium) Some recovered code has Chinese-language comments. Zimperium says that only describes how the code was written, not who deployed it, so it ties its conclusions to the code and infrastructure only. The best defense is patching, because every CVE in these chains is already fixed. Apple even pushed an expanded iOS 18.7.7 update to more devices to block DarkSword, so users should check Settings for the newest version offered for their phone. People at higher risk, such as journalists, activists, and executives, should turn on Lockdown Mode. Everyone should treat unexpected “Open in Safari” prompts as a stop sign. Security teams should require patched iOS builds on all devices, including personal ones used for work. Mobile threat defense tools can flag odd crashes, unexpected restarts, and disabled code signing. Teams should also keep diagnostic logs for high-risk users, because the malware deletes local traces. Site owners should audit third-party scripts and enforce a strict Content Security Policy. For now, those figures should be treated as developing estimates rather than a final accounting of recovered funds or the exchange’s ultimate losses. Binance.com users ( Binance.US was not affected) should check their accounts, avoid follow-up scams, and respond quickly if they spot signs of a separate compromise. Go directly to official updates. Open the Binance app or navigate to its support site yourself. Avoid logging in through unexpected messages claiming that you must urgently verify your account or claim compensation. Binance has asked customers to rely on official channels. Review your account and report anything unexpected. Check your transaction history and account security settings. If you find activity you do not recognize, contact Binance through its official support service . Binance’s support center includes options to disable an account and reset a password or two-factor authentication. Never give anyone your authentication codes. Treat requests for login codes as a warning sign, even if the person claims to be helping with the incident. Be wary of anyone promising to recover cryptocurrency. The FBI published a warning in 2023 that fake recovery services target people who have already lost cryptocurrency. Preserve evidence if you lose money to a related scam. items.title: Hackers Weaponize OpenAI API in NIK C2 Framework for Credential Theft and Remote System Control
items.summary: A new malware framework called NIK C2 is turning the OpenAI API into a tool for cybercriminals. Its Windows implant can dump passwords, record every keystroke, take hidden control of a desktop, and send the stolen data to an AI model for analysis, all inside the same session. The tool is a Go-based, 64-bit Windows remote access program. It talks to its server over TLS-secured WebSockets on port 443. It also uses an HTTP backup channel that checks in about every 250 milliseconds. All traffic is locked with AES-256-GCM encryption, and the implant rotates between three server tiers so a single takedown does not cut it off. Researchers at Cisco Talos identified the malware and published their findings on October 29, 2026. Talos found a live server in the wild and said, with moderate confidence, that NIK C2 is a working framework and not a proof of concept. The samples point to at least three versions, which suggests a skilled team that keeps adding features. Abusing OpenAI is not new. The earlier OpenAI Assistants API backdoor called SesameOp used the service to hide its command traffic. NIK C2 goes a step further by using the model as a built-in analyst. Hackers Weaponize OpenAI API The AI feature runs through a command named ai_generate . The operator sends a prompt, an API key, and a model name. The implant builds a request and sends it to the OpenAI Chat Completions endpoint from the victim’s computer. It waits up to 60 seconds, reads the answer, and returns the text to the attacker’s panel along with token-usage counts. If no model is named, it defaults to gpt-4. The most worrying detail is the key fallback. If the attacker leaves out an API key, the implant reads the OPENAI_API_KEY variable on the victim’s machine. NIK C2 implant’s operational architecture (Source – Cisco Talos) OpenAI then bills the victim, and the logs show the victim’s key, so nothing points back to the attacker. Talos calls this a deliberate design choice. This kind of AI-enabled malware is getting more attention from defenders. Talos has also released the open-source CAIRN toolkit , which hunts for AI endpoints, prompt templates, and API-key patterns inside suspicious files. Because normal apps use the same AI services, blocking those domains alone is not practical. Credential Theft, Remote Control, and Screen-Locking Ransomware The implant supports more than 52 commands. For theft, it copies browser databases from Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, and Firefox. It also grabs saved Wi-Fi passwords, Discord tokens, and desktop crypto wallets such as Exodus, Electrum, and Bitcoin Core. It also targets wallet extensions such as MetaMask, Coinbase Wallet, and Phantom. Two search patterns hunt the whole disk for files with names like “seed,” “mnemonic,” “private,” or “secret.” A keylogger streams each keystroke live to the attacker. Hidden VNC gives full desktop control that the victim cannot see. The implant also offers proxy tunnels and RDP session control to move deeper into a network. To stay hidden, the implant renames itself to names like svchost.exe and csrss.exe and patches AMSI so PowerShell scripts are not scanned. It also skips the UAC prompt with a fodhelper trick. It marks itself as a critical process, so ending it in Task Manager triggers a Blue Screen of Death. The ransomware module is simple but fast. It backs up the Master Boot Record, writes an HTML lock screen with the attacker’s Bitcoin or USDT wallet details, and opens it through the Windows mshta.exe utility , a trusted tool that attackers often misuse. A registry Run key named “SystemLock” brings the screen back after every restart. It does not encrypt files, so it leaves little forensic evidence. A separate bootkit-prep feature checks UEFI, BIOS, and Secure Boot status.
