A new malware framework called NIK C2 is turning the OpenAI API into a tool for cybercriminals. Its Windows implant can dump passwords, record every keystroke, take hidden control of a desktop, and send the stolen data to an AI model for analysis, all inside the same session.

The tool is a Go-based, 64-bit Windows remote access program. It talks to its server over TLS-secured WebSockets on port 443.

It also uses an HTTP backup channel that checks in about every 250 milliseconds. All traffic is locked with AES-256-GCM encryption, and the implant rotates between three server tiers so a single takedown does not cut it off.

Researchers at Cisco Talos identified the malware and published their findings on October 29, 2026. Talos found a live server in the wild and said, with moderate confidence, that NIK C2 is a working framework and not a proof of concept.

The samples point to at least three versions, which suggests a skilled team that keeps adding features. Abusing OpenAI is not new.

The earlier OpenAI Assistants API backdoor called SesameOp used the service to hide its command traffic. NIK C2 goes a step further by using the model as a built-in analyst.

Hackers Weaponize OpenAI API

The AI feature runs through a command named ai_generate. The operator sends a prompt, an API key, and a model name.

The implant builds a request and sends it to the OpenAI Chat Completions endpoint from the victim’s computer. It waits up to 60 seconds, reads the answer, and returns the text to the attacker’s panel along with token-usage counts. If no model is named, it defaults to gpt-4.

The most worrying detail is the key fallback. If the attacker leaves out an API key, the implant reads the OPENAI_API_KEY variable on the victim’s machine.

NIK C2 implant’s operational architecture (Source – Cisco Talos)

OpenAI then bills the victim, and the logs show the victim’s key, so nothing points back to the attacker. Talos calls this a deliberate design choice. This kind of AI-enabled malware is getting more attention from defenders.

Talos has also released the open-source CAIRN toolkit, which hunts for AI endpoints, prompt templates, and API-key patterns inside suspicious files. Because normal apps use the same AI services, blocking those domains alone is not practical.

Credential Theft, Remote Control, and Screen-Locking Ransomware

The implant supports more than 52 commands. For theft, it copies browser databases from Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, and Firefox. It also grabs saved Wi-Fi passwords, Discord tokens, and desktop crypto wallets such as Exodus, Electrum, and Bitcoin Core.

It also targets wallet extensions such as MetaMask, Coinbase Wallet, and Phantom. Two search patterns hunt the whole disk for files with names like “seed,” “mnemonic,” “private,” or “secret.”

A keylogger streams each keystroke live to the attacker. Hidden VNC gives full desktop control that the victim cannot see. The implant also offers proxy tunnels and RDP session control to move deeper into a network.

To stay hidden, the implant renames itself to names like svchost.exe and csrss.exe and patches AMSI so PowerShell scripts are not scanned.

It also skips the UAC prompt with a fodhelper trick. It marks itself as a critical process, so ending it in Task Manager triggers a Blue Screen of Death.

The ransomware module is simple but fast. It backs up the Master Boot Record, writes an HTML lock screen with the attacker’s Bitcoin or USDT wallet details, and opens it through the Windows mshta.exe utility, a trusted tool that attackers often misuse.

A registry Run key named “SystemLock” brings the screen back after every restart. It does not encrypt files, so it leaves little forensic evidence. A separate bootkit-prep feature checks UEFI, BIOS, and Secure Boot status.

The data could enable targeted scams, harassment, stalking, or physical threats. DHS employees should follow agency guidance, verify unexpected contact, and report threats to security. A group of hackers calling themselves the Department of Peace says it stole and published the personal details of more than 41,000 people working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The department says it is aware of a potential breach. The group, which also claimed the theft of contract documents from the DHS in March, gave the data to Swiss hacktivist maia arson crimew, who published it in collaboration with the transparency collective DDoSecrets. The latter also published the BlueLeaks data dump that listed law enforcement officers’ details in 2020. The aim of publishing the data was to replace “anonymity with accountability,” DDoSecrets co-founder Emma Best said in an online statement. According to TechCrunch , timestamps on the records suggest the data was taken around mid-August. The group said it had launched the attack in response to a July 17 statement by DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, in which he promised to “turn up the heat” with traffic stops. What was stolen? The data files published online, which the publishers have called “Icepick,” span staff at nearly 7,000 offices. They include the names, work email addresses, phone numbers, office addresses, job titles and membership in internal DHS groups. The employees impacted include almost 6,600 Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) employees. ICE is the DHS unit responsible for immigration enforcement and deportations in the US. The dataset also carried details of over 21,000 Customs and Border Protection (CBP) employees, along with information on people who work at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). The data dump revealed less information than the ShinyHunters’ FBI data heist in September, which reportedly contained Social Security numbers, emergency contacts, medical records and home addresses. Nevertheless, this is more than just a phone book of folks in the DHS. For one thing, it doesn’t take much to cross-reference data. Reuters matched six DHS employees’ data to credit bureau records and breach data from a dark web intelligence platform. Online activists regularly use open-source intelligence (OSINT) to “doxx” people from very few clues, meaning that even a leak of basic identity information can put someone in danger. In fact, the creators of a separate searchable version say they added information through automated and manual research. So some details shown in that version may not have come from the data stolen from DHS. Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know. SEE PLANS The data in this case also included membership of groups within Active Directory, a Microsoft tool that contains identity information about computer users. Active Directory controls who can access different internal tools, services, and third-party software within an organization. The files listed over 200 CBP users in a group that could access the facial recognition tool Mobile Fortify. Other groups reference a service called Penlink, which the company claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. According to the Guardian , job titles in the data dump show which agents were assigned to sensitive jobs such as special operations, surveillance, and undercover work. How did they get the data? The Department of Peace said that it got to the information via a single sign-on (SSO) service provided by identity company Okta. SSO is a prized target for hackers because a single authentication can get a user into many different workplace services and applications. Okta says it has no evidence its data or systems were compromised, but that doesn’t rule out someone abusing a DHS account with stolen credentials. DHS told reporters it was aware of a potential breach. One DHS employee whose data showed up in the breach told Reuters they hadn’t heard anything about it. What DHS employees can do now The leaked records include work contact details and internal group memberships. This information could help attackers create convincing messages or calls, and may expose some employees to unwanted attention or threats. DHS has warned about the risk of harassment, stalking, and physical harm. It is not yet clear whether the leak has led to specific threats or affected any operations. If you work for DHS: Follow security advice and instructions from the DHS. Treat unexpected calls, emails, and texts about your role or colleagues with caution. Verify them through a contact method you already trust, and never share passwords or MFA codes. Change any personal passwords you’ve reused for work, and turn on MFA where available. Follow your agency’s process for work accounts. Report suspicious contact or threats to your agency’s security team. If you believe there’s an immediate danger, contact law enforcement. Do you think your information might have been leaked in a data breach? Check out the Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection service. Someone’s got their eye on your personal information. Make sure it’s us. PROTECT YOUR IDENTITY

items.title: Pre-SIEM Detection for MSSPs
items.summary: tl;dr Prime Detect runs detection rules on your clients’ event streams before data reaches the SIEM. It applies Sigma rules to events in transit, tags each match with a severity and a MITRE ATT&CK technique, and links related matches into attack chains. In client testing, about 7% of telemetry was tagged. MSSPs use Prime Detect to give every client the same 20,000+ detections regardless of which SIEM that client runs, to send less data into SIEMs they pay to operate, and to keep each client’s data inside its own pipeline. It works alongside the SIEMs you already run. It does not replace them. Contact Sales Why MSSPs are moving detection ahead of the SIEM An MSSP’s detection coverage is usually set by whatever each client’s SIEM can hold. That creates three problems that grow with every client you add. Uneven coverage. Clients run different SIEMs with different rule limits. The same threat can be caught for one client and missed for another, depending on the platform underneath. Ingest cost. Where you operate the SIEM, every event ingested is a cost against your margin, whether it carries a threat signal or not. Engineering load. Your detection engineers spend their time porting and tuning the same rules across platforms instead of building the detections clients actually pay for. Prime Detect moves detection upstream. Rules run on events as they stream through the pipeline, before any SIEM ingests them. Coverage depends on the compute you assign, not on each client’s SIEM. You then decide, per client, what reaches the SIEM. What Prime Detect does Detection in the stream Applies Sigma rules to events in transit, before SIEM ingest Runs 20,000+ detection rules plus your own custom detections, with no fixed rule ceiling Tags every match with a severity and a MITRE ATT&CK technique Links related matches into attack chains, so analysts see a sequence of activity instead of isolated alerts Tagged telemetry you can route Tags about 7% of telemetry, based on client testing Sends tagged events to the SIEM and the rest to warm or cold storage, by your rules Produces structured, ATT&CK-labeled events that AI triage and SOAR tools can use directly Deployment and control Runs on Kafka and Kubernetes you or your clients operate Keeps data inside the pipeline, with no outbound connection required Deploys air-gapped or in the cloud Available open source or under an Enterprise license How it fits with the SIEMs you already run Prime Detect sits between the event pipeline and the SIEM. Nothing in the SIEM has to change, so it works across a mixed client base. MSSPs typically deploy it in one of two ways: Shared, multi-tenant: one Prime Detect deployment in your environment, with detections and routing set per tenant. Per client: a deployment inside the client’s own infrastructure, for clients with strict data residency or air-gap requirements. Rollout follows the same three steps either way: Forward everything to the SIEM as today, with Detect tags added to matched events. Add a SIEM index or dashboard that raises Detect-tagged events as high-priority alerts. Once tuned, route untagged events to warm or cold storage to cut ingest. What Prime Detect does not do It does not replace the SIEM for centralized logging, search, investigation, or retention. It does not decide whether an incident is significant or reportable. Your incident process makes that call. It does not make data transfer decisions for you. Where data goes, and under which agreement, stays with your firm and your clients. NIS2, DORA, HIPAA, and GDPR: where Prime Detect fits MSSPs carry their own obligations and inherit their clients’. NIS2 defines managed security service providers in Article 6(40) and lists them in Annex I, so many MSSPs are covered entities in their own right. With direct ingestion, logs go into the SIEM and detection rules run there. Pre-SIEM detection runs the rules on events in transit, before the SIEM ingests them. MSSPs can run a shared multi-tenant deployment with detections and routing set per tenant. They can also deploy inside a client’s own infrastructure when data residency or an air gap requires it. Under Article 23, they must give an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of a significant incident and a notification within 72 hours. Under DORA Article 28, financial clients remain fully responsible for their own compliance when they use an MSSP, so they will expect evidence of what you detect. What does HIPAA require for audit trails and incident reporting? The HIPAA Security Rule, 45 CFR 164.312(b), requires mechanisms that record and examine activity in systems containing electronic protected health information. Does pre-SIEM detection create GDPR data transfer issues? Not by itself. Prime Detect runs inside your or your client’s pipeline and needs no outbound connection, so detection adds no transfer of personal data. Where the rest of the data goes, and under which Chapter V mechanism, remains your firm’s decision. Will Prime Detect commoditize our detection engineering service? It shifts where your engineers spend their time. Baseline coverage comes from the 20,000+ rule library, which SOC Prime keeps adding to. Your team can focus on client-specific detections, threat hunting, and tuning, which is the work clients see as your differentiator.

Under Article 23, they must give an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of a significant incident and a notification within 72 hours. Under DORA Article 28, financial clients remain fully responsible for their own compliance when they use an MSSP, so they will expect evidence of what you detect.

What does HIPAA require for audit trails and incident reporting?

The HIPAA Security Rule, 45 CFR 164.312(b), requires mechanisms that record and examine activity in systems containing electronic protected health information. Under 164.308(b) and 164.314(a), a business associate must report security incidents it becomes aware of to the covered entity, including breaches of unsecured protected health information.

Does pre-SIEM detection create GDPR data transfer issues?

Not by itself. Prime Detect runs inside your or your client’s pipeline and needs no outbound connection, so detection adds no transfer of personal data. Where the rest of the data goes, and under which Chapter V mechanism, remains your firm’s decision.

Will Prime Detect commoditize our detection engineering service?

It shifts where your engineers spend their time. Baseline coverage comes from the 20,000+ rule library, which SOC Prime keeps adding to. Your team can focus on client-specific detections, threat hunting, and tuning, which is the work clients see as your differentiator.

items.title: Researchers Hacked Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Codex, VS Code, and Claude Desktop Embedded Browsers
items.summary: Security flaws in the embedded browsers of Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Codex, VS Code, and Claude Desktop could enable code execution, file theft, and address-bar spoofing on developer machines . The findings published on October 29 show how browser features built into AI assistants can break security boundaries when given extra access to their host apps. The researchers named the attack class EMBRACE, short for an embedded browser trusted like a real one. These are separate flaws sharing one design problem. Features meant to help assistants preview projects, read pages, and track tabs gave untrusted content powers it should not have. According to Forever report, Cursor exposed a window.cursorBrowser.send() bridge that allowed any loaded page to send content into the agent’s instruction box without a user gesture. Embedded Browser Flaws in Popular AI Coding Tools Exploited Attackers could abuse its element-selected channel to hide instructions inside HTML attributes. The visible item looked harmless, while the agent received command fragments and instructions to join them into an npm installation command. A single Enter keypress could approve execution. When Cursor’s sandbox blocked installation, the agent independently retried outside it, allowing the package’s preinstall script to launch Calculator. Proof of execution: the package’s `preinstall` launched Calculator from a cold start in an empty workspace (source: Forever security ) Success depended on the model and was not guaranteed. The finding adds another browser entry point to risks covered in earlier Cursor prompt injection research . GitHub Copilot’s browser preview accepted address updates supplied by the page itself. It checked the address format but did not confirm that the reported location matched the page actually loaded. Researchers made an attacker-controlled page display github.com/login in the preview’s address bar. The agent also received that false location, although the page remained on the attacker’s server. A fake login form could therefore appear beneath a trusted address and mislead both the user and the assistant. Claude Desktop and VS Code restricted file access on the main page but failed to apply the same checks inside web workers, which run scripts in the background. A malicious local preview could start a worker and read files outside its project folder. Codex needed no worker bypass. Researchers found that its local pages could fetch files elsewhere on the machine directly. On macOS, the team usedDS_Store metadata to discover filenames and expand the search across folders. Their test collected SSH keys, .env files, npm tokens, and private documents. The demonstration sent data to a local receiver. An attacker could instead use a remote server. Delivery required opening a malicious local page, potentially through a link generated by the assistant itself. These findings sit alongside earlier Claude sandbox escape coverage . Forever Security says Cursor patched its flaw on October 1. GitHub independently fixed the spoofing issue in Copilot 1.1.29 on October 13, after researchers confirmed it in version 1.1.27. At publication, Codex and VS Code remained unpatched. Microsoft rejected the report on Workspace Trust, while OpenAI did not respond. Anthropic accepted its issue after an initial rejection, but the report gives no clear patch status. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Palo Alto Confirms Active PHP2Shell Exploitation Targeting Exposed PAN-OS Management Interfaces
items.summary: Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that attackers are actively exploiting PHP2Shell vulnerabilities against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet. In its October 29, 2026, update, Unit 42 said it independently verified attacker tools used to combine the PHP flaws with a Linux kernel vulnerability and gain root access. The vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, each carry a critical CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. They can allow remote code execution without a login. Palo Alto said roughly 0.02% of its global installed base had public management interfaces configured and was impacted. Its teams have contacted those customers individually, according to the Unit 42 threat brief . The confirmation updates the earlier picture covered in Cyber Security News’ report on PHP vulnerabilities affecting PAN-OS , when the vendor had not reported malicious exploitation against its products. PHP2Shell Enables Remote Code Execution Both flaws involve unsafe memory handling when PHP stops processing a request after an error. CVE-2026-109618 affects out-of-memory handling through longjmp() , a function that jumps out of the current operation. That sudden exit can leave request data partly initialized. Cleanup routines may then read or act on that invalid data, creating a path to code execution. CVE-2026-109619 leaves shared internal state pointing to memory that PHP has already freed. A later request handled by the same worker can reach those stale references before normal setup resets them. Attackers can use this condition to make the process execute their code. The PHP Group’s security advisory identifies PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed deployments as exposed. Fixed releases are PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. Unit 42 counted more than 22.6 million exposed instances potentially vulnerable worldwide. That figure describes possible PHP exposure, not confirmed breaches or affected Palo Alto firewalls. Dream Research reported finding campaign artifacts showing 25 compromised PAN-OS firewall and management servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. The count included three systems in a US government-affiliated environment. The attacker used a custom PHP2Shell implementation aimed at the PAN-OS management web server. Crafted upload requests created memory pressure, leaked an address, and manipulated memory structures to execute commands as the restricted nobody user. A separate Linux kernel flaw, Fragnesia, tracked as CVE-2026-46300, then enabled root access. Cyber Security News’ report on the 25-server campaign explains the wider impact. Dream found evidence of webshell placement, internal tunneling, LDAP credential extraction, and Active Directory enumeration. However, it could not confirm whether later password spraying or attempts to create backdoor accounts succeeded. This confirmation should not be confused with Unit 42’s retracted October 23 update. That earlier account linked activity at a European government agency to PHP2Shell, but investigators could not establish that these specific flaws provided initial access. The October 29 update separately confirms the PAN-OS campaign. PAN-OS Patches and Immediate Protection Palo Alto’s security advisory limits the affected surface to the management HTTPS interface and XML API. PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama are covered. GlobalProtect portals, gateways, Clientless VPN and Captive Portal are not affected by these PHP flaws. A dataplane interface is exposed only when a management profile is attached. Administrators should immediately remove public management access, allow only trusted internal IP addresses, and install the correct PAN-OS hotfix. Fixed options include 12.2.4-h1, 12.1.10-h3, 11.2.16-h1, 11.1.16-h4 and 10.2.18-h13, with additional fixes for other maintenance releases. Palo Alto says these updates address both PHP vulnerabilities and interrupt the observed chain. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

items.title: How to Export Logs from Elasticsearch and Kibana
items.summary: Use a short Python script with the official client’s helpers.scan, or the _search API with a point in time (PIT) and search_after. For quick pulls of up to 10,000 rows, ES|QL with format=json works straight from Kibana’s Dev Tools. Kibana Discover can generate a report too, but not in a format LogTotal reads today. If your integration preserved it, event.original holds the raw log line. Elastic is one of the most common foundations for in-house security analytics, from Elastic Security to self-built stacks. Prime Core has 23,722 detection rules for Elastic, mapped to 671 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Authentication. Create an API key in Stack Management → API keys with read and view_index_metadata on the indices you need. Send it as Authorization: ApiKey . On Elastic Cloud, the Elasticsearch endpoint is on your deployment’s overview page. Know where the data lives. Elastic Agent integrations write to data streams named logs- - . Linux authentication logs from the System integration, for example, land in logs-system.auth-default. Check for event.original . Many integrations don’t keep the raw line by default; it’s a “preserve original event” option. If it’s missing, the parsed fields are what you have, and that’s fine for a JSON upload. Data tiers. Searches against cold or frozen tiers are slower. Keep windows tight when the data is old. The examples follow the current Elastic documentation, checked October 2026. Option 1: Python with helpers.scan (recommended) import json, os from elasticsearch import Elasticsearch, helpers es = Elasticsearch("https://my-deployment.es.example.com:443", api_key=os.environ["ES_API_KEY"]) query = {"query": {"range": {"@timestamp": { "gte": "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z", "lt": "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"}}}} with open("elastic_auth_1019.jsonl", "w") as out: for hit in helpers.scan(es, index="logs-system.auth-*", query=query, size=1000): out.write(json.dumps(hit["_source"]) + "\n") For raw lines, write hit[“_source”].get(“event”, {}).get(“original”, “”) instead of the whole document. Option 2: ES|QL for quick pulls In Kibana Dev Tools: POST /_query?format=json { "query": """ FROM logs-system.auth-* | WHERE @timestamp >= "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z" AND @timestamp < "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, source.ip, message | LIMIT 10000 """ } Two catches. ES|QL returns 1,000 rows unless you set LIMIT, and it tops out at 10,000. The JSON response also comes as columns plus values, not as records. To turn it into one object per line, save the query body as query.json and run it through jq: curl -sS -H "Authorization: ApiKey $ES_API_KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ "https://my-deployment.es.example.com/_query?format=json" -d @query.json \ | jq -c '.columns as $c | .values[] | [$c, .] | transpose | map({(.[0].name): .[1]}) | add' > esql_1019.jsonl Option 3: Export logs from Kibana UI (Discover) For smaller investigations, Kibana Discover lets you find, filter, and export logs directly from the browser without writing scripts. Open Discover. Sign in to Kibana and navigate to Analytics → Discover , or select Discover from the main navigation. Select your data. Choose the data view containing the logs you need, such as logs-system.auth-*. Make sure it includes the relevant Elasticsearch indices or data streams. Set the time range. Use the time picker in the upper-right corner to select the investigation period. Narrow the window to avoid exporting unnecessary events. Filter the logs. Use the search bar and available filters to isolate relevant events. For example, enter event.category: authentication to focus on authentication activity. Select the fields. Add useful columns such as @timestamp, host.name, user.name, source.ip, and message. If available, include event.original to preserve the raw log content. Export the results. Open More → Export → Tab results as CSV (in some versions, Share → CSV Reports ). Generate the report and download the CSV file. If the export is not downloaded immediately, find it under Stack Management → Reporting . Alternative: Copy logs as JSON. For a small selection of events, select the relevant rows in Discover, open the Selected menu, and choose Copy documents as JSON . Paste the copied content into a text editor and save it as a .json file. Only the fields included in the current table selection may be copied. Limitations. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix 401 or 403 API key lacks privileges on the indices Add read and view_index_metadata Result window is too large More than 10,000 hits in one _search Use helpers.scan or PIT with search_after ES|QL returns exactly 1,000 rows Default limit Add LIMIT (max 10,000) No event.original field The integration didn’t preserve it Export the parsed document instead Timeouts Old data on cold or frozen tiers Narrow the window; run it in pieces FAQ What about Elastic Security alerts? Alerts live in their own indices (.alerts-security.alerts-*). Exporting alerts is a different job from exporting the logs behind them; for LogTotal, export the logs. Does this work for OpenSearch? The idea is the same, the clients differ.
items.summary_html:
Use a short Python script with the official client’s helpers.scan, or the _search API with a point in time (PIT) and search_after. For quick pulls of up to 10,000 rows, ES|QL with format=json works straight from Kibana’s Dev Tools. Kibana Discover can generate a report too, but not in a format LogTotal reads today. If your integration preserved it, event.original holds the raw log line.

Elastic is one of the most common foundations for in-house security analytics, from Elastic Security to self-built stacks. Prime Core has 23,722 detection rules for Elastic, mapped to 671 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

Authentication. Create an API key in Stack Management → API keys with read and view_index_metadata on the indices you need. Send it as Authorization: ApiKey . On Elastic Cloud, the Elasticsearch endpoint is on your deployment’s overview page.

Know where the data lives. Elastic Agent integrations write to data streams named logs--. Linux authentication logs from the System integration, for example, land in logs-system.auth-default.

Check for event.original. Many integrations don’t keep the raw line by default; it’s a “preserve original event” option. If it’s missing, the parsed fields are what you have, and that’s fine for a JSON upload.

Data tiers. Searches against cold or frozen tiers are slower. Keep windows tight when the data is old.

The examples follow the current Elastic documentation, checked October 2026.

Option 1: Python with helpers.scan (recommended) 
import json, os
from elasticsearch import Elasticsearch, helpers

es = Elasticsearch("https://my-deployment.es.example.com:443", api_key=os.environ["ES_API_KEY"])
query = {"query": {"range": {"@timestamp": {
    "gte": "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z", "lt": "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"}}}}

with open("elastic_auth_1019.jsonl", "w") as out:
    for hit in helpers.scan(es, index="logs-system.auth-*", query=query, size=1000):
        out.write(json.dumps(hit["_source"]) + "\n")

For raw lines, write hit[“_source”].get(“event”, {}).get(“original”, “”) instead of the whole document.

Option 2: ES|QL for quick pulls

In Kibana Dev Tools:

POST /_query?format=json
{
  "query": """
    FROM logs-system.auth-*
    | WHERE @timestamp >= "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z" AND @timestamp < "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"
    | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, source.ip, message
    | LIMIT 10000
  """
}

Two catches. ES|QL returns 1,000 rows unless you set LIMIT, and it tops out at 10,000. The JSON response also comes as columns plus values, not as records. To turn it into one object per line, save the query body as query.json and run it through jq:

curl -sS -H "Authorization: ApiKey $ES_API_KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  "https://my-deployment.es.example.com/_query?format=json" -d @query.json \
  | jq -c '.columns as $c | .values[] | [$c, .] | transpose | map({(.[0].name): .[1]}) | add' > esql_1019.jsonl
Option 3: Export logs from Kibana UI (Discover)

For smaller investigations, Kibana Discover lets you find, filter, and export logs directly from the browser without writing scripts.

  1. Open Discover. Sign in to Kibana and navigate to Analytics → Discover, or select Discover from the main navigation.
  2. Select your data. Choose the data view containing the logs you need, such as logs-system.auth-*. Make sure it includes the relevant Elasticsearch indices or data streams.
  3. Set the time range. Use the time picker in the upper-right corner to select the investigation period. Narrow the window to avoid exporting unnecessary events.
  4. Filter the logs. Use the search bar and available filters to isolate relevant events. For example, enter event.category: authentication to focus on authentication activity.
  5. Select the fields. Add useful columns such as @timestamp, host.name, user.name, source.ip, and message. If available, include event.original to preserve the raw log content.
  6. Export the results. Open More → Export → Tab results as CSV (in some versions, Share → CSV Reports). Generate the report and download the CSV file. If the export is not downloaded immediately, find it under Stack Management → Reporting.

Alternative: Copy logs as JSON. For a small selection of events, select the relevant rows in Discover, open the Selected menu, and choose Copy documents as JSON. Paste the copied content into a text editor and save it as a .json file. Only the fields included in the current table selection may be copied.

Limitations. CSV reports are intended for moderate-sized exports and have row-count and file-size limits that depend on the Kibana version and configuration. Exporting a Discover session definition as JSON does not export the log events themselves.

For LogTotal, use a supported log format. When JSONL is required, export the records using the Python or Elasticsearch API methods described below, or convert the exported data into one JSON object per line before uploading.

Step 3: Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal
  1. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file.
  2. Sanitize. Look it over before you continue.
  3. Review. 
When it goes wrong SymptomLikely causeFix401 or 403API key lacks privileges on the indicesAdd read and view_index_metadataResult window is too largeMore than 10,000 hits in one _searchUse helpers.scan or PIT with search_afterES|QL returns exactly 1,000 rowsDefault limitAdd LIMIT (max 10,000)No event.original fieldThe integration didn’t preserve itExport the parsed document insteadTimeoutsOld data on cold or frozen tiersNarrow the window; run it in pieces
FAQ

What about Elastic Security alerts?

Alerts live in their own indices (.alerts-security.alerts-*). Exporting alerts is a different job from exporting the logs behind them; for LogTotal, export the logs.

The idea is the same, the clients differ.

items.title: Trezor Warns of Suspected Spy Implant in Crypto Wallet That Could Steal Recovery Phrases
items.summary: Trezor has warned that a suspected hardware implant inside a Trezor Safe 5 could steal recovery phrases and send them over a mobile network. The warning covers every Trezor model bought from CryptoBilis from March 2026 onward, although only one suspected device has been reported. In its October 30 security notice , Trezor urged affected users to move funds to a newly created wallet with a new seed. The company has not examined the device and has received no reports of stolen funds from CryptoBilis buyers. The March cutoff is a precautionary scope for customer action, not proof that every device sold since then was altered. The confirmed extent and operation of the suspected Trezor implant remain subject to laboratory examination. Suspected Implant Targets the Wallet Screen The report came from a customer in Indonesia who bought the Safe 5 through CryptoBilis on Tokopedia in August 2026. Trezor received the disclosure on October 28, reviewed photos, and interviewed the customer by video. The device is being sent to its security lab.[ trezor ] According to the report, an extra circuit board sits between the wallet’s main board and screen. It contains a cellular module and antenna. The added hardware allegedly reads information shown on the display, including the wallet backup, and sends it over a mobile network while the device is plugged in. That would make the screen connection a possible theft point. Rather than needing to break the wallet’s core security, an attacker could capture the recovery words when they appear during setup. This remains a reported method, not a finding confirmed through Trezor’s own testing. A stolen recovery phrase can let someone restore a wallet elsewhere and control its funds. Cybersecurity News has also covered fake crypto wallet screens that seek the same secret through false recovery prompts. The suspected implant would target displayed information instead of relying on a user entering words into fake software. The warning follows a separate investigation involving Ledger wallets supplied by CryptoBilis. According to Trezor, Ledger began investigating customer fund losses on October 9 and later confirmed physical tampering in some devices. Cybersecurity News previously reported Ledger’s confirmation of an unauthorized hardware implant in a CryptoBilis device. Trezor removed CryptoBilis from its authorized reseller network on October 9 and began checking customer devices. Despite the shared reseller, Trezor has not identified the attackers or confirmed that the same group targeted both brands. It is working with Ledger and other parties investigating the incident. Trezor also credited SEAL 911, the Security Alliance’s emergency response service, for helping with the report and customer support planning. The customer who reported the suspected Trezor implant had already moved his funds before finding it. Trezor says it has received no reports involving other resellers. Its warning also covers stores selling devices supplied by CryptoBilis, not just purchases made directly from the reseller. What Affected Trezor Owners Should Do Trezor says moving the existing wallet backup onto another device does not fix the risk. Users need a fresh wallet with a newly generated seed, then must transfer their funds to it. Anyone who has not set up an affected device should leave it unused and never enter an existing recovery phrase. If another secure hardware wallet is unavailable, Trezor recommends temporarily using a software wallet or familiar exchange. Its sending guide explains the transfer process. Users should carefully check the full receiving address before sending funds. Customers should not rely on weighing or opening their devices to rule out tampering. Trezor says weight differences can have other causes and there is no dependable home inspection method. Eligible CryptoBilis buyers can contact official Trezor Support for a replacement shipped directly or a voucher covering a new device. They should keep the original wallet. Trezor also warns that scammers may exploit the incident through fake emails, letters, or calls. Support will never ask for a recovery phrase.

items.title: Anthropic hacked to deliver remote access trojan to Claude developer laptops worldwide
items.summary: Yesterday, Anthropic were compromised and Cursor VS Code extension used by tens of millions of developers for Claude access was delivering a remote access trojan via an SSH reverse backdoor. The malware allowed hands on and automated remote access to developer laptops and desktops, in a supply chain attack. items.summary_html:
Yesterday, Anthropic were compromised and Cursor VS Code extension used by tens of millions of developers for Claude access was delivering a remote access trojan via an SSH reverse backdoor. The malware allowed hands on and automated remote access to developer laptops and desktops, in a supply chain attack.

Anthropic has not informed customers, and the malicious version was silently deleted without telling anybody.

The extension itself auto updated in Cursor to the malicious version. Cursor say around 5000 developer systems were impacted.

Phorion were the first to notice the malicious activity on endpoints:

Official Claude Code Extension Compromise: Security Advisory | Phorion

The compromised version was 2.1.313. This version was replaced 8 hours ago by Anthropic, with version 2.1.314, which appears to remove the backdoor from the extension but I’m not sure if it still contains no malicious code. It does not remove the SSH backdoor from systems already infected, nor the prior recon activity.

You may notice 2.1.313 is missing from OpenVSX, Visual Studio Marketplace and Cursor:

Cursor has admitted the issue:

Security notice - malicious version of Anthropic.claude-code (2.1.313) identified in the Cursor Extension Marketplace · Cursor

a maliciously modified version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was made available in the Cursor VS Code extension Marketplace. The extension runs malicious code that attempts to install a persistent SSH backdoor. Specifically, it:
Collects host and user information: hostname, username, OS, architecture, home directory path, environment variable names, working directories, configured Git email, and public IP.
Attempts to add an attacker-controlled SSH key to authorized_keys, enable the local SSH service, and open a reverse SSH tunnel. Outside of highly unusual circumstances where Cursor was started with administrator privileges, due to errors in the malicious code, this step would fail.
Attempts to make the reverse SSH tunnel persistent via a LaunchAgent (macOS) or a scheduled task that attempts to run as SYSTEM with a Startup-script fallback (Windows). Background scripts retry the tunnel roughly every 60 seconds.
Reports host details and backdoor status via HTTP POST to /beacon on port 8099.

To hunt for the malicious version with Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, I have published KQL queries:

ThreatHunting/AdvancedHuntingQueries/AnthropicSupplyChainAttack.kql at master · GossiTheDog/ThreatHunting

There is some wordsmithing in the Cursor blog, for example: “This malicious version of the extension was not developed by Anthropic” — it was, in fact, uploaded as Anthropic’s verified account. “Developed” is doing some heavy lifting — of course Anthropic didn’t develop the backdoor, there was a security incident leading to a supply chain attack.

Notable customers who run Claude Code and Cursor on laptops include Binance, amongst thousands of others.

This is an emerging situation, follow me on Mastodon for updates — @gossithedog@cyberplace.social:

Cyberplace

Network IoCs:

  • VSIX SHA-256 (darwin-arm64 — Mac): 432ccdee3801f99e52b8fe31f69ea9870118e96ea7ef9ecabed1479621b5ab62
  • Modified VSIX SHA-256 (win32-x64): 3de1722901165769893bef57c72594e9a54459faa23f3091b136b79966edd081
Network
  • Reverse SSH tunnel: 134[.]209[.]82[.]225 port 22
  • C2: hxxp://134[.]209[.]82[.]225:8099/beacon (HTTP POST)
  • Local beacon attempt: 127[.]0[.]0[.]1:8099/beacon (HTTP POST, loopback)
  • Public IP lookups to ifconfig[.]me / api[.]ipify[.]org — legitimate services; access alone is not an indicator

Anthropic hacked to deliver remote access trojan to Claude developer laptops worldwide was originally published in DoublePulsar on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: How to Export Event Data from CrowdStrike Falcon
items.summary: For a targeted pull, run your query in Falcon’s Advanced Event Search and export the results as JSON. For bulk raw telemetry, Falcon Data Replicator (FDR) delivers your events to an S3 bucket as gzipped JSON, one event per line. Keep in mind what you’re getting: Falcon’s own sensor telemetry (process, network, DNS, logon events), not the hosts’ original Windows or Linux logs. Falcon telemetry is some of the richest endpoint data a SOC has, and it’s often the first thing an IR partner asks for. Prime Core has 23,742 detection rules for CrowdStrike data, mapped to 674 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get it out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Access. Event search needs a Falcon role that allows it. FDR needs its own subscription, plus an API client with FDR scope; CrowdStrike gives you the bucket, queue and credentials. Retention. How far back event data goes depends on your subscription, often days to a few months. Check before you promise anyone history. Event names. Falcon telemetry is organized by event_simpleName. The ones you’ll use most: ProcessRollup2 (process start), NetworkConnectIP4, DnsRequest, UserLogon. Knowing them makes queries much faster to write. CrowdStrike’s documentation sits behind the Falcon login. This guide is based on it, plus the public FalconPy and FDR projects, checked October 2026. Option 1: Advanced Event Search Scope the query tightly, and don’t reduce it with table() before exporting, because that drops fields: #event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ComputerName=WS-042 Set the time range, run the search, then export the results as JSON or CSV. If CSV is selected, specify in ‘Fields to export’ choose ‘Select all. Option 2: Falcon Data Replicator (bulk) FDR is the route for volume. CrowdStrike writes batches of gzipped JSON files to an S3 bucket and announces each new batch on an SQS queue. For continuous collection, consume the queue (CrowdStrike publishes a sample consumer). For a one-off, list the bucket, pick the batches covering your window, and download them: export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=' ' export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=' ' aws s3 ls s3:// / / --recursive | less aws s3 cp s3:// / / / ./fdr/ --recursive Then filter to the host you care about, by its agent ID: zcat ./fdr/*.gz | jq -c 'select(.aid == " ")' > ws042_fdr.jsonl Each line is one event. FDR volume adds up fast, so filter by aid and event_simpleName before you upload. Step 3: Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix No export option, or results are capped Role permissions or a UI limit Check your role; split the time range; use FDR for volume Nothing older than a certain date Subscription retention Check FDR archives or your SIEM AccessDenied on the FDR bucket Credentials rotated, or FDR not enabled Get current FDR credentials Fields you expected are missing table() trimmed them Export without table() FDR files are huge No filtering Filter by aid and event_simpleName FAQ Can I get Windows Event Logs out of Falcon? Not from the sensor telemetry: Falcon doesn’t collect raw Windows event logs by default. Export them from the host What about detections and alerts? Those are available through the Falcon API (FalconPy makes it easy), but they’re alerts, not raw telemetry. For LogTotal, export the events behind them.

items.title: How to Export Logs from Microsoft Sentinel
items.summary: Sentinel data lives in a Log Analytics workspace, so an export is a KQL query plus a way to save the results as JSON. The simplest is the Azure CLI: az monitor log-analytics query returns one JSON object per row. The portal’s export button produces a spreadsheet-style file that LogTotal doesn’t read today, so use the CLI or PowerShell for uploads. Sentinel collects from everywhere: Windows, Linux, Entra ID, Microsoft 365, firewalls, clouds. That makes it the natural place to pull an investigation slice from. Prime Core has 23,700 detection rules for Microsoft Sentinel, mapped to 674 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get the data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Permissions. Log Analytics Reader or Microsoft Sentinel Reader on the workspace is enough. The workspace ID. The CLI wants the workspace GUID, from the workspace’s overview page, not its name. Know your tables. The ones that matter most: SecurityEvent (Windows), Syslog (Linux), SigninLogs and AuditLogs (Entra ID), OfficeActivity (Microsoft 365), CommonSecurityLog (CEF from firewalls and other appliances), AzureActivity, plus any custom _CL tables. Retention tiers. Data in interactive retention can be queried directly. Data that has aged into long-term retention can’t: you need a search job or a restore first. Some table plans (Basic, Auxiliary) also limit what KQL can do. Where you write KQL. Depending on how your tenant is set up, that’s Advanced hunting in the Microsoft Defender portal or Logs in the Azure portal. The queries are the same. The commands follow Microsoft’s documentation, checked October 2026. Step 1: Write the query Keep it to events. No summarize if you want logs back. For Linux SSH activity: Syslog | where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-10-19) .. datetime(2026-10-20)) | where Computer == "web-03" | where ProcessName in ("sshd", "sshd-session") For Windows logons and account changes on a domain controller: SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-10-19) .. datetime(2026-10-20)) | where Computer startswith "DC-01" Run it in the portal first and check the row count. items.summary_html:
Sentinel data lives in a Log Analytics workspace, so an export is a KQL query plus a way to save the results as JSON. The simplest is the Azure CLI: az monitor log-analytics query returns one JSON object per row. The portal’s export button produces a spreadsheet-style file that LogTotal doesn’t read today, so use the CLI or PowerShell for uploads.

Sentinel collects from everywhere: Windows, Linux, Entra ID, Microsoft 365, firewalls, clouds. That makes it the natural place to pull an investigation slice from. Prime Core has 23,700 detection rules for Microsoft Sentinel, mapped to 674 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get the data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

Permissions. Log Analytics Reader or Microsoft Sentinel Reader on the workspace is enough.

The workspace ID. The CLI wants the workspace GUID, from the workspace’s overview page, not its name.

Know your tables. The ones that matter most: SecurityEvent (Windows), Syslog (Linux), SigninLogs and AuditLogs (Entra ID), OfficeActivity (Microsoft 365), CommonSecurityLog (CEF from firewalls and other appliances), AzureActivity, plus any custom _CL tables.

Retention tiers. Data in interactive retention can be queried directly. Data that has aged into long-term retention can’t: you need a search job or a restore first. Some table plans (Basic, Auxiliary) also limit what KQL can do.

Where you write KQL. Depending on how your tenant is set up, that’s Advanced hunting in the Microsoft Defender portal or Logs in the Azure portal. The queries are the same.

The commands follow Microsoft’s documentation, checked October 2026.

Step 1: Write the query

Keep it to events. No summarize if you want logs back. For Linux SSH activity:

Syslog
| where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-10-19) .. datetime(2026-10-20))
| where Computer == "web-03"
| where ProcessName in ("sshd", "sshd-session")

For Windows logons and account changes on a domain controller:

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-10-19) .. datetime(2026-10-20))
| where Computer startswith "DC-01"

Run it in the portal first and check the row count.

Step 2: Export as JSON

Azure CLI:

az login
az monitor log-analytics query \
  --workspace  \
  --analytics-query "Syslog | where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-10-19) .. datetime(2026-10-20)) | where Computer == 'web-03'" \
  --output json > sentinel_web03_1019.json

jq -c '.[]' sentinel_web03_1019.json > sentinel_web03_1019.jsonl

The first run may ask to install the log-analytics extension. Say yes.

PowerShell (Az module):

Connect-AzAccount
$kql = "SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-10-19) .. datetime(2026-10-20)) | where Computer startswith 'DC-01'"
(Invoke-AzOperationalInsightsQuery -WorkspaceId '' -Query $kql).Results |
  ForEach-Object { $_ | ConvertTo-Json -Compress } | Out-File sentinel_dc01_1019.jsonl -Encoding utf8

Query results are capped in rows and size. For busy tables, split the window into hours and run the export once per slice.

Step 3: Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal
  1. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. 
  2. Sanitize. 
  3. Review.

FAQ

Do I get raw Windows events?

You get the parsed SecurityEvent rows, with the original event data in the EventData column. Not an EVTX file. For EVTX, export from the host.

If you use the unified Defender portal, advanced hunting can query Defender and Sentinel tables together.

items.title: How to Export Advanced Hunting Results from Microsoft Defender XDR
items.summary: Run your query in Advanced hunting , then send the same query to Microsoft Graph’s runHuntingQuery to get the results as JSON. The portal’s export button produces a spreadsheet-style file that LogTotal doesn’t read today. Advanced hunting keeps 30 days of data, so anything older has to come from Sentinel or wherever you stream Defender data. Defender XDR holds endpoint, identity, email and cloud app telemetry in one queryable place, which makes it the first stop in most Microsoft-shop investigations. Prime Core has 17,197 detection rules for Microsoft Defender data, mapped to 659 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to pull a slice out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Permissions. For Graph, you need the ThreatHunting.Read.All permission. The signed-in user also needs a Defender role that allows advanced hunting. Limits. Queries time out after a few minutes, and results are capped. Plan to split by time or by device. The tables. DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceNetworkEvents, DeviceLogonEvents, DeviceFileEvents, DeviceRegistryEvents, DeviceEvents (a mixed bag, including ASR and AMSI events), EmailEvents, IdentityLogonEvents, and AlertInfo with AlertEvidence. The time column is Timestamp. The examples follow Microsoft’s documentation, checked October 2026. Step 1: Write the query DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-10-19) .. datetime(2026-10-20)) | where DeviceName startswith "ws-042" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256 Run it in the portal first. Device names in Defender are often FQDNs, which is why startswith works better than ==. Step 2: Export through Microsoft Graph Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "ThreatHunting.Read.All" $kql = @" DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-10-19) .. datetime(2026-10-20)) | where DeviceName startswith "ws-042" "@ $resp = Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method POST ` -Uri "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/security/runHuntingQuery" ` -Body (@{ Query = $kql } | ConvertTo-Json) -ContentType "application/json" $resp.results | ForEach-Object { $_ | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress } | Out-File ws042_proc_1019.jsonl -Encoding utf8 Each row comes back as one JSON object per line. For several days or several devices, loop over day-sized windows to stay under the limits. Step 3: Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix 403 from Graph Missing ThreatHunting.Read.All consent or Defender role Grant consent; check your role Query times out or returns partial results Too much data in one query Narrow the time window or the device set Nothing older than 30 days Advanced hunting retention Use Sentinel or your streaming destination Row count stops at a round number Result cap Split the window No rows for a known device Name mismatch (short name vs FQDN) Use startswith or has FAQ Can I get the raw EVTX from a device? Yes, with Live Response in Defender for Endpoint: getfile pulls files, including exported EVTX, from a machine. Is this the same as Sentinel? No, though they overlap in the unified Defender portal. Sentinel keeps longer history.

items.title: Binance Faces Largest Crypto Heist – $6.36 Billion Reportedly Stolen by North Korean Group
items.summary: Binance reportedly lost approximately $6.36 billion in cryptocurrency on October 29, 2026, after an attacker drained wallets across ten blockchains. TRM Labs describes the incident as the largest cryptocurrency theft ever recorded, with most of the stolen funds transferred out within about 20 minutes of the attack. Its investigation attributes the operation to TraderTraitor, a North Korean-linked hacking group known for targeting cryptocurrency platforms and financial organizations to steal digital assets. According to TRM, Binance acknowledged a security incident, suspended withdrawals on several networks, and said user funds were safe. The reported loss exceeds four times the $1.5 billion Bybit theft. Earlier reporting on the Bybit multistage attack investigation explains how compromised infrastructure enabled another major cryptocurrency theft, although Binance’s initial entry point remains unknown. Binance Hit by Biggest Crypto Heist in History Researchers from TRM identified malicious sweeper contract activity that allowed the attacker to repeatedly drain a Binance Ethereum hot wallet. Their published Binance hack analysis describes harmful smart contract code rather than a named endpoint malware family. TRM attributes the operation to TraderTraitor with high confidence, citing blockchain records and intelligence gathered outside the blockchain. Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft. The operator received three small Tornado Cash withdrawals starting October 28, then deployed and tested attack code against several wallets. A final rehearsal preceded installation of the same code on a Binance hot wallet by approximately four hours, suggesting a planned operation rather than an opportunistic transfer. The first recorded theft occurred on the XRP Ledger between 20:05 and 20:09 UTC, when five Binance wallets transferred 233.46 million XRP. Solana and Optimism transfers followed. At 20:20 UTC, a Bitcoin hot wallet sent 18,270 BTC to the attacker, who immediately split the funds into smaller amounts through a peel chain. Ethereum activity exposed the attack’s central technical feature: EIP-7702 delegation. This mechanism lets a wallet authorize smart contract code to control its behavior. At 20:20 UTC, the operator submitted 50 authorizations signed by Binance’s wallet, directing it toward an attacker-controlled sweeper. Unlike previously documented TraderTraitor cloud compromise campaigns , this report does not establish how access was first obtained. Each authorization covered a consecutive nonce, the counter used to track wallet activity. Preparing multiple signatures increased the chance that one would match the wallet’s current counter when executed. One matched. Three minutes and 24 seconds later, a single sweep transferred 167,464 ETH and 63 tokens, including 1.615 billion USDT. The delegation remained active, allowing six further sweeps as fresh deposits arrived. The compromised wallet also controlled execution for another Binance smart account, enabling the removal of 823 million USDC. Meanwhile, wallets across other networks produced ordinary signed transfers. TRM therefore suspects compromised signing infrastructure, not an Ethereum-only authorization phishing incident. Binance had not published a root cause in the report. Frozen Funds, Laundering Activity, and Defensive Priorities TRM valued the stolen assets at their prices when transferred, producing the $6.36 billion estimate. Ethereum accounted for approximately $3.79 billion, followed by Bitcoin at $1.47 billion and Tron at $628 million. Its figures reflect blockchain observations through October 30 at 00:30 UTC, meaning subsequent movements or price changes could alter later assessments. Issuers and network responders restricted approximately $2.7 billion. Tether, Circle, Ripple, and World Liberty Financial froze stablecoins, while Arbitrum’s Security Council removed 8,426 ETH and 74.6 million ARB from the attacker’s control. These actions limited access to funds; they did not establish that the assets had been returned to Binance. The attacker also converted approximately 325 million USDT into roughly 122,300 ETH through market makers and trading contracts. Another wallet deposited 60 million USDT into Aave and borrowed about 19,760 ETH. Earlier investigations into Lazarus cryptocurrency laundering networks illustrate why tracing counterparties matters, although those findings should not be treated as proof of participants in this incident. TRM recommends screening deposits and trading counterparties, alerting on unexpected wallet delegations, and rejecting unapproved EIP-7702 authorizations. Exchanges should separate signing systems and approval paths across blockchains and wallet tiers. Treasury teams also need tested revocation procedures because a malicious delegation can keep redirecting incoming funds after the initial theft. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Indicator type Source-reported observation Wallet delegation Unexpected EIP-7702 code on treasury wallets Signing behavior Batch of 50 consecutive-nonce authorizations Fund movement Repeated sweeps of incoming deposits Bitcoin laundering Peel-chain outputs of 1,000 and 100 BTC Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally defanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: How to Export Logs from Google SecOps (Chronicle)
items.summary: For small, targeted pulls, run a UDM search and call the same search through the Google SecOps API to get JSON. For raw logs in their original format, the Data Export API copies logs for a time range and log type into a Cloud Storage bucket you own. The UI’s export produces a spreadsheet-style file that LogTotal doesn’t read today. Google SecOps keeps a year of data by default at Google scale, and it’s increasingly where security teams look first. Prime Core has 20,031 detection rules for Google SecOps, mapped to 663 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Raw logs or UDM events? Google SecOps keeps both: the raw logs as ingested, and normalized UDM events. When the raw logs are syslog or JSON, they’re usually the better input for LogTotal. UDM JSON works too. Permissions. Access is granted through IAM roles on the SecOps instance. A data export also needs permission to create exports and a bucket the SecOps service account can write to. Retention. Standard retention is 12 months. Log types. Every feed has a log type label, such as WINEVTLOG for Windows event logs. Note the ones you need before you export. The steps follow Google’s documentation, checked October 2026. Endpoints differ by region and API version, so check them against your instance. Option 1: UDM search through the API Write the search in the UI first, for example principal.hostname = “web-03”, and check the results. Then run it through the API with a time range: TOKEN=$(gcloud auth print-access-token) curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ "https:// -chronicle.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/ /locations/ /instances/ :udmSearch?query=principal.hostname%3D%22web-03%22&timeRange.startTime=2026-10-19T00:00:00Z&timeRange.endTime=2026-10-20T00:00:00Z&limit=10000" \ | jq -c '.events[]' > secops_web03_1019.jsonl Option 2: Raw logs with the Data Export API For larger windows, or when you want logs exactly as they arrived: Create a Cloud Storage bucket and give the SecOps service account write access to it. Create a data export for your time range and log type, pointing at the bucket. Poll the export until it finishes. Download the files: gcloud storage cp -r gs://my-secops-export/ / ./secops-export/ The files hold the original log lines for that log type. Decompress them if needed, then upload. Option 3: Export logs through the Google SecOps UI For quick investigations or smaller log samples, you can export search results directly from the Google SecOps interface without using the API. Open Search. Sign in to Google SecOps and navigate to Investigation > Search . Run a search. Enter a UDM query, for example principal.hostname = “web-03” , or search raw logs. Set the time range and click Run Search . Review results. Check the matching events. For UDM searches, use the Column Manager to select the fields you want to export. Download the logs. UDM events: In the Events table, click Download and select Download as CSV . You can also select Download as CSV (with raw logs) to include the original log entries. Raw logs: In the Raw Logs results table, click More > Download as CSV . Save the file. Google SecOps downloads the results as a CSV file. Limitations. UI exports use CSV rather than JSON or JSONL, which LogTotal doesn’t currently support. Raw log searches are limited to 10,000 results per query. For larger exports, narrow the time range or use the Data Export API. To analyze the exported data in LogTotal, extract the original log entries into a supported raw log format or use the API export methods described above. Step 3: Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix 403 or permission denied Missing IAM role on the instance Ask for API access on the SecOps project Export fails to write The SecOps service account can’t write to the bucket Grant it write access Search results stop short Result limit Narrow the time range, or use Data Export 404 from the API Wrong region or instance ID in the URL Copy them from your instance settings Raw logs missing for some sources Some log types keep less raw detail Export UDM events instead FAQ Is Chronicle the same thing? Yes. Google SecOps is the current name; many docs and APIs still say Chronicle. UDM or raw: which should I upload? Raw, when it’s syslog or JSON, because LogTotal sees what the source actually sent. UDM is a good fallback, and handy when you need the normalization.

For larger windows, or when you want logs exactly as they arrived:

  1. Create a Cloud Storage bucket and give the SecOps service account write access to it.
  2. Create a data export for your time range and log type, pointing at the bucket.
  3. Poll the export until it finishes.
  4. Download the files:
gcloud storage cp -r gs://my-secops-export// ./secops-export/

The files hold the original log lines for that log type. Decompress them if needed, then upload.

Option 3: Export logs through the Google SecOps UI

For quick investigations or smaller log samples, you can export search results directly from the Google SecOps interface without using the API.

  1. Open Search. Sign in to Google SecOps and navigate to Investigation > Search.
  2. Run a search. Enter a UDM query, for example principal.hostname = “web-03”, or search raw logs. Set the time range and click Run Search.
  3. Review results. Check the matching events. For UDM searches, use the Column Manager to select the fields you want to export.
  4. Download the logs.
    • UDM events: In the Events table, click Download and select Download as CSV. You can also select Download as CSV (with raw logs) to include the original log entries.
    • Raw logs: In the Raw Logs results table, click More > Download as CSV.
  5. Save the file. Google SecOps downloads the results as a CSV file.

Limitations. UI exports use CSV rather than JSON or JSONL, which LogTotal doesn’t currently support. Raw log searches are limited to 10,000 results per query. For larger exports, narrow the time range or use the Data Export API. To analyze the exported data in LogTotal, extract the original log entries into a supported raw log format or use the API export methods described above.

Step 3: Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal
  1. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. 
  2. Sanitize. 
  3. Review. 
When it goes wrong SymptomLikely causeFix403 or permission deniedMissing IAM role on the instanceAsk for API access on the SecOps projectExport fails to writeThe SecOps service account can’t write to the bucketGrant it write accessSearch results stop shortResult limitNarrow the time range, or use Data Export404 from the APIWrong region or instance ID in the URLCopy them from your instance settingsRaw logs missing for some sourcesSome log types keep less raw detailExport UDM events instead
FAQ

Is Chronicle the same thing?

Yes. Google SecOps is the current name; many docs and APIs still say Chronicle.

UDM or raw: which should I upload?

Raw, when it’s syslog or JSON, because LogTotal sees what the source actually sent. UDM is a good fallback, and handy when you need the normalization.

items.title: Unauthorized OpenAI Codex and Claude Code Relays Disable AI Sandboxes and Redirect Enterprise Data
items.summary: An unauthorized AI relay service is installing genuine OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code tools on company computers, then changing their settings to send requests through third-party servers. The setup also removes sandbox controls, creating a path for sensitive business data to leave approved systems. Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team documented the activity in an October 29 report. Researchers observed the service across a dozen organizations since early 2026. Most were in mainland China, with other deployments involving multinational firms connected to South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia. Affected industries include semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, shipping, electronics, petrochemicals, and data center services. The key distinction is configuration. Researchers found neither a modified client nor a vulnerability in Codex or Claude Code. The genuine tools follow settings introduced by the relay. Sandbox Controls and Credentials Replaced Users appear to run a setup command themselves, often within minutes to half an hour of installing an AI coding tool through npm. Researchers found no automated or exploit-based delivery. A fileless PowerShell or bash script arrives from a lookalike domain such as vibe.aiok[.]me . It checks for Node.js and the requested coding tool, installs missing components, and then applies the relay settings. Because users receive a working application, the extra setup can look routine. The script rewrites ~/.codex/config.toml or ~/.claude/settings.json . It changes base_url or ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to relay-controlled infrastructure and installs relay-issued credentials. User-level environment variables preserve these settings after a restart. For teams examining unfamiliar setup scripts, ANY.RUN’s interactive sandbox offers a separate analysis environment with live interaction and reporting. This differs from the coding agent’s own sandbox, which limits actions during normal use. In Codex, the script sets sandbox_mode to danger-full-access . It also enables network access for the write sandbox and disables telemetry and error reporting through DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 and DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING=1 . These changes remove safeguards while suppressing signals that might otherwise reach the vendors. On one host, the script ran claude /logout , removed ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , then ran claude /login . This cleared an existing session before relay credentials took over. Researchers could not establish whether every deployment followed that sequence, reads the Symantec report . The service rotated through at least eight domains imitating OpenAI or Anthropic services. Its subscription-style Claude tokens could suggest pooled account resale, but researchers said this was not proof of its business model. Related reporting on Codex and Claude Code hijacking through Downloads folders shows a separate route to endpoint redirection. Here, however, the setup script changes the settings directly rather than relying on malicious instructions inside files. The relay can see prompts, files, and secrets sent through it, and could alter responses. With sandbox protection removed, a malicious response could lead to commands running with the user’s account privileges. Symantec found no evidence that the operator had exploited this position. Observed redirection must not be confused with confirmed data theft. Separate coverage of AI coding agent security flaws highlights why permission controls matter. This case adds another concern: genuine software can become unsafe when an unapproved service controls its settings. Defenders should review endpoint URLs, sandbox settings, and user-level credential variables. PowerShell or bash download-and-execute commands shortly after npm installation deserve attention. Network monitoring should flag coding tools contacting destinations outside approved AI endpoints. Relay-issued variables also warrant review because other applications may inherit them. These checks help separate sanctioned deployments from unapproved access without treating every legitimate AI installation as malicious activity. Investigate suspicious scripts before they reach developer systems. Explore ANY.RUN’s interactive analysis features to observe behavior, inspect network activity, and support incident triage. items.title: CISA Warns of GitLab Integer Overflow Vulnerability Exploited in Attacks
items.summary: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has warned that attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-97229 . This GitLab vulnerability could allow code execution without logging in. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 29, 2026, confirming evidence of active exploitation and raising the urgency for organizations running affected GitLab servers. The vulnerability affects GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition. It involves an integer overflow or wraparound caused by insufficient checks on regular expressions inside CI/CD configurations. A specially crafted expression could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server. Cybersecuritynews.com previously covered the technical details in its report on the GitLab code execution vulnerability . Regular expressions are text patterns used to match or filter data. In this case, the dangerous input reaches GitLab’s regular expression compiler through a CI/CD configuration. These configurations define automated development tasks. Processing a malicious pattern could affect the server itself, not just cause a pipeline task to fail. GitLab Integer Overflow Vulnerability Exploited An integer overflow occurs when a calculation produces a number outside the range a program can store. The resulting value can become unexpectedly small or negative. MITRE’s CWE-190 description explains that these errors can cause crashes, memory corruption, or unauthorized code execution, depending on how the software uses the value. GitLab assigned the flaw a maximum CVSS score of 10.0. Earlier reporting identified affected versions as 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.4, and 19.4 before 19.4.2. Those branches received fixes on October 12. Administrators should review their installed release and follow the current vendor update guidance. The supplied catalog entry lists November 1, 2026, as the remediation deadline and marks forensic triage as required under BOD 26-04. It lists ransomware use as unknown. That status does not establish a ransomware link, and CISA’s public alert does not identify attackers, victims, or the scale of exploitation. CISA’s October 29 alert explains that BOD 26-04 requires federal civilian agencies to prioritize high-risk vulnerabilities on exposed assets. The directive also requires, where applicable, checks for signs that attackers compromised a system before updates were applied. CISA encourages other organizations to adopt similar risk-based patching practices. Administrators must also avoid confusing this issue with CVE-2026-110264, a separate GitLab regular expression vulnerability disclosed later in October. Cybersecuritynews.com’s coverage of that separate GitLab server vulnerability explains that installing the earlier CVE-2026-97229 update does not fix the newer issue. Reviewing both advisories helps teams choose an update that addresses both vulnerabilities rather than leaving another code execution path open on their GitLab servers.
